Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 1:

﴿Yā-Sīn﴾ The discussion of it is the same as the discussion of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) that occur at the beginnings of the surahs. Among what has been said about it is that it is one of the names of Allah the Exalted. This was narrated by Ashhab from Malik, and it was stated by Ibn al-'Arabi. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means "O human" (ya insan), in the language of Abyssinia (al-Habasha). And from him as well, that it has the same meaning in the dialect of Tayy. I do not think this is authentically reported from him, because writing it in the codices of the Qur'an as two letters contradicts that.

Among people there are those who claim that Yā-Sīn is one of the names of the Prophet (ﷺ). Isma'il ibn Bakr al-Himyari, the well-known poet of the Rafidah, whom they call al-Sayyid al-Himyari, built on this his verse:

O soul, do not exhaust yourself in sincere love, striving for affection except for the family of Yasin (ali Yasina).

He probably took this from the words of Allah the Exalted in Surat al-Saffat: ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130]. It has been said that it means the family of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Among people there are those who said that Yā-Sīn is an abbreviation of "Yā Sayyid" (O master), addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is weakened by the pronunciation of the reciters, who pronounce it with a nun (Yā-Sīn, with final nun sound).

Among people there are those who name their sons with this word, and this is common in the Egyptian and Syrian lands. Among them is Shaykh Yasin ibn Zayd al-Din al-'Ulaymi al-Himsi, who died in the year 1061 (AH), author of

page 345

al-Ta'aliq al-Qayyima. He writes his name according to how it is pronounced, not according to the spelling of the letters (huruf al-tahajji), although people may be heedless and write it with two letters as the opening of this surah is written.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ashhab said: I asked Malik, "Is it proper for anyone to name himself Yasin?" He said: "I do not think it is proper, because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Yā-Sīn. By the wise Qur'an﴾; a person would be saying, 'My name is Yasin.'" Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a remarkable statement, because a servant may not be named with one of the names of Allah if it carries a meaning of His, such as "Knowing" (alim) or "Powerful" (qadir). Malik only prohibited naming with this because it is one of the names of Allah whose meaning is not known, so its meaning may be something exclusive to the Lord, and a servant should not venture upon it lest he expose himself to danger; so consideration requires lifting it from him. End of quotation. There is room for scrutiny in this.

Pronouncing the name "Yā" without elongation is a lightening (takhfif), as in Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad.

[Page 346]

**"By the wise Qur'an. Indeed, you are among the messengers, upon a straight path."** The oath by the Qur'an is a metonymy (kināya) for its exalted rank and its great honour with God, the Exalted. This is the purpose of the first verses of this surah. The purpose of this oath is to affirm the statement together with that exaltation.

"Al-Qur'an" is a proper noun by predominance (ʿalam bi-l-ghalaba) for the Book revealed to Muhammad ﷺ from the time of his mission until his death, for its miraculous character (iʿjaz) and its legislation (tashrīʿ). It has been discussed previously in His words, ﴿and you do not recite from it any Qur'an﴾ in Surat Yunus.

"Al-Ḥakīm" may mean "al-Muḥkam" with a fatḥa on the kāf, that is, made firm and perfected, and iḥkām is perfection of a thing's essence in what is intended from it.

It may also mean "possessor of wisdom (ḥikma)", and describing the Qur'an with this is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), because it contains wisdom.

The clause ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ is the answer to the oath. The emphasis of this statement by the oath, the particle of emphasis (inna), and the lām of initiation is in view of its being intended as an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the polytheists who denied the message. It is thus a consolation (taʾnīs) for the Prophet ﷺ and an allusion to the polytheists. So the emphasis with respect to him is an increase in confirmation, and with respect to the implied (kināy) meaning it serves to refute their denial. Rhetorical purposes do not conflict with one another.

**"Upon a straight path"** is a second predicate of *inna*, or a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the subject of *inna*. Its purpose is to awaken attention to the greatness of his law (sharīʿa), after establishing that he is a messenger like the other messengers.

"ʿAla" here indicates metaphorical elevation, which means firm establishment (tamakkun), as previously mentioned in His words, ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ in Surat al-Baqara. The purpose of predicating this of the addressee is not to inform that he is upon a straight path, since that is already known from the information that he is one of the messengers. It is known that the intended "messengers" are those sent from God. Rather, the purpose is to combine the state of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, with the state of his religion, so that the knowledge that his religion is a straight path becomes independent knowledge and not implicit.

The straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm) is the guidance that leads to success in the Hereafter. It is the religion with which the Prophet ﷺ was sent and the character which God taught him. It is likened to a straight path with no crookedness, in that it is trustworthy in conveying one to the intended goal, without the traveller having to hesitate on it.

Thus Islam contains guidance in both lives, and its follower is like the traveller on a straight path, with no bewilderment in his journey that might overtake him until he reaches the intended place.

The Qur'an contains the religion, so the Qur'an is part of the straight path.

The indefiniteness of "ṣirāṭ" serves to convey its magnification.

﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿so that you may warn a people whose forefathers were never warned, so they are heedless﴾. This refers back to the Wise Qur'an, since it is what was sent down from God. After the oath had completed its answer, the discourse returned to one of the purposes of the oath, which is to honour the one sworn by, so it was described as ﴿the revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾.

Most reciters read ﴿تَنْزِيلُ﴾ (tanzīl) in the nominative (rafʿ), taking it as the predicate of an omitted subject, which is known from context. This is one of the cases of omitting the subject (ḥadhf al-musnad ilayhi, the ellipsis of the subject), which al-Sakkakī called the omission that follows customary usage (al-ḥadhf al-jārī ʿalā mutābaʿat al-istiʿmāl). The reason is that when they attributed a statement to something and then reported about it, they were in the habit of omitting its pronoun, which is the subject, to indicate that it is honoured, as if it were too evident to need mention. An example is the verse of Ibrahim al-Ṣūlī, or ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr al-Asadī, or Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd al-Kātib, from the verses of the Ḥamāsa (anthology) in the chapter on guests:

*"I will thank ʿAmr if my death is delayed, for favours he did not boast of, even though they were great."*

*"A youth whose wealth is not hidden from his friend, nor does he show complaint when the sandal slips."*

Its estimate is: "He is a youth" (huwa fatan).

Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim, and Khalaf read ﴿تَنْزِيلَ﴾ in the accusative (naṣb), with the estimate "I mean" (aʿnī). The meaning is: "I mean from my oath a Qur'an that I have sent down." This emphasis is an increase in honouring its status, and it is equivalent to the omission of the subject found in the reading in the nominative.

Tanzīl is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of the passive participle (bi-maʿnā al-mafʿūl), and it is predicated of the subject with the verbal noun for emphasis in establishing that it is sent down.

The revelation is attributed to God through the two attributes, the All-Mighty and the Most Merciful, because what the Qur'an contains can only be among the effects of God's might, which is that it brings people to the truth and to the path of guidance without flattery or weakness, along with its warning and threat against disobedience and disbelief. It can also be among the effects of His mercy, which is that the Qur'an sets out proofs, brings the distant near, and reveals realities to those who look, along with its glad tidings for those who are in God's good pleasure. This is what was explained afterwards, in summary, by His words ﴿so that you may warn a people whose forefathers were never warned, so they are heedless﴾, and in detail by His words ﴿the word has certainly come true concerning most of them﴾ [Yāsīn: 7], and by His words ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a noble reward﴾ [Yāsīn: 11].

So the lām in ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ﴾ (li-tundhira, "so that you may warn") is connected to ﴿تَنْزِيلُ﴾, and it is the lām of causation (lām al-taʿlīl), giving the reason for the sending down of the Qur'an.

Warning alone is mentioned because the first thing the Prophet ﷺ began to convey to the people was warning them all with what was contained in the first surah revealed, from His words ﴿No! Surely man transgresses﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 6] ﴿when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 7], and so on, and with what is contained in Surah al-Muddaththir. This is because the people as a whole were in a state that did not please God, so their condition called for warning so that they would quickly give up what they were entangled in.

As for the people described as those whose forefathers were never warned, they are either the ʿAdnānī Arabs, for centuries passed in which no warner came to them, and their forefathers passed away without hearing any warner. The counting of their forefathers begins from their highest grandfather in the main line of their lineage, by which they were distinguished as a stock, and this is ʿAdnān, because he is the root of the Arabized Arabs (al-ʿArab al-mustaʿribah). Or the intended people are the people of Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ, at the beginning of his mission, directly addressed the call to the people of Makkah and its surroundings, so they were the ones whom God willed to receive the religion and in whom the community of Islam would take root. Then they were the bearers of the Sharīʿah and the helpers of the Messenger ﷺ in conveying his call and supporting it. The people of Yathrib joined them, and they were Qaḥṭānī, so they became the Helpers (anṣār). Then the faith of the tribes of the Arabs followed one after another.

He based on this His words ﴿فَهم غافِلُونَ﴾ (fahum ghāfilūn, "so they are heedless"). That is, because their forefathers were not warned, they became characterised by heedlessness as a settled attribute. That is, they are heedless of what the Messengers and the laws bring, so they are in ignorance and error, since misguidance piled up among them year after year and generation after generation.

This state includes all whom the Prophet ﷺ called, whether those who later believed or those who did not believe.

Heedlessness (al-ghafla), in its literal sense, is being oblivious of something and not remembering it. Here it is a metonymy (kināya) for neglect and turning away from what deserves to be drawn attention to, as in the words of al-Nābigha:

*"Some people who do not know my character say: 'Perhaps Ziyād, may you have no father, is heedless.'"*

﴿Indeed the word has come true against most of them, so they do not believe.﴾ This is an elaboration of the condition of the people to whom Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent to warn. They are of two kinds: a group upon whom warning had no effect, and a group who followed the Reminder (al-dhikr) and feared God, and so benefited from the warning. He made clear that the word of punishment has come true against most of the people, i.e., God knew that they would not believe, owing to the aversion from good with which He had created their minds, so He established this in His knowledge and wrote that they would not believe. Thus the fa' (fa) is for deriving the negation of the belief of most of them from the saying that has come true against most of them.

"Haqqa" means "was established and occurred," so it does not admit of annulment. "Al-qawl" (the word) is a verbal noun intended to mean what God, exalted, intended concerning them, so it is a saying of the category of the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi, speech of the soul), or of what God revealed to His messengers.

The definite article in "al-qawl" is the definite article of genus, and the thing said is omitted because its being derived from it indicates it.

The estimate: "Indeed the word has come true," i.e., the inner word, which is what is written in His knowledge, exalted be He, that they will not believe.

This verse is an apposition of badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition) to the clause ﴿Indeed, the word has come into effect upon most of them, so they do not believe﴾ [Ya-Sin: 7], for the negation of their faith includes what this verse contains of placing shackles on their necks, literally or figuratively.

Ja'l (placing, making) means the bringing into being of a thing; that is, We made their state like the state of those who have shackles on their necks, reaching up to their chins, so that they are raised-headed (muqmahun). It is possible that this is a figurative image (tamthil), in which the state of their turning away from reflecting upon the Qur'an, from the call of Islam, and from contemplating its clear proofs is likened to the state of a people upon whose necks were placed heavy shackles that rise up to their chins, so that they are like those who are muqmahin, that is, those who raise their heads and lower their gaze, not turning right or left, so they look at nothing around them. This makes it a comprehensive figurative image (tamthiliyyah).

The mention of ﴿so they reach up to the chins﴾ serves to establish that the shackles are fastened tight against the bones of the chins, such that when the one shackled among them wishes to turn or to lower his head, his chin is pinned, and so he is compelled to remain still. This is an imagined state of these shackles, and not every shackle is like this state.

This figurative image is also capable of being distributed, so that each part of the composite figure is likened to a part of the other state: the aversion within their souls from good is likened to the shackles, and their turning away from reflection and fairness is likened to the raising of the head (iqma'h).

The fa' in His saying ﴿so they reach up to the chins﴾ is a conjunction upon the clause ﴿We have placed shackles on their necks﴾, meaning: We placed shackles, that is, We brought them up to the chins.

Ja'l here is literal, and it is what was created in their souls of the disposition of arrogance and obstinacy.

Al-aghlal is the plural of ghull (with a dammah on the ghayn), which is a broad ring of iron like a necklace, having sides on one of its faces and two ends facing its sides, in which there are parallel holes. The ring is tightened at its two ends around the neck of the shackled person by an iron rod with a head like a small ball, which slides into the holes; when it reaches its ball-like head, it settles, preventing the shackle from loosening or slipping off. This was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And those are the shackles upon their necks﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5], in Surat al-Ra'd.

The fa' in His saying ﴿so they are muqmahun﴾ is a consequence (tafri') upon the clause ﴿so they reach up to the chins﴾.

Al-muqmah is in the form of the passive participle, meaning one who has been made qami(h), that is, one who has his head raised, looking upward, and lowers his gaze. It is said: qamahahu al-ghull, when the shackle made his head raised and lowered his gaze. Thus its meaning is composed of two things. Al-adhqan is the plural of dhaqan (with fatha on the dhal and the qaf sukun... vocalised dhaqan), which is the meeting place of the two jaws. This was discussed in al-Isra'.

It is also possible that His saying ﴿Indeed, We have placed shackles on their necks﴾, etc., is a warning of what will befall them on the Day of Resurrection, when they are driven to Hell in shackles, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿When the shackles are on their necks and the chains; they will be dragged through the boiling water, then in the Fire they will be kindled﴾ [Ghafir: 71], in Surat Ghafir. In that case the verb ja'alna is future in meaning, expressed in the past form to affirm its certain occurrence, like His saying ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], meaning: We will place shackles on their necks.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 9:

﴿And We have set before them a barrier and behind them a barrier﴾ This is a climax in their deprivation of guidance, were they to reflect: their hearts' harshness does not accept drawing conclusions from proofs and arguments, such that they do not shift from what they are in. Their condition is therefore likened to the condition of those who are placed between two barriers, namely two walls: a barrier before them and a barrier behind them. So if they attempted to move from their place and to strive toward their aim, they would not be able to do so, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So they were not able to proceed, nor could they return﴾ [Ya-Sin: 67], and the saying of Abu al-Shish:

Desire has halted me where you are, so there is no one behind me who is late to it, nor one ahead of it.

This has been stated explicitly in the saying:

"Of the calamities, may you have no father, that I have been struck with barriers upon the earth,
I do not find my way therein to the place of a hillock between al-'Udhayb and the land of Murad."

The barrier (sadd) has been discussed in Surat al-Kahf.

In Mafatih al-Ghayb: The impediment to faith is either within the self or outside of it. For them both impediments exist: within the self, the fetter (ghull); and from outside, the barrier (sadd). So their gaze does not fall upon themselves, so they do not see the signs that are within themselves, because the one with raised head does not see himself; and their gaze does not fall upon the horizons, because those between the two barriers do not see the horizons, so the signs are not made clear to them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat: 53].

The repetition of the verb "We placed" (ja'alna) in the first sense, in the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, We have put fetters around their necks﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8] and so on, is an emphasis of this placing. As for the second sense, in the meaning of ﴿Indeed, We have put fetters around their necks﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8], the repetition of the verb "We placed" is because it is a placing that occurs in this world, which is distinct from the placing that occurs on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "sadda" with a ḍammah, which is the name of a wall that blocks between an inside and an outside. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read it with a fatḥah, which is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a name for that which is blocked.

* * *

﴿So We covered them, and they do not see﴾ This is a consequence of both of the two objects: ﴿We have put fetters around their necks﴾ [Ya-Sin: 8] and ﴿We have set before them a barrier and behind them a barrier﴾, because in both verbs there is an impediment to the states of sight.

The speech dispenses with mentioning what follows secondarily from their being likened to those placed between two barriers, namely their inability to shift from their condition.

Al-Ighsha' is placing a covering (ghisha'), which is that which veils a thing. The intended meaning is: We covered their sights. So in the speech there is an elision of a possessive term (muḍaf), indicated by the context, and it is emphasised by the consequence stated in His saying "so they do not see." The placing of the subject (musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate (musnad fi'li) serves to convey the strengthening of the judgement, that is, the confirmation of their not seeing.

Verse 10: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the clause "they do not see" (lā yubṣirūn); that is, your warning and its absence are equal with respect to them. The particle (ʿalā) here has its figurative sense of elevation (istiʿlāʾ majāzī), and here it indicates association (mulābasah); it is connected to (sawāʾ), which signifies "it has become equal" (istawā). A parallel to this was mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The hamzat al-taswiyah (the hamza of equalization) originally serves as an interrogative, then it was used for equalization by way of metonymic figurative usage (al-majāz al-mursal). This became so widespread that equalization was counted among the meanings of the hamza, due to its frequent use in this sense together with the word sawāʾ, which conveys the verbal-noun sense (al-maṣdariyyah). Since the hamza was used with the meaning of equalization, am (أم) was used in the sense of waw (and). It has also come in its literal usage in the verse of Buthayna:

sawāʾun ʿalaynā yā Jamīl ibn Maʿmar idhā mittu baʾsāʾ al-ḥayāti wa līnuhā
("It is the same for us, O Jamil ibn Ma'mar, whether, when you die, [we face] the hardship of life or its ease.")

The clause "they will not believe" (lā yu'minūn) is explanatory, clarifying that the equality of warning and its absence with respect to them is that they do not believe.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah Ya-Sin (36), verse 11:**

﴿Indeed, you can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a noble reward.﴾ When His words ﴿It is all the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ (36:10) included that warning, in the case of those against whom the Word has come true, that they will not believe, is no different from not warning them, this might give the impression that warning is futile for others and for some of the virtue of the people of faith. So He followed it with an explanation of the benefit of warning with regard to those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful unseen.

"The Reminder" (al-dhikr) means the Qur'an.

"Following" (al-ittiba') is in its literal sense tracing and walking behind someone. Here it is used metaphorically for turning toward something and caring for it, because one who follows something takes care to trace it. Following the Reminder means affirming it and believing in what it contains, because reflecting upon it leads to acting by it, as is reported in the story of the faith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). He found a tablet on which Surah Ta-Ha was written at the house of his sister, so he began reading and reflecting upon it, and then he believed.

The polytheists used to turn away from listening to the Qur'an and would prevent people from listening to it. What illustrates this is the story of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul at the beginning of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) settling in Medina: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by the gathering of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy, dismounted, greeted them, and recited the Qur'an to them until he finished. 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy said: 'O man, what you say is better than your talk, if it is true. So sit in your house, and whoever comes to you, speak to him, and whoever does not come to you, do not force it upon him.'"

Since turning toward listening to the Qur'an leads to belief in what it contains, because it enters the heart, as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "Indeed it has a sweetness, and upon it is a radiance; its lowest part is abundant, and its highest part is fruitful." The phrase "follows the Reminder" was followed by the clause ﴿and fears the Most Merciful unseen﴾. Thus the intended meaning of following the Reminder is its most complete form, which is not followed by turning away. It leads to the obedience of those who follow it to what it calls them to.

The fear of the Most Merciful is their piety in their innermost selves. These are the believers, given prominence to honour them and the warning. This is the counterpart to His words ﴿Certainly the Word has come true against most of them﴾ (36:7), and it is the remainder of the detailing of His words "so that you may warn a people." The purpose is to strengthen the Messenger's (ﷺ) motivation in warning, and to praise those who accepted his warning and believed.

So the meaning of the verb "you warn" (tundhir) is the warning whose effect follows from it, namely fear and obedience, as if it were said: "You only warn, so the one who follows the Reminder is warned," meaning that this is their condition, because they have believed and they are mindful.

The use of the past-tense verb form indicates the certainty of following and fear. The intended meaning is the beginning of following.

Then, on the basis of this praise, came the command to give good tidings to these people of forgiveness for what was in the time of ignorance and for what they commit of minor lapses.

The combination of "you warn" and "give good tidings" contains the rhetorical embellishment of antithesis (tibaq), and it shows that the beginning of their affair is warning and its outcome is good tidings.

The "reward" (ajr) is the recompense for faith and acts of obedience. Describing it as "noble" is because it is the best of its kind, as was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿Indeed, a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾ (27:29) in Surah al-Naml.

The expression by the attribute "the Most Merciful" rather than the name of Majesty (Allah) is for two reasons. The first is that the polytheists used to deny the name "the Most Merciful," as He said: ﴿They said, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ (25:60).

The second is an indication that His mercy does not require that He not be feared. The believer fears Allah while knowing His mercy, so he hopes for mercy.

The restriction (al-qasr) derived from His words ﴿Indeed, you can only warn one who follows the Reminder﴾ is the restriction of warning to the one attached to "who follows the Reminder" and fears Allah. This is according to the interpretation (ta'wil) by which the meaning of the verb "you warn" was interpreted, that is, that the benefit of warning is achieved, and this is a true restriction. If you insist on keeping the verb "you warn" in its apparent usage, which indicates the occurrence of its verbal nouns, then the restriction is a claimed one (id'a'i), by treating the warning of those who did not follow the Reminder and did not fear as the status of no warning, in the absence of its benefit.

**[Page 355]**

Verse 12: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forward and what they left behind, and We have enumerated everything in a clear record.﴾

When the restriction in His words ﴿You can only warn those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful unseen﴾ [Yasin: 11] was implied, it negated that warning could apply to those who did not follow the Reminder and did not fear the Most Merciful. This contained an allusive metonymy (kinaya ta'ridiyya) that those who did not benefit from the warning are in the position of the dead, since they do not benefit from what benefits every intelligent person, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿That he may warn whoever is alive﴾ [Yasin: 70], and as He said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [An-Naml: 80]. Following this, the discourse digressed (istitrad) into a transition (takhallus) to establishing the Resurrection. The success (tawfiq) that surrounds those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful is like the bringing to life of the dead, because the state of polytheism is a state of misguidance resembling death, and bringing someone out of it is like reviving the dead. Thus this verse, by its explicit meaning, contained knowledge of the reality of the Resurrection, and by its allusive meaning contained a symbol and two implicit metaphors (isti'arat): the metaphor of "the dead" for the polytheists, and the metaphor of "the living" for rescue from polytheism. The indicator (qarina) is the shift from one speech to another, due to what the shift suggests regarding the precedence of presence in the imagination, so that it encompasses the speaker, from what was being spoken about concerning his matter, to speech about what has occurred to him. These indications are among the consequences of the context and are not among the necessary implications of the meaning of the structure. This is one of the most subtle forms of transition by means of the particle ﴿inna﴾ (إنَّ), because the connection between what is transitioned from and what is transitioned to requires acuity, and this is the situation of addressing the intelligent person mentioned in the introduction to the science of meanings (ilm al-ma'ani).

Accordingly, the position of the clause ﴿Indeed, We bring the dead to life﴾ is a fresh resumptive beginning (istinaf ibtida'i), for the purpose of warning those who did not follow the Reminder and did not fear the Most Merciful, who are the ones required by the negative aspect in the restrictive form.

It is also permissible that the "bringing to life" be a metaphor for rescue from polytheism, and "the dead" a metaphor for the people of polytheism. Then the bringing to life of the dead is the granting of success (tawfiq) to those among the people who believe, to faith, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose example is in darkness?﴾ [Al-An'am: 122], and so on.

Then the clause is a favour (imtinan) upon the believers by making faith easy for them, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He opens his breast to Islam﴾ [Al-An'am: 125]. The position of the clause relates to His words ﴿So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a noble reward﴾ [Yasin: 11].

What is meant by recording ﴿what they have sent forward﴾ is a metonymy for the promise of reward for their good deeds and reward for their traces.

This interpretation suits the fresh resumptive beginning, so that the transition, by beginning a speech, alerts the listener to what the speaker considered within the folds of his discourse.

The emphasis by the particle ﴿inna﴾ (إنَّ) is regarded in terms of the explicit meaning, as is customary. And the word ﴿nahnu﴾ (نَحْنُ) is a pronoun of separation (damir fasl), not for emphasis, though it is an additional emphasis. The meaning is: We bring them to life for recompense, and therefore He conjoined ﴿and We record what they have sent forward﴾, that is, We enumerate for them their deeds, good and bad, which they sent forward in the world, in order that We may recompense them.

The conjunction of this clause is an incorporation (idmaj) of warning and threat, that they will be called to account for their deeds and recompensed for them.

The metonymy here is a metonymy for enumeration and for nothing among their deeds escaping or being neglected. It is what is expressed by the records of deeds that the noble scribes record.

**[Page 356]**

Thus what is meant by ﴿what they have sent forward﴾ is the deeds they did before death. Their deeds in this worldly life are likened to things they send forward to the Hereafter, as a traveller sends forward his baggage and loads.

As for ﴿traces﴾ (آثار), they are the traces of deeds and not the deeds themselves, by the indicator of its being contrasted with ﴿what they have sent forward﴾, like what they leave behind of good or evil among people and in souls.

What is intended by that is what they knew to be in accordance with the legal obligations or in contradiction to them. ﴿And their traces﴾ likewise. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever establishes a good practice (sunna hasana), he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection; and whoever establishes an evil practice, he will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their deeds."

So traces are the causes (musabbabat) of causes they acted upon. The intention is not the recording of everything they did, because no religious benefit that would entail recompense results from that. This is a promise and a threat, each taking its share of it.

It has been transmitted from Jabir that "the Prophet (ﷺ) learned that the Banu Salima wished to move from their dwellings at the far end of Madina to near the mosque, and they said: 'The areas are empty.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: 'O Banu Salima, stay in your dwellings, your traces will be recorded.' He said it twice." Related by Muslim. It means the traces of their feet in walking to congregational prayer.

In the narration of al-Tirmidhi from Abu Sa'id, it adds: that he recited to them ﴿and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾, thus making "traces" general to the sensory and the non-sensory. This corresponds to the second view regarding the position of the clause ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾, and it proceeds according to what we established in the ninth introduction. The narrator of the hadith from al-Tirmidhi imagined that this verse was revealed concerning that, but the context of the verse contradicts it, and its Meccan character refutes it.

Enumeration (ihsa'): its reality is counting and reckoning, and here it is a metonymy for comprehensiveness, precision, and nothing being absent from the mention and specification, because enumeration and reckoning necessitate that not one of the counted things be missed.

The imam (إمام): that which is followed in guidance according to what it indicates. Al-Nabigha said:

"They built the glory of life upon an imam..."

He applied "imam" to the Book, because the Book is followed for what it contains of reports and stipulations. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Fearing oppression and mutual contention; but can the desires undo what is in the written scrolls?"

The intended meaning of ﴿every thing﴾ according to the apparent sense is every thing of people's deeds, as the context indicates. So the mention of ﴿every thing﴾ is for the purpose of conveying comprehensiveness and generality regarding what they sent forward and their traces, of great and small. Thus the word ﴿kulla﴾ (كُلَّ) is an explicit text for generality, from the relative pronoun and from the definite plural with a genitive construction. Therefore the clause ﴿and We have enumerated every thing in a clear record﴾ is an emphasis of ﴿and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾, and an explanation of its general sense, and its conjunction without separation is considered because of the additional benefit it contains.

It is also permissible that what is meant by ﴿every thing﴾ is everything that exists, of beings and deeds. The enumeration would then be enumeration of knowledge, that is, the attachment of knowledge to known things at the time of their occurrence, and the clear record would be the knowledge of Allah, may He be exalted. The sense of "in" is that of encompassment, meaning that nothing escapes His knowledge just as the contained does not escape the container.

The knowledge of Allah was called an imam because the attachments of His divine will and power proceed in accordance with it. Thus the clause ﴿and We have enumerated every thing﴾ according to this is a concluding statement (tadhyil) conveying that recording is not restricted to the deeds of people that proceed in accordance with the legal obligations or their opposite, but rather encompasses all existing beings. And since "thing" (shay') is synonymous with "existent" (mawjud), it is permissible that by "every thing" is meant what exists actually, or what precedes existence, which is the possible. Then its enumeration would be knowledge that it will be or will not be, and the measures of its existence and its states, as in His words: ﴿And He has enumerated everything by number﴾ [Al-Jinn: 28].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 13–14:

﴿And strike for them an example: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it﴾ ﴿when We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, and they said, "Indeed, we are messengers to you."﴾ It follows the description of their aversion and heedlessness toward benefiting from the guidance of the Qur'an with a threat of a worldly punishment, since at the end of this story comes His saying: ﴿It was but one cry, and at once they were extinguished﴾ [Ya-Sin: 29].

Ḍarb (striking, i.e., setting forth) is a well-known metaphorical usage meaning placing or making, as in "he struck his seal" and "I struck a tent." It is used here in the sense of making, and it was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example (an yaḍriba mathalan mā)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: make the companions of the town and the messengers sent to them a likeness for the people of Makkah and your sending to them.

"Lahum" (for them) may be connected to "iḍrib" (strike), meaning strike an example for their sake, that is, so that they may take heed, like His saying ﴿He has struck for you an example from yourselves﴾ [al-Rum: 28]. It may also be an attribute of "mathal," meaning strike a likeness for them, like His saying ﴿So do not strike forth comparisons for Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 74].

Mathal (example) means likeness, so His saying ﴿and strike for them an example﴾ means "and set forth a likeness," that is, liken their situation in denying you to a likeness from the earlier ones. Since mathal had come to predominate in the sense of a likeness in state, and ḍarb is more general, it was made the object of "iḍrib," meaning set forth their state by a likeness to it; thus a difference arises between "iḍrib" and "mathalan" in terms of consideration. "Mathalan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

"Aṣḥāba al-qaryah" (the companions of the town) is in the accusative as an explanation (bayān) of "mathalan," or as an apposition (badal). It may also be the first object of "iḍrib," with "mathalan" as the second object, like His saying ﴿Allah struck an example: a town﴾ [al-Nahl: 112].

The meaning is that the state of the polytheists of Makkah is like the state of the companions of the town who were made an example.

As for the town, the exegetes said, from Ibn 'Abbas, that it is "Antakiyah" (Antioch), a city in Syria bordering the lands of the Greeks.

As for the messengers sent to it, Qatadah said they were among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) whom 'Isa (peace be upon him) sent, and that this was when 'Isa had been raised. They mentioned their names, with differences in that.

The verification of the story: 'Isa (peace be upon him) called only the Children of Israel to his religion, and the religion with which he was sent was only a completion of what divine wisdom required to be completed from the Law of the Torah. But 'Isa instructed the disciples not to neglect forbidding people from worshipping idols. So whenever they saw a vision, or a thought occurred to them to head to a land of the lands of Israel or what bordered it, or an inspiration arose in their souls to head to a land, they knew that this was a revelation from Allah to fulfil the testament of 'Isa (peace be upon him). This was around the year forty after the birth of 'Isa (peace be upon him).

Exegetes differed on specifying the three messengers who were sent to the people of Antioch, and in the variations of the names. What agrees with what is in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles among the books of the New Testament is that "Barnabas" and "Saul," called "Paul," were among the disciples of the ḥawāriyyūn, and they were described as being of the prophets; they were in Antioch as messengers for teaching. And they were strengthened by the disciple "Silas." The exegetes mentioned that the third was "Simeon," but there is nothing in the Book of Acts that requires that Paul and Barnabas were strengthened by Simeon. It occurs in the thirteenth chapter of it that there was a prophet in Antioch named "Simeon."

The deniers were those who were residents of Antioch, from among the Jews and the Greeks. There is in the Acts of the Apostles nothing but general words about the denial and the dialogue that took place between the messengers and those to whom they were sent. It mentions that there was a group of Jews there who attacked the truthfulness of the call of Paul and Barnabas and stirred up against them the women of those who believed in 'Isa from the notable people of the city, from the Greeks and others, until "Paul and Barnabas" were compelled to leave Antioch and headed for Iconium and its surroundings, and the Jews of some of those cities opposed them. The Christian rabbis in those cities decided to return Paul and Barnabas to Antioch. After their return, what had happened to them the first time happened to them again, especially in the matter of the obligation of circumcision upon whoever enters the religion. So Paul and Barnabas went to Jerusalem to consult the ḥawāriyyūn, and the rabbis of Jerusalem decided to support them with two men

صفحة ٣٦٠
from the prophets, namely "Barsabas" and "Silas." As for "Barsabas," he did not remain. As for "Silas," he stayed with "Paul and Barnabas," preaching to the people. Perhaps that was by revelation from Allah to them and to their companions from the ḥawāriyyūn. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿when We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third﴾: when We sent to them two and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, attributing the sending and the strengthening to Allah.

Ta'zīz is strengthening, and in this root there is the sense of making the one strengthened mighty; the best view is that ta'zīz is support.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "fa-'azaznā" with the first zay lightened; the verb 'azza, in the sense of "to be mighty," is synonymous with 'azzaza, as they say shadda and shaddada. The rest read it with the zay doubled.

The emphasis of their saying "Indeed, we are messengers to you" is due to their denial by them, so they emphasized the statement with a moderate emphasis, and this is called a talabī (responsive) form.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for the sake of concern with the matter of those to whom they were sent, whose faith in 'Isa was intended.

What agrees with what is in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles among the books of the New Testament is that "Barnabas" and "Saul," called "Paul," were among the disciples of the ḥawāriyyūn, and they were described as being of the prophets; they were in Antioch as messengers for teaching. And they were strengthened by the disciple "Silas." The exegetes mentioned that the third was "Simeon," but there is nothing in the Book of Acts that requires that Paul and Barnabas were strengthened by Simeon. It occurs in the thirteenth chapter of it that there was a prophet in Antioch named "Simeon."

The deniers were those who were residents of Antioch, from among the Jews and the Greeks. There is in the Acts of the Apostles nothing but general words about the denial and the dialogue that took place between the messengers and those to whom they were sent. It mentions that there was a group of Jews there who attacked the truthfulness of the call of Paul and Barnabas and stirred up against them the women of those who believed in 'Isa from the notable people of the city, from the Greeks and others, until "Paul and Barnabas" were compelled to leave Antioch and headed for Iconium and its surroundings, and the Jews of some of those cities opposed them. The Christian rabbis in those cities decided to return Paul and Barnabas to Antioch. After their return, what had happened to them the first time happened to them again, especially in the matter of the obligation of circumcision upon whoever enters the religion. So Paul and Barnabas went to Jerusalem to consult the ḥawāriyyūn, and the rabbis of Jerusalem decided to support them with two men

صفحة ٣٦٠
from the prophets, namely "Barsabas" and "Silas." As for "Barsabas," he did not remain. As for "Silas," he stayed with "Paul and Barnabas," preaching to the people. Perhaps that was by revelation from Allah to them and to their companions from the ḥawāriyyūn. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿when We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third﴾: when We sent to them two and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, attributing the sending and the strengthening to Allah.

Ta'zīz is strengthening, and in this root there is the sense of making the one strengthened mighty; the best view is that ta'zīz is support.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "fa-'azaznā" with the first zay lightened; the verb 'azza, in the sense of "to be mighty," is synonymous with 'azzaza, as they say shadda and shaddada. The rest read it with the zay doubled.

The emphasis of their saying "Indeed, we are messengers to you" is due to their denial by them, so they emphasized the statement with a moderate emphasis, and this is called a talabī (responsive) form.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for the sake of concern with the matter of those to whom they were sent, whose faith in 'Isa was intended.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 15:

﴿They said: "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has revealed nothing. You are only lying."﴾ The people of Antioch and the cities nearby were a mixture of Jews and idol-worshippers among the Greeks. So the saying "You are only human beings like us" is fitting to be uttered by worshippers of idols, and it is evident, given their belief that the gods do not send messengers nor reveal to anyone. For this reason it has come in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles that some of the Greeks from the city of "Lystra" saw a miracle from the prophet Paul, and they said in Greek: "The gods have taken the likeness of men and have descended to us." So they called "Barnabas" "Zeus," that is, the planet Jupiter, and "Paul" "Hermes," that is, the planet Mercury. The priest of Zeus came to them with bulls to sacrifice to them and garlands to place upon them. When Paul and Barnabas saw that, they tore their garments and cried out: "We are only human beings like you, and we admonish you to turn away from these falsehoods to the living God who created the heavens and the earth..." etc.

صفحة ٣٦١

And it is fitting to be uttered by the Jews, who did not give victory to the prophets, because that saying implies that they [the messengers] and the rest of the Jews are equal, and that there is no superiority for them through what they claim of prophethood; and it implies the denial that God sent down anything, that is, after the Torah. So among the miracles of the Qur'an is the gathering of the saying of both groups in these two clauses.

And the choice of the description "the Most Merciful" in the report of the disbelievers' saying, "and the Most Merciful has revealed nothing," is because it is suitable for the creed of both groups: the Greeks do not know the name of God, and the Lord of lords in their view is "Zeus," who is the source of mercy in their belief; and the Jews used to avoid pronouncing the name of God, which in their language is "Yahweh," so they substitute attributes for it.

The exception in (﴿إنْ أنْتُمْ إلّا تَكْذِبُونَ﴾) is an interrogative-style restrictive construction (istifham mufarragh) detached from omitted predicates, so the clause "tukadhdhibun" (you lie) occupies the position of the predicate with respect to the pronoun "antum" (you).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 16–17:

﴿They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you."﴾ ﴿And our duty is only the clear conveyance.﴾ This dialogue is related in the manner of reporting conversations, by recounting the words of the speakers without a conjunction.

And ﴿Our Lord knows﴾ is an oath (qasam), because it is an invocation of God as witness to the truthfulness of their statement. It is an ancient oath which the Arabs carried over in the Jahiliyya, and al-Harith ibn 'Abbad said:

"I was not among its (the war's) cutters down; God knows it, and I am today roasting in its heat."

It appears that it was an emphatic oath among them, because of how rarely it occurs in their speech, and it hardly occurs except in an important context. According to the scholars of the Muslims, it is an oath like other oaths, and there is expiation (kaffara) for breaking it.

Some scholars of the Hanafiyya said that they hold an opinion that one who swears by it falsely incurs apostasy (riddah), because he attributed to God's knowledge something contrary to reality, so it leads to making God's knowledge ignorance. This aims at emphasis and warning; otherwise, how could anyone be judged an unbeliever on remote implications?

The insistence on strong emphasis with the oath was necessitated by what they saw of the firm determination of many people of the town to deny them. This degree of emphasis is called ḍarb inkārī (the denial-type emphasis).

As for their words ﴿And our duty is only the clear conveyance﴾, this is an admonition, which they gave to the people so that they would know that no benefit accrues to them from the people's faith, and a declaration to them of their disassociation from responsibility for the people remaining in polytheism. Such a thing by its nature stirs thoughtful reflection in the people's souls.

al-Balagh (conveyance): a verbal noun (ism masdar) from ablagha, meaning to deliver a report. God says: ﴿If upon you is only the conveyance﴾ [al-Shura: 48], and He says: ﴿This is a conveyance for mankind﴾ [Ibrahim: 52]. The word balagh is not used for conveying persons.

The jurists say, regarding the hire of ships and mounts, that among it is that which is "on balagh," meaning on reaching a specific place, between the lessor and the lessee.

al-Mubin (the clear): an attribute of al-balagh, i.e., the conveyance that is clear in its indication, which is the one without ambiguity or evasion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 18:

﴿They said, "Indeed, we consider you a bad omen. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment from us will surely touch you."﴾ When the proof overwhelmed them from every side, and the words of the messengers, ﴿And upon us is only the clear conveyance﴾ [Ya-Sin: 17], reached the souls of the people of the town to the point of shame and humiliation, because the proof had failed them, and they had marked themselves with obstinacy and rejection toward those who sought their benefit, they turned to concealing their shame and their being silenced by wrapping up the cause for rejecting their call in something they thought would convince the messengers to abandon their call. They presumed that what they were claiming was a hidden matter, with no one able to dispute it except its inventor. This was by their claiming that they had taken omen from them and that a misfortune had come upon them from them. The defeated party must always resort to a feeble excuse.

Al-tatayyur (taking omen) originally means striving to know what a bird signifies, good or evil, from the kind of bird that appears and from the manner in which it flies off or comes. Then it was applied to every event which someone imagines was the cause of some harm befalling him, and it became synonymous with tasha'um (ill omen).

In a hadith: "There is no contagion, and no tiyarah (ill omen); the ill omen is only in the one who takes omen." It is in this sense that the term is used in this verse, that is, they said, "Indeed, we have taken you as an ill omen."

The meaning of "bikum" (by you) is "by your call." They do not mean that a calamity of evil befell the town, affecting all its people, such as drought, plague, or something similar of general harm, coinciding with the arrival of the messengers or with their call. Some exegetes have permitted this, but the meaning is rather that no one is free in this life from being struck by something disagreeable. It is the habit of people of foolish fancies and deficient minds to attribute events to what coincides with them without knowing their causes, and then to choose, in identifying the coincidences of misfortune, things that do not suit their desires and that they dislike, and to identify among the coincidences of good omen what they desire and what their natures accept. In this way they deceive themselves, as is the way of people of weak intellect. Thus the source of all causes for them returns to the states of their own souls and their appetites, as God Most High related about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours"; and if evil afflicted them, they attributed it to Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131], and He related about the polytheists of Makkah that if ﴿evil afflicts them, they say, "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [al-Nisa: 78].

It is also possible that they meant by the ill omen that their call had caused disputes and disagreement among the people of the town. When the souls of the people of the town agreed that the explanation of every disagreeable event that befalls any of them is that it is due to these messengers, their word became united upon that, so they said, ﴿Indeed, we consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning that one of them or a group would say it, and all the people of the town would agree with them.

Then they moved on to demanding that they cease this call, so they said, ﴿If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment from us will surely touch you.﴾ With this, they compelled Paul and Barnabas to leave Antioch, and they went out to Iconium, and the miracle of Paul appeared in Iconium, then in Lystra, then in Derbe. The Jews in each of these cities continued to oppose the messengers, persecute them, and stir the people against them, so harm and affliction touched them from this, and Paul was stoned in the city of Lystra until they thought he had died.

The lam in ﴿la-in lam tantahu﴾ is a preparatory lam for an oath, by which is related what they uttered of an oath in their speech.

[p. 364]

﴿They said: "Your omen is with you. Is it because you have been admonished? Rather, you are a people who transgress."﴾ The speech of the messengers is related using words that are synonymous with it and convey its meaning in Arabic idiom, as an allusion to the idolaters of Quraysh, to whom the town was offered as a parable. The messengers did not mention the root *tiyarah* (ill omen) or *tayr* (birds). They said only what indicates that the misfortune of the people is connected to their own selves, not to something brought to them by the messengers. So it is related in words that match this in the speech of the Arabs, as an allusion to the polytheists of Makkah. This is in the position of *tajrid* (abstraction) in giving the parable: in relating the story, attention is paid to the circumstances of those who are likened to the people of the story. Since *tiyarah* in the sense of misfortune (*shu'm*) is derived from the name of the bird (*tayr*), the root of derivation is taken into account in it.

The use of *tair* (bird) in the sense of misfortune has also come in the words of the Exalted in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿Indeed, their omen is with Allah﴾ [al-A'raf 7:131], in the manner of *mushakalah* (rhetorical correspondence).

The meaning of ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ is: the bird to which you attribute misfortune is with you, that is, in your souls. They meant that if you reflected, you would find that the cause of what you have named a misfortune is your disbelief and your bad hearing of admonitions. For those who listened to the best of speech followed it and did not transgress against you. You are the ones who preferred sedition and kindled hatred and grudges. So you are indeed the cause of the evil that befell the situation in the town.

The last part of their speech points to this idea when they said ﴿Is it because you have been admonished?﴾ by way of the rhetorical interrogation of denial (*al-istifham al-inkari*) entering upon the conditional *in* (if). It is an interrogation about an omitted element indicated by the preceding speech. That omitted element is restricted by the condition, whose answer is also omitted, being dispensed with by the interrogation about it. The two have one meaning, except that Sibawayh prefers that when interrogation and condition combine, one brings what fits the interrogation had it been stated explicitly. Likewise, when it is omitted, the implied element should be suited to the interrogation. The estimated sense is: "Do you consider it an omen that you were admonished, if you were admonished?" This is indicated by the statement of the people of the town: ﴿We have taken you as an omen﴾, that is, by your words. They rejected that the misfortune came from their admonition by saying ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress.﴾ That is: there is no ill omen in what you claim, but you are a people who disbelieve, whose minds have been covered by illusions, so you took what was beneficial to you as harm to you, and you placed things other than in their proper causes, through your immersion in ignorance, disbelief and corruption of belief. Among your transgression is your belief in misfortune and in luck.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿Is it because you have been admonished?﴾ with the interrogative hamzah entering upon *in* (if), which has a kasrah on its hamzah and is conditional, with the *kaf* doubled. Abu Ja'far read *a-in dhukirtum* with both hamzahs pronounced with fatha and the *kaf* lightened, from *dhukirtum* (you were mentioned). The interrogation is then affirmative (*taqrir*), meaning: "Because we mentioned your names when we called you, has misfortune settled among you?", as a metaphor for their being worthy that their names should be a misfortune.

[p. 365]

In the mention of the word "people" (*qawm*) there is an indication that transgression is firmly established among them, and that their peoplehood is sustained by it, as was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 365 continues]

This is connected to the account of the dialogue, already under way, between the people of the town and the three messengers. It is meant to show the gulf between the state of the obstinate among the people of the town and the state of the believing man among them, who admonished them with a far-reaching exhortation, and who was one of a small group from the town's people.

You may take the clause ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man, running﴾ as coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause "there came to it the messengers", and you may also take it as coordinated with the clause ﴿They said: "Indeed, we are sent to you"﴾ [Yāsīn 36:14].

By "the city" (al-madīnah) here is meant the very town mentioned in His words "the people of the town" [Yāsīn 36:13]. It is expressed here as "the city" for variety of expression (tafannun). Thus "farthest" (aqṣā) is an adjective of an elided noun which is, in meaning, the noun governing "the city" in the genitive. The sense is: "from the far edge of the city", that is, from its outer edge. The benefit of stating that he came "from the farthest part of the city" is to indicate that faith in God appeared among the people of the outskirts of the city (rabaḍ al-madīnah) before it appeared in the heart of the city. This is because the heart of the city is the dwelling of its rulers and of the rabbis of the Jews, who are further from fairness and from examining whether what the messengers call them to is true. Most of its inhabitants follow its great men, because of their attachment to them and their fear of their might. By contrast, the people at the edges of the city are closer to independence of judgement and less concerned with others, since most of the people at the edges of the city earn their own living, being close to the desert Bedouin.

With this, the reason becomes clear for placing "from the farthest part of the city" before "a man", in order to praise the people of the farthest part of the city, and that good may be found at the edges what is not found at the centre, and that the weak are the first to accept faith, since the mighty among them, with their luxury and grandeur, do not bar them from the truth. For it is customary that such people dwell in the middle of the city. Abū Tammām said:

"It was the protected middle, then events joined with it until it became an edge."

As for His words, Exalted is He, in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ, ﴿And there came a man from the farthest part of the city, running﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:20], the arrangement there follows the original order, since there is no reason for placing it first, given that the man there was an adviser and was not a caller to faith.

On this basis, this man is not mentioned in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, and this is among the matters in which the Qur'an is distinguished by informing us of it. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and his companions that his name was Ḥabīb ibn Murrah. It was said that he was a carpenter, and it was said otherwise. When the messengers approached the city, he saw them and saw a miracle (muʿjizah) or a marvel (karāmah) of theirs, and so he believed. It was also said that he had been a believer before this. It is not improbable that this man whom the exegetes described as a carpenter is the one called "Simon" who is known as "the Niger", mentioned in the eleventh chapter of the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, and that the description "carpenter" is a distortion of "Niger". For among the names that occur in the words of the exegetes, from Ibn ʿAbbās, is the name "Shamʿūn al-Ṣafā" or "Simʿān". This name does not occur in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles.

The description of the man as "running" (yasʿā) indicates that he came hastily, and that news had reached him of the people of the city's resolve to stone the messengers or to torment them. So he wished to advise them out of concern for them and for the messengers. This is praise of this man, indicating that he is one who is to be emulated in hastening to change what is wrong.

The clause "he said: O my people" (qāla yā qawmi) is an inclusive apposition (badal ishtimāl) of the clause "a man came", because his coming, given that it was for this purpose, is among the things that the coming included.

His opening his address to them by calling them with the description of "people" (qawmiyyah) for him is intended to suggest that what he is about to say to them is pure advice, because he loves for his people what he loves for himself.

"Following" (ittibāʿ) means compliance (imtithāl). The term "following" has been borrowed for it, by way of comparison: taking up another's opinion is likened to the follower in his course.

The definiteness of "the messengers" (al-mursalīn) is for prior reference (ʿahd).

[Page 366]

The clause ﴿Follow those who ask no reward of you﴾ reinforces the clause "Follow the messengers" [Yāsīn 36:20], with the added indication of the reason for following them, namely the clear signs of truthfulness and sincere advice in their message. For they call to guidance, and no benefit accrues to them from it. Thus their call is purely for the purpose of guiding those to whom they are sent. This is a comprehensive word of wisdom, meaning: "Follow those with whom you lose nothing of your worldly goods and gain the soundness of your religion."

The phrase "who ask no reward of you" was placed before "and they are rightly guided" in the relative clause only because the people were in doubt about the truthfulness of the messengers, and one of the motives for their denial was the accusation that they were seeking some benefit for themselves from it. For when attachment to love of wealth had dominated the people, and they had become distant from grasping lofty aims, they took every striving that appears in a man to be for the sake of his own benefit. So he put first what removes from them this suspicion, so that they might be prepared to reflect on what they are being called to. Also, this is of the nature of clearing (takhliyah) with respect to the messengers and those to whom they are sent, and clearing precedes adornment (taḥliyah). So the clause "who ask you no reward" was more important in the relative clause.

"Reward" (ajr) is true of every worldly benefit that accrues to someone from his work, so it includes wealth, standing, and leadership. Since it was denied of them that they ask a reward, it was denied of them that they aim, by their call, at some worldly benefit that would accrue to them.

After that, the position was prepared for the clause ﴿and they are rightly guided﴾, that is, they are characterised by being guided to what brings everlasting felicity. They call you only to follow their way. So when they are rightly guided, what they call you to by following them is a call to guidance. Thus this clause, by its position after the preceding one, contains praise of the messengers and of what they call to, and an encouragement to follow them.

Know that this verse was cited by al-Qazwīnī in al-Īḍāḥ wa al-Talkhīṣ as an example of iṭnāb (amplification) called īghāl (extension), which is to bring, after the completion of the intended meaning, another statement that completes the meaning without it, for a purpose. From what we have explained it is clear to you that His words "and they are rightly guided" were not mere addition, but were for the sake of the admonition depending on it, and that "who ask no reward of you" was like a preparation for it. We excuse the author of al-Talkhīṣ by saying that for an example, assumption and supposition suffice.

[Page 367]

The first clause of the relative was verbal and negative, because the aim is to negate that a request for reward should arise from them, let alone its continuing and persisting. The second clause was nominal, to affirm their guidance and its continuance, such that one need not fear for whoever follows them that at some time he might be unguided.

His words ﴿And why should I not worship Him who originated me, and to whom you will be returned?﴾ are coordinated with the clause "Follow the messengers". He intended to inform them that he had followed the messengers and renounced the worship of idols. He expressed the speech in the form of a rebuking interrogative, and with the formula "what is to me that I do not...", which is normally used by a speaker in response to one who has objected to an act of his, or whom wonder at his act has seized, or who expresses this in his heart. Therefore it contains the indication that they had been objecting to his calling them to affirm the messengers who came with the oneness of God. For that implies that he had preceded them in doing what he had commanded them.

The interrogative "mā" is in the position of the nominative of the inceptive (mubtada'), and the genitive phrase in His words "to me" (lī) is the predicate of the interrogative "mā".

The clause "I do not worship" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun. The meaning: "And what would be to me in a state of not worshipping Him who originated me?" That is, nothing prevents me from worshipping the One who created me. This statement is used as an allusion (taʿrīḍ) at them, as if he were saying: "What is to me that I do not worship, and what is to you that you do not worship Him who originated you?" This is indicated by the words "and to Him you will be returned", since he made the attribution to their pronoun to strengthen the sense of allusion. He began by attributing the statement to himself so that it would appear as advice to himself, while in fact he intended to advise them, so that he might be gentle with them and conciliate them, and make them hear the truth in a manner that does not arouse their anger, and so that they would be more ready to accept it, seeing that he wants for them only what he wants for himself.

Then he followed it with the refutation of worshipping idols, returning to the method of allusion with His words ﴿Shall I take other gods besides Him?﴾. This is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) of explanatory type (istiʾnāf bayānī), because it suggests a question about whether benefit has been obtained through the intercession of those gods with the One who originated him. The interrogative is one of denial: "I deny to myself that I should take other gods besides Him", that is, "I do not take gods."

"Taking" (ittikhādh) is a reflexive form (ifti‘āl) from "taking" (akhdh), which is seizing. Seizing suggests the acquisition of what was not previously there. So "taking" suggests that it was made, and this completes the allusion to those addressed, that they made the idols into gods, though they are not gods, because the true God is not made by being made, but deserves divinity intrinsically.

[Page 368]

He described the supposed gods, who are assumed to be taken, with a conditional clause in His words ﴿If the Most Merciful wills me harm, their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me﴾. The intent is an allusion to those addressed for taking those gods, on the ground that they intercede for them with God and bring them near to Him in nearness. And from the fact that they cannot avert harm, it is known that they are incapable of bringing benefit, because the motives for averting harm from a master are stronger and more important, and the disgrace attaching to the patron for his inability to do so is greater.

He used the description "the Most Merciful" rather than the proper name "God" for the reason already mentioned just above, in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿They said: "You are only a human like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing."﴾ [Yāsīn 36:15].

"Rescue" (inqādh) means deliverance from defeat, distress, or bewilderment. That is: their intercession with God, who has willed harm for me, will not benefit me, and they will not rescue me from harm if it befalls me.

Since their intercession was negated of benefit to the one interceded for, it was also negated of them, by implication, that they should intercede, because whoever knows that he will not be interceded for does not intercede. So it is as if he said: "Shall I take other gods besides Him, for whom there is no intercession with God?", to refute their belief that they are intercessors whose intercession is accepted. And since their intercession does not benefit, due to their weakness and their not being equal to God, who harms and benefits, in the attributes of divinity, it was more fitting that they should not be able to rescue. The shift from the implied meaning (dalālat al-fahwā) to the explicit meaning (dalālat al-manṭūq) is mentioned because the context is one of explicitness, since it relates to faith, which is the foundation of righteousness.

[Page 367]

The first clause of the relative was verbal and negative, because the aim is to negate that a request for reward should arise from them, let alone its continuing and persisting. For that implies that he had preceded them in doing what he had commanded them.

The interrogative "mā" is in the position of the nominative of the inceptive (mubtada'), and the genitive phrase in His words "to me" (lī) is the predicate of the interrogative "mā".

This statement is used as an allusion (taʿrīḍ) at them, as if he were saying: "What is to me that I do not worship, and what is to you that you do not worship Him who originated you?" The interrogative is one of denial: "I deny to myself that I should take other gods besides Him", that is, "I do not take gods."

So "taking" suggests that it was made, and this completes the allusion to those addressed, that they made the idols into gods, though they are not gods, because the true God is not made by being made, but deserves divinity intrinsically.

[Page 368]
