He expressed the speech in the form of a rebuking interrogative, and with the formula "what is to me that I do not...", which is normally used by a speaker in response to one who has objected to an act of his, or whom wonder at his act has seized, or who expresses this in his heart. Therefore it contains the indication that they had been objecting to his calling them to affirm the messengers who came with the oneness of God. For that implies that he had preceded them in doing what he had commanded them.

The interrogative "mā" is in the position of the nominative of the inceptive (mubtada'), and the genitive phrase in His words "to me" (lī) is the predicate of the interrogative "mā".

The clause "I do not worship" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun. The meaning: "And what would be to me in a state of not worshipping Him who originated me?" That is, nothing prevents me from worshipping the One who created me. This statement is used as an allusion (taʿrīḍ) at them, as if he were saying: "What is to me that I do not worship, and what is to you that you do not worship Him who originated you?" This is indicated by the words "and to Him you will be returned", since he made the attribution to their pronoun to strengthen the sense of allusion. He began by attributing the statement to himself so that it would appear as advice to himself, while in fact he intended to advise them, so that he might be gentle with them and conciliate them, and make them hear the truth in a manner that does not arouse their anger, and so that they would be more ready to accept it, seeing that he wants for them only what he wants for himself.

Then he followed it with the refutation of worshipping idols, returning to the method of allusion with His words ﴿Shall I take other gods besides Him?﴾. This is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) of explanatory type (istiʾnāf bayānī), because it suggests a question about whether benefit has been obtained through the intercession of those gods with the One who originated him. The interrogative is one of denial: "I deny to myself that I should take other gods besides Him", that is, "I do not take gods."

"Taking" (ittikhādh) is a reflexive form (ifti‘āl) from "taking" (akhdh), which is seizing. Seizing suggests the acquisition of what was not previously there. So "taking" suggests that it was made, and this completes the allusion to those addressed, that they made the idols into gods, though they are not gods, because the true God is not made by being made, but deserves divinity intrinsically.

[Page 368]

He described the supposed gods, who are assumed to be taken, with a conditional clause in His words ﴿If the Most Merciful wills me harm, their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me﴾. The intent is an allusion to those addressed for taking those gods, on the ground that they intercede for them with God and bring them near to Him in nearness. And from the fact that they cannot avert harm, it is known that they are incapable of bringing benefit, because the motives for averting harm from a master are stronger and more important, and the disgrace attaching to the patron for his inability to do so is greater.

He used the description "the Most Merciful" rather than the proper name "God" for the reason already mentioned just above, in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿They said: "You are only a human like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing."﴾ [Yāsīn 36:15].

"Rescue" (inqādh) means deliverance from defeat, distress, or bewilderment. That is: their intercession with God, who has willed harm for me, will not benefit me, and they will not rescue me from harm if it befalls me.

Since their intercession was negated of benefit to the one interceded for, it was also negated of them, by implication, that they should intercede, because whoever knows that he will not be interceded for does not intercede. So it is as if he said: "Shall I take other gods besides Him, for whom there is no intercession with God?", to refute their belief that they are intercessors whose intercession is accepted. And since their intercession does not benefit, due to their weakness and their not being equal to God, who harms and benefits, in the attributes of divinity, it was more fitting that they should not be able to rescue. The shift from the implied meaning (dalālat al-fahwā) to the explicit meaning (dalālat al-manṭūq) is mentioned because the context is one of explicitness, since it relates to faith, which is the foundation of righteousness.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error﴾ is the answer to the rebuking interrogative. The particle "then" (idhan) is the apodosis to the negated, not to the negation. That is: if I were to take other gods besides God, I would be in manifest error.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾ is placed in the position of the final purpose of the address and the conclusion from the proof. This is a declaration of his faith and a recording against them that God is their Lord, not those idols.

The declaration was emphasised by the sequential particle in "so listen to me", as a call to ensure that they hear, in case they are heedless.

[Page 370]

﴿It will be said: "Enter Paradise." He said: "Would that my people knew"﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured.﴾

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'nāf bayānī*, a clause that answers a question the listener would naturally ask) addressing what the listener awaits: learning what he encountered from his people after he confronted them with that forceful address. Did they accept his guidance, or did they turn away from it and abandon him, or did they harm him as the advocates of truth who oppose the whims of the multitude are harmed? The answer is given by what His words ﴿It will be said: "Enter Paradise"﴾ indicate. This is the most important matter for the Muslims, and they are among those intended by the knowledge of such a story, so that their certainty and steadfastness in faith may increase. As for the polytheists, their share of this parable is what has preceded and what comes later in His words ﴿It was but a single cry, and behold, they were extinguished.﴾

In His words ﴿It will be said: "Enter Paradise"﴾ there is an allusion (*kināya*, metonymy or indirect expression) to his being killed as a martyr in exalting the Word of God. This is because placing the command to enter Paradise immediately after his exhortation, without any transition, implies by way of *dalālat al-iqtiḍā'* (implication required by the meaning) that he died and that they killed him for opposing their religion. Some exegetes said: they killed him by stoning. Others said: they burned him. Others said: they dug a pit for him and buried him alive.

This man of faith was admitted into Paradise immediately after his death, because he was among the martyrs, and the martyrs have the distinction of being hastened into Paradise, entering it without delay. In the ḥadīth: "The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise."

The one who says "Enter Paradise" is God, exalted is He.

The one addressed is the man who came from the farthest part of the city. The pronoun of the one addressed was not mentioned with the preposition *lām* because the saying mentioned here is a creative saying (*qawl takwīnī*), whose addressee is not intended; rather, the intent is to narrate its occurrence, since when it occurs its effect occurs, as in His saying ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Naḥl: 40].

Since the parable does not relate that he left the place where he delivered his exhortation, this indicates that he died in that very place. It is understood from this that he died slain at that time or as a result of it.

He pursued this meaning through the way of allusion and did not state explicitly that they killed him, passing over this meaning in regard to the polytheists, lest it gladden them that his people had killed him, so that they make it part of what the parable was struck with, against them and against the Messenger ﷺ, and so that they hope to kill the Messenger ﷺ.

[Page 371]

This allusion is understood only by the people of Islam, among whom the necessary connection between martyrdom in the way of God and entering Paradise is established. As for the polytheists, they suppose that this is in the Hereafter. Eloquent speech may contain subtleties whose benefit is specific to some of the listeners.

The clause ﴿He said: "Would that my people knew"﴾ is also a resumptive explanatory clause, because the listener expects to know what he said when joy overwhelmed him at entering Paradise. The meaning is: entering Paradise did not distract him from the condition of his people; he wished that they would know what he had received from his Lord, so that they would know the excellence of faith and believe. He did not wish their destruction, nor did he gloat over them. Thus he was characterized by restraint of anger and by forbearance toward the ignorant. That is because in the world of realities the soul is directed only to pure goodness, and there is no worth in base shares and trivial matters.

The particle *bi* (with) was introduced before the object of *ya'lamūna* (they know) to imply the meaning of "they would be informed," because there is no hope that they would attain knowledge of that through observation and inference.

The *mā* in His words ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*), meaning: that they would know of the forgiveness of my Lord and His making me among the honoured.

By "the honoured" is meant those upon whom God's honour descends, and they are the angels, the prophets, and the best of the righteous. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 26], meaning the angels and Jesus, peace be upon them.

* * *

[Page 5]

﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down.﴾ ﴿It was but a single cry, and behold, they were extinguished.﴾

This is a return to the story of the people of the city, after the narrative had moved away from them to mention the believing man who came from the farthest part of the city advising them. This return occurred because the people are the people of that man.

The clause ﴿And We did not send down upon his people﴾ etc. is conjoined to the clause ﴿It will be said: "Enter Paradise"﴾, so it is likewise a resumptive explanatory clause, because the listener is eager to know what happened to this man and to his people, whom he advised but who did not heed him. When he explained to the listener what had happened to the man, there was conjoined to it an explanation of what happened to the people after him.

The opening of the story of their punishment in this world with a negation of one form of retribution is a preparation for the intended point: that nothing befell them except what befell their like of the punishment of annihilation. That is, We did not send down hosts of created beings from the heaven to fight his people, or We did not send down hosts of angels from the heaven to destroy them. Their punishment was only a single cry from a single angel, which destroyed them all.

The *min* in His words ﴿min ba'dihi﴾ ("after him") is superfluous (*mazīda*) in the adverbial expression, to stress the connection of the thing modified to the adverb. Its original use is the initial *min* (of origin), and the annexation of *ba'd* to the pronoun of the man is according to an understood, commonly elided, noun: "after his death," as in His saying ﴿When he said to his sons: "What will you worship after me?"﴾ [al-Baqara: 133].

[Page 6]

The *min* in His words ﴿min jund﴾ ("any host") is emphatic (*mu'akkida*) for the generality of *jund* in a negative context. The *min* in His words ﴿min al-samā'﴾ ("from the heaven") is initial (of origin). In the use of the particle *min* three times with differing meanings there is an embellishment of paronomasia (*jinās*).

In this there is an indirect reproach (*ta'rīḍ*) to the polytheists of Mecca, when they said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee﴾ [al-Isrā': 92], that is, that you bring God, whom you claim sent you, and with Him His host of angels to avenge you.

The clause ﴿And We were not going to send down﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*mu'taridha*) placed between the two kinds of punishment, the negated and the affirmed, with the purpose of refuting the polytheists: the custom of God has not been to send down hosts upon the deniers, and the affair of the disobedient is less than this concern.

The *ṣayḥa* (cry) is the single instance of crying, in the pattern *fa'la*, so describing it as "single" is an emphasis on the sense of unity, lest it be supposed that the intended meaning is the single type among the types. The word *ṣayḥatan* (a cry) is in the accusative as the predicate of *kānat* (it was) after an exceptive construction with a deleted antecedent (*istithnā' mufarragh*). The attachment of the feminine *tā'* to the verb together with the accusative *ṣayḥatan* indicates that the deleted antecedent of the exception is the punishment or the cry implied by "a single cry," that is: the punishment or the cry was not anything but a cry whose attribute is that it is single, and so on to the end. Abū Ja'far read *ṣayḥatun* with the nominative, taking *kānat* as complete (*tāmma*), meaning: nothing occurred except a single cry.

The coming of *idhā* (the sudden "then") of sudden occurrence in the clause that follows from ﴿It was but a single cry﴾ serves to convey the speed of their extinction by that cry.

This cry is a thunderbolt, as God, exalted is He, said, relating about Thamūd: ﴿So the cry seized them﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 73].

The *khumūd* (extinction) is the going out of a fire. It is used metaphorically (*isti'āra*) for death after a life full of strength and tyranny, so that the speech contains a comparison of the state of their life to the blazing of a fire and the state of their death to the extinguishing of a fire. Thus two metaphors arise: one explicit (*taṣrīḥiyya*, openly stated), and the other implicit (*makniyya*, veiled), whose sign is the first. These are the two metaphors contained in the verse of Labīd:

*"Man is but like a meteor and its light: it turns to ash after it was shining."*

[Page 7]

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We made them a harvest, extinguished﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 15] has preceded in the Sura of al-Isrā'. Thus this brevity in the verse is wondrous, since the meaning of Labīd's verse is achieved in three words.

This points to a great event that befell the people of Antioch after the call of the messengers, and it is a mark of honour for the martyrs among the followers of Jesus, peace be upon him. If the cry was a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd, then those who were extinguished by it were the entire population of the city, and perhaps they were all unbelievers after the death of the man who admonished them and after the messengers had left the city. But history does not record the occurrence of such an event in Antioch, so it is possible that history omitted some events, especially in times of turmoil and strife.

When he explained to the listener what had happened to the man, there was conjoined to it an explanation of what happened to the people after him.

The opening of the story of their punishment in this world with a negation of one form of retribution is a preparation for the intended point: that nothing befell them except what befell their like of the punishment of annihilation. That is, We did not send down hosts of created beings from the heaven to fight his people, or We did not send down hosts of angels from the heaven to destroy them. Their punishment was only a single cry from a single angel, which destroyed them all.

The *min* in His words ﴿min ba'dihi﴾ ("after him") is superfluous (*mazīda*) in the adverbial expression, to stress the connection of the thing modified to the adverb. Its original use is the initial *min* (of origin), and the annexation of *ba'd* to the pronoun of the man is according to an understood, commonly elided, noun: "after his death," as in His saying ﴿When he said to his sons: "What will you worship after me?"﴾ [al-Baqara: 133].

[Page 6]

The *min* in His words ﴿min jund﴾ ("any host") is emphatic (*mu'akkida*) for the generality of *jund* in a negative context. The *min* in His words ﴿min al-samā'﴾ ("from the heaven") is initial (of origin). In the use of the particle *min* three times with differing meanings there is an embellishment of paronomasia (*jinās*).

In this there is an indirect reproach (*ta'rīḍ*) to the polytheists of Mecca, when they said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee﴾ [al-Isrā': 92], that is, that you bring God, whom you claim sent you, and with Him His host of angels to avenge you.

The clause ﴿And We were not going to send down﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*mu'taridha*) placed between the two kinds of punishment, the negated and the affirmed, with the purpose of refuting the polytheists: the custom of God has not been to send down hosts upon the deniers, and the affair of the disobedient is less than this concern.

The *ṣayḥa* (cry) is the single instance of crying, in the pattern *fa'la*, so describing it as "single" is an emphasis on the sense of unity, lest it be supposed that the intended meaning is the single type among the types. The word *ṣayḥatan* (a cry) is in the accusative as the predicate of *kānat* (it was) after an exceptive construction with a deleted antecedent (*istithnā' mufarragh*). The attachment of the feminine *tā'* to the verb together with the accusative *ṣayḥatan* indicates that the deleted antecedent of the exception is the punishment or the cry implied by "a single cry," that is: the punishment or the cry was not anything but a cry whose attribute is that it is single, and so on to the end. Abū Ja'far read *ṣayḥatun* with the nominative, taking *kānat* as complete (*tāmma*), meaning: nothing occurred except a single cry.

The coming of *idhā* (the sudden "then") of sudden occurrence in the clause that follows from ﴿It was but a single cry﴾ serves to convey the speed of their extinction by that cry.

This cry is a thunderbolt, as God, exalted is He, said, relating about Thamūd: ﴿So the cry seized them﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 73].

The *khumūd* (extinction) is the going out of a fire. It is used metaphorically (*isti'āra*) for death after a life full of strength and tyranny, so that the speech contains a comparison of the state of their life to the blazing of a fire and the state of their death to the extinguishing of a fire. Thus two metaphors arise: one explicit (*taṣrīḥiyya*, openly stated), and the other implicit (*makniyya*, veiled), whose sign is the first. These are the two metaphors contained in the verse of Labīd:

*"Man is but like a meteor and its light: it turns to ash after it was shining."*

[Page 7]

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We made them a harvest, extinguished﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 15] has preceded in the Sura of al-Isrā'. Thus this brevity in the verse is wondrous, since the meaning of Labīd's verse is achieved in three words.

This points to a great event that befell the people of Antioch after the call of the messengers, and it is a mark of honour for the martyrs among the followers of Jesus, peace be upon him. If the cry was a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd, then those who were extinguished by it were the entire population of the city, and perhaps they were all unbelievers after the death of the man who admonished them and after the messengers had left the city. But history does not record the occurrence of such an event in Antioch, so it is possible that history omitted some events, especially in times of turmoil and strife.

[Page 370]

﴿It will be said: "Enter Paradise." He said: "Would that my people knew"﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured.﴾

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'nāf bayānī*, a clause that answers a question the listener would naturally ask) addressing what the listener awaits: learning what he encountered from his people after he confronted them with that forceful address. Did they accept his guidance, or did they turn away from it and abandon him, or did they harm him as the advocates of truth who oppose the whims of the multitude are harmed? The answer is given by what His words ﴿It will be said: "Enter Paradise"﴾ indicate. This is the most important matter for the Muslims, and they are among those intended by the knowledge of such a story, so that their certainty and steadfastness in faith may increase. As for the polytheists, their share of this parable is what has preceded and what comes later in His words ﴿It was but a single cry, and behold, they were extinguished.﴾

In His words ﴿It will be said: "Enter Paradise"﴾ there is an allusion (*kināya*, metonymy or indirect expression) to his being killed as a martyr in exalting the Word of God. This is because placing the command to enter Paradise immediately after his exhortation, without any transition, implies by way of *dalālat al-iqtiḍā'* (implication required by the meaning) that he died and that they killed him for opposing their religion. Some exegetes said: they killed him by stoning. Others said: they burned him. Others said: they dug a pit for him and buried him alive.

This man of faith was admitted into Paradise immediately after his death, because he was among the martyrs, and the martyrs have the distinction of being hastened into Paradise, entering it without delay. In the ḥadīth: "The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise."

The one who says "Enter Paradise" is God, exalted is He.

The one addressed is the man who came from the farthest part of the city. The pronoun of the one addressed was not mentioned with the preposition *lām* because the saying mentioned here is a creative saying (*qawl takwīnī*), whose addressee is not intended; rather, the intent is to narrate its occurrence, since when it occurs its effect occurs, as in His saying ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Naḥl: 40].

Since the parable does not relate that he left the place where he delivered his exhortation, this indicates that he died in that very place. It is understood from this that he died slain at that time or as a result of it.

He pursued this meaning through the way of allusion and did not state explicitly that they killed him, passing over this meaning in regard to the polytheists, lest it gladden them that his people had killed him, so that they make it part of what the parable was struck with, against them and against the Messenger ﷺ, and so that they hope to kill the Messenger ﷺ.

[Page 371]

This allusion is understood only by the people of Islam, among whom the necessary connection between martyrdom in the way of God and entering Paradise is established. As for the polytheists, they suppose that this is in the Hereafter. Eloquent speech may contain subtleties whose benefit is specific to some of the listeners.

The clause ﴿He said: "Would that my people knew"﴾ is also a resumptive explanatory clause, because the listener expects to know what he said when joy overwhelmed him at entering Paradise. The meaning is: entering Paradise did not distract him from the condition of his people; he wished that they would know what he had received from his Lord, so that they would know the excellence of faith and believe. He did not wish their destruction, nor did he gloat over them. Thus he was characterized by restraint of anger and by forbearance toward the ignorant. That is because in the world of realities the soul is directed only to pure goodness, and there is no worth in base shares and trivial matters.

The particle *bi* (with) was introduced before the object of *ya'lamūna* (they know) to imply the meaning of "they would be informed," because there is no hope that they would attain knowledge of that through observation and inference.

The *mā* in His words ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*), meaning: that they would know of the forgiveness of my Lord and His making me among the honoured.

By "the honoured" is meant those upon whom God's honour descends, and they are the angels, the prophets, and the best of the righteous. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 26], meaning the angels and Jesus, peace be upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 30:

﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ This is a tadhyil (concluding summation), and it is part of the speech of Allah, Exalted. It takes the place of lamentation over the nations that denied the messengers, and it encompasses the community intended by the parables that precede it, from His saying ﴿And strike for them a parable: the people of the town﴾ [Ya-Sin: 13], and the continuity of this evil custom among them.

So the definite article in "al-'ibad" (the servants) is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins) used for totality (al-istighraq), and it is an assumed (id'a'i) totality, in which the condition of the majority among the nations to which a messenger comes is taken into account, because in this context there is no objection to the scarcity of those who affirmed the messengers and supported them, so it is as if all of them had denied.

And "al-'ibad" is a name for humankind, and it is the plural of "'abd" (servant). The "'abd" is the one owned (al-mamluk), and all people are servants of Allah, Exalted, because He is their Creator and the One who disposes of them. Allah, Exalted, said ﴿as provision for the servants﴾ [Qaf: 11], and al-Mughira ibn Habna said:

"The servants have become in evil, having no relief except al-Muhallab after Allah, and the rain."

It is pluralized as "'abid" and "'ibad." The first plural has become predominant for "'abd" in the sense of owned slave, and the second plural for "'abd" in the sense of human being, and this is a fine specification in Arabic usage.

And al-hasra (lamentation) is the intensity of regret mixed with grieving over a lost benefit.

Page 8
The particle of address here is merely for alerting to the gravity of what follows, so that the hearer attends to it. Its entry into sentences whose intended meaning is an expression (insha') of a meaning in the speaker's own self, rather than a report, is frequent. Thus the combination of that expression with the particle of alerting is a proclamation of what is in the speaker's self of the implication of the expression, as in the sayings: "ya khaybatan" (O disappointment), "ya la'natan" (O curse), "ya wayli" (O my woe), "ya farhi" (O my joy), "ya laytani" (O would that I), and similar. A woman of Tayy said, from the verses of al-Hamasa:

"O the loss of the youths, when they ascend it, in the belly of al-Shara, like a stallion, bridled and saddled."

And the verse of the Book:

"O curse of Allah upon the peoples, all of them, and the righteous, upon Simʿan from Jar."

The address may occur in such a case with the hamza, as in the saying of Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi:

"Alhafa for the villages of Sahbal, when the calamities and the bold enemy drove against us."

The origin of this address is that the meaning which stirs the expression is treated as a rational being, so the speaker addresses it by name to request its presence, as if he said: "This is your station, so be present," just as one who is intended in a grave matter is called. Then it transfers from that to expressing what has befallen the speaker of need for that one called. Then this became common and widespread until the metaphor and metonymy in it were forgotten, and it became merely an alert to what comes after it, while the concern is present in both states.

This has been mentioned at His saying, Exalted, ﴿O would that I had been with them﴾ [An-Nisa': 73] in Surat an-Nisa', and His saying ﴿O woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend﴾ [Al-Furqan: 28] in Surat al-Furqan.

The occurrence of such a thing in the speech of Allah, Exalted, is a representation of the state of the servants of Allah in their denying the messengers of Allah, by the state of one whom his family laments, having fallen into a destruction from which they wished to spare him.

The clause ﴿no messenger comes to them﴾ is an explanation of the aspect of the lamentation over them, because His saying ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾, although it came after mention of the people of the town, when it generalized over all the servants, there arose an ambiguity regarding the aspect of generality. So its clarification came that all the servants are equal to those who were made into a parable and those for whom the parable was struck, in that state represented, and that the admonitions and the warnings reaching them from the messenger sent to every nation among them, and from observing the generations who denied the messengers and so perished, did not benefit them. Thus the aspect of the lamentation over them became known in general from this verse, and then in detail from His saying after it ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed﴾ [Ya-Sin: 31], etc.

The exception in His saying ﴿but they were mocking him﴾ is an exception of general states (mufarragh) from the pronoun in "ya'tihim" (comes to them); that is, no messenger comes to them in any state of theirs except in the state of their mocking him.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before "yastahzi'un" (they mock) is for emphasis on the messenger, indicating the enormity of mocking him, together with the suitability of the verse-ending (fasila) through this fronting. Thus two purposes were attained from it, one of meaning and one of rhetorical embellishment (badi').

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 31:

﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that they will not return to them?﴾ This sentence is an explanation (bayan) of the sentence ﴿There does not come to them a messenger but that they mock him﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30], because it details the generality (ijmal) that is derived from His saying ﴿There does not come to them a messenger but that they mock him﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30]. The outcome of that mockery of the Messenger was the destruction of those who mocked. Thus, the failure of every nation that denied its messenger to take heed of the fate of the deniers before it stirs regret over them and over their likes, just as their mockery of the Messenger, their lack of insight into his call, his warning, and the proofs of his truthfulness, stirred it.

The pronoun in "yaraw" (they have seen) refers to the servants (al-'ibad), as the coherence of the pronouns requires. The reference in it is a rhetorical generality ('umum idda'i), as was mentioned just before. Therefore, it is necessary to exclude from it the first nation that denied its messenger, namely the people of Noah, for no destruction of a nation that had denied its messenger had preceded them. This is an exclusion by the evidence of reason, because His saying "before them" guides, upon reflection, to the fact that it does not include the first nation to which a messenger was sent.

It has been said that the pronoun of "Have they not seen" may refer to what the pronoun of ﴿And set forth to them a parable﴾ [Ya-Sin: 13] refers to, and the parable would have ended with the sentence ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30] and the verse. This is far-fetched, because it would require that the sentence be conjoined to the sentence "And set forth to them a parable," just as the sentence ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have brought to life﴾ [Ya-Sin: 33] and the verse was conjoined, and the sentence ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37], and the sentence ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41] were conjoined.

Page 10
There is no need for this consideration in the reference, and you have already known the justification of the first consideration for validating the generality.

The interrogation may be a denial (inkari): their heedlessness of the destruction of the generations has been placed in the position of lack of knowledge, so they are rebuked for lack of knowledge of that, which is a known and famous matter. It may also be that the interrogation is confirmatory (taqriri), built upon the negation of knowledge of the destruction of the generations, to exhaust their excuse, so that they have no recourse but to acknowledge that they are doers; their acknowledgment is then more binding upon them, because they asked in the form of a negation, so it was open to them to deny that.

The seeing, under both assumptions, is cognitive (ilmiyya) and not visual (basariyya), because the destruction of the generations was not witnessed by a nation that came after the nation that had been destroyed before it.

The verb of seeing is suspended (mu'allaq) from acting by the presence of kam, because kam, whether it is interrogative or declarative, has the front of the sentence; for the declarative kam is transferred from the interrogative, and what has the front of the sentence does not let what precedes it govern what follows it.

And "kam" is in the position of the accusative by "ahlakna" (We destroyed): its meaning is an ambiguous multitude, explained by His saying "from the generations," and kam occupies the position of the object of "ahlakna."

And "qablahum" (before them) is an adverbial complement (zarf) of "ahlakna," and the meaning of qablahum is: before their existence.

And His saying, "that they to them do not return" is a substitutive of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the sentence "ahlakna," because destruction includes non-return; the verbal noun formed from "an" and what follows it was substituted for the meaning of the sentence ("kam ahlakna qablahum min al-qurun"), because the meaning of that sentence is the multitude of destruction and the multitude of those destroyed. The verb of seeing governs "annahum ilayhim la yarji'un" by way of consequence, due to the dominance of the meaning of the verb over the sentence "kam ahlakna," because suspension voids the action in the wording but not in the locus.

The benefit of this substitution is to fix the depiction of the destruction for the sake of increasing the warning, and to bring that image to mind in the destruction, i.e., a destruction with no hope of return to the world, for what destruction involves of non-return to family and loved ones increases the regret in clarity.

Page 11
And "ilayhim" is connected to "yarji'un" (they return), and its being placed before its complement is for the sake of the rhyme (fasila).
The pronoun in "ilayhim" refers to the servants, and the pronoun in "annahum" refers to the generations.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 32:

﴿And indeed, all of them, they will all be brought before Us.﴾ I see that its conjunction with the clause (﴿that they, to them, do not return﴾ [Ya-Sin: 31]) occupies the position of a precaution (ihtiras) against the assumption of those addressed by the Qur'an that the statement ﴿that they, to them, do not return﴾ [Ya-Sin: 31] confirms their belief in the negation of resurrection (al-ba'th).

The particle (an) may be a lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy (thaqilah) an, and the more eloquent usage is to leave it inoperative (ihmal) regarding what follows it. Most often the predicate of the noun is accompanied by a lam called al-lam al-fariqah (the distinguishing lam), because it distinguishes between the lightened (mukhaffafah) in-, derived from the heavy, and the negating in- (an-nafiyah), so that the affirmative predicate is not confused with the negated predicate, which would contradict the speaker's intention. On this reading, his saying ”lamma“ with a light mim, as Al-Jumhur read (lamma jami'un), is composed of the distinguishing lam and the extra (za'idah) ma for emphasis (li-l-ta'kid). It is also possible that (in) is a negating particle meaning ”la“ (not), and that (lamma) with a heavy mim is a particle of exception (harf istithna') meaning ”illa“ (except), which occurs after negation and similar constructions such as an oath. Likewise Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Abu Ja'far read. The implied sense: ”and not all of them, except they will be brought before Us.“

﴿Kull﴾ (kullun) is the subject (mubtada'), and its tanwin is the tanwin of compensation (tanwin al-'iwad) for what it is annexed to (kull), i.e., all the generations (kull al-qurun), or all of those mentioned among the generations and those addressed.

﴿Jami'﴾ (jami') is a noun on the pattern fa'il, meaning majmu' (gathered), and is the opposite of scattered (mutafarriq). It is said: "he gathered things together" (jam'a ashya'a kadha) when he made them close and connected after they had been dispersed and distant.

The meaning: all the generations will be brought before Us gathered together, i.e., their bringing is not at different times nor in multiple places. Thus the word ﴿kull﴾ conveys that the bringing encompasses them such that no group escapes from them, and the word ﴿jami'﴾ conveys that they are brought together, so neither of the two words is sufficient without mention of the other. Do you not see that if it were said: "And indeed most of them, when all of them are brought before Us," there would be a contradiction between most of them and all of them; i.e., most of them come gathered together. So ﴿jami'﴾ is raised as a predicate in the reading with light ”lamma“, and as an exception in the reading with heavy ”lamma“.

﴿Muhdarun﴾ is an adjective (na't) of ﴿jami'﴾ in both readings. The adjective took into account the meaning of the modified noun, so the plural marker was attached to it, as in the verse of Labid:

"They were emptied, and there were in them the gathered ones, so they set out early from them, and their threshold and thumam were left behind."

The bringing (al-ihdar) is the bringing for reckoning, recompense and punishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 33:

"﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have revived it and brought forth from it grain, so from it they eat.﴾" It is connected (ʿuṭifa) to the story of (﴿And present to them a parable: the companions of the town﴾ [Yasin: 13]), for it presents a parable of the state of their aversion and their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), and what that state includes of association (shirk), denial of the Resurrection (al-baʿth), and harm to the Messenger (ﷺ), together with the consequence of all of that. Then this detailed account followed in order to refute what those beliefs included, namely the denial of the Resurrection and of associating partners with Allah.

It began with an indication of the nearness of the Resurrection, due to the transition from His saying ﴿And indeed, all of them will be brought before Us, present﴾ [Yasin: 32], on the basis that these signs are not free of their indication that Allah alone has disposal over affairs, and in that is an affirmation of His Oneness (tawhid al-wahdaniyya).

"Sign" (āya) is the subject (mubtadaʾ); "for them" (lahum) is a qualifier of "sign"; "the earth" (al-arḍ) is the predicate of "sign"; and "dead" (al-mayyita) is a qualifier of "the earth."

The clause "We have revived it" (aḥyaynāhā) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the earth," and it is a restricted circumstantial clause, because the reviving of the earth is the basis for the indication of the possibility of resurrection after death. Or the clause "We have revived it" may be an explanation (bayān) of the clause "﴿and a sign for them is the earth﴾," clarifying the place of the sign within it; or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from the clause "﴿and a sign for them is the earth﴾"; or an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), as if a questioner had asked: "How was the dead earth?"

Page 13
The death of the earth is its drying and barrenness due to its being devoid of plant life within it, and its reviving is the emergence of plants from it, of herbage, pasture and crops.

Nafiʿ and Abu Jaʿfar read "al-mayyita" with a doubled yāʾ (shadda). The rest read it with a single yāʾ (takhfif). The meaning is one, and the two are equivalent in usage.

"Al-habb" is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) of ḥabba, which is the seed of a plant, such as a grain of wheat or barley. It was discussed earlier at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿like a grain that grows seven ears﴾, in Surat al-Baqara.

The bringing forth of the grain from the earth means bringing it out from its vegetation, so it came from it through an intermediary. This is an interweaving (idmāj) of a favour (imtinān) within the course of the argument, and for this reason ﴿so from it they eat﴾ is connected to it by fāʾ. The placing of "from it" before "they eat" is for emphasis, drawing attention to the blessing, and for the sake of the rhyme of the verse (riʿāyat al-fāṣila).

[Page 14 header not translated]

﴿And We made in it gardens of palm trees and grapevines, and We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾ ﴿so that they may eat of its fruit, and what their hands have made. Will they not then be thankful?﴾ This is from the revival of the earth by causing trees bearing fruit to grow. This revival is more wondrous and more lasting, although the revival by the growth of grain and herbage is clearer as a sign, because it comes about quickly.

The gardens were mentioned earlier, at the beginning of Surat al-Ra'd.

The gushing of springs was discussed earlier, at His saying, ﴿And indeed, among stones are some from which rivers burst forth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-thamar (fruit), with two fatḥas or with two ḍammas, refers to what palm trees and grapevines yield, of kinds of fruit and kinds of grapes. The thamarah (single fruit) stands to the fruit as the grain (ḥabb) stands to the spike (sunbulah). The majority of readers recited ﴿thamarihi﴾ with two fatḥas. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf recited it with two ḍammas.

Al-nakhīl (palm trees) is a collective noun (ism jam') of nakhl.

Al-a'nāb is the plural of 'inab, which is applied both to the grapevine plant and to its fruit. The plurality of al-nakhīl and al-a'nāb is considered in terms of the multiplicity of kinds of their fruit-bearing trees, hence the plural "kinds" of its fruit.

The pronoun in ﴿min thamarihi﴾ refers to what has been mentioned, meaning: from the fruit of what we have mentioned, as in the saying of Ru'bah:

*In it are streaks of black and white,*
*as if, on the skin, it were the spreading of white leprosy.*

It was said to him: "Why did you not say, *kaannahā* (as if it)?" He said: "I meant *ka'anna dhālika* (as if that), woe to you." This was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68], in Surat al-Baqarah.

It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the palm trees, while the grapevines are left unmentioned, since it is known that they are like the palm trees. As in the saying of al-Azraq ibn Ṭarafah ibn al-'Amūd al-Qarā'iyy al-Bāhilī:

*He threw me with a sin, of which I was guilty, while my father*
*was innocent, and because of the well he threw me.*

He did not say *barī'ayn* (two innocent ones), since it is known that his father was like him.

It is also permissible for *mā* in His saying ﴿wa mā 'amilathu aydīhim﴾ to be a relative pronoun (ma-mawṣūlah) coordinated with *thamarihi*, meaning: "that they may eat of the fruit of what their hands have made." In that case it becomes an interpolation (idmāj) that guides to tending the gardens through labour, watering and care, so that their yield is more abundant. The pronoun in *'amilathu* on this reading refers to the relative pronoun.

It is also permissible for *mā* to be negative, and the pronoun refers to what has been mentioned of grain, palm trees and grapevines. The meaning is: that they did not create those things. This is more emphatic in expressing divine favour and more suited to the context of the verse, which is in the manner of an argument (istidlāl).

The majority recited ﴿wa mā 'amilathu﴾ with the pronoun-suffix *hā'* (-hu), referring to what has been mentioned of grain, palm trees and grapevines. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Abū Bakr (from 'Āṣim) and Khalaf recited ﴿wa mā 'amilat﴾ without the *hā'*, and it is likewise written so in the Kufan codex. This is in accordance with the omission of the object when it is known.

It is also permissible that the omission of the object is for the purpose of generality. The estimated meaning is: "and what their hands made of any of that, anything." Both omissions are common.

Upon this is based the interrogative of denial (istifhām al-inkār), because they did not thank Him, by taking rivals to Him who brought into being this wondrous creation.

The imperfect verb was used to emphasise their disbelief, since God deserves that they repeatedly thank Him; so how do they persist in associating others with Him?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 36:

﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of what they do not know.﴾ This is an interjected statement (i'tiraD) placed between the clause ﴿And a sign for them is the earth﴾ [Ya-Sin: 33] and the clause ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37]. What prompted it was the mention of the reviving of the earth and the bringing forth of grain and trees from it, for in that there are states and a wondrous origination that reminds one of the magnifying of the One who deposited these crafts with His wisdom. Thus the argument from the creation of pairs is included in passing (idmaj).

Here "Subhana" (Glory be) is used to create the declaration of God's exaltation (tanzih) above the states of the polytheists, an exaltation above everything unfitting to His divinity, the greatest of which is associating partners with Him, and this is the intended meaning here.

The use of the relative pronoun (alladhi) with the Exalted Essence serves to indicate the basis for the declaration of exaltation and magnification. The discussion of "Subhana" has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah and elsewhere. "Al-azwaj" is the plural of "zawj," which is applied to each of the male and female of animals, and "zawj" is also applied to the meaning of a category distinguished by its properties among existing things, by analogy with the category of male and the category of female, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53], which has passed in Surat Ta-Ha. The first usage is the more common, as is taken from the words of al-Raghib, and it is the one that fits the transfer of the word from the "zawj" that is a second member for another. It is therefore permissible to understand "al-azwaj" in this verse in the first meaning, so that it is a reminder of the creation of the kinds of animals, of which there are male and female, and "min" in the three places is then initial (ibtida'iyyah), related to the verb "khalaqa" (created).

صفحة ١٦
This is an inclusion (idmaj) of the mention of another of the signs of the sole creation, for the creation of animals with the powers within them for their reproduction, the protection of their species and the production of their benefits, is the most delicate of creations in workmanship and the deepest in wisdom, and the most closely bound to the favour upon man, in that the benefits of animals were made for him, as in the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun. For this reason it was singled out among the other creations by being joined to glorifying its Creator, as an honouring of its status and a varied recounting of the greatest of the offspring arising from the origination of the power of life in the earth and the emergence of the kinds and categories of living beings from it, as the beginning with the mention of "what the earth grows" before anything else of the beginnings of creation indicates; for it is the earliest in forming the materials of animal life, since the male and female come into being from the sperm, and the sperm comes into being from the powers of the foods obtained from consuming plants. This is the meaning of His words ﴿of what the earth grows, and of themselves﴾, that is, and of what comes into being in them from their animal parts.

The pronoun of the plural of rational beings is used by way of giving precedence (taghlib) to the human species, given that it is the one intended by the lesson of this verse, and in order to arrive at specifying it with the lesson in His words ﴿and of what they do not know﴾.

The indication of His words, exalted is He, ﴿and of what they do not know﴾ points to secrets deposited in the creation of the kinds and categories of animals, which are what distinguished their species from one another, and distinguished their categories and males from their females, and deposited in them the spirit by which they are distinguished from plants, through the governing of their affairs according to the readiness of each species and each category, until it reaches the highest of the species in ascent, which is the human species. So the meaning of ﴿of what they do not know﴾ is: of what they do not know in detail, though they may perceive it in general, for the one who reflects knows that among created things there are hidden secrets whose understanding has not reached the grasp of their essence. Among these is the spirit, for God, exalted is He, has said ﴿Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾ [al-Isra': 85].

People may differ in grasping some of those properties, in general and in detail, and then be equal in not knowing others. Some groups or generations may be distinguished by knowing something of the subtleties of creation through discovery, experiment, or tracing traces that others did not know, and then they are equal in what remains concealed beneath the veil of hiddenness among the subtleties of formation. Through this general awareness of them, they were counted within the consideration of the sign of the creation of pairs from all directions. If "al-azwaj" in His words ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ is understood in the second meaning of this word, namely its application to categories and kinds, as in His words ﴿So We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53], then "min" in the three places is explanatory (bayaniyyah), and what follows it is in the sense of an explanatory apposition or a detailed substitute for the general "al-azwaj." The meaning is: all the pairs, which are: what the earth grows, and themselves, and what they do not know. His words ﴿and of what they do not know﴾ indicate an omitted element whose estimate is: and what they do know, and this is by the indication of allusion.

He singled out the kinds of plants for mention because by them is the sustenance of people's livelihood and the livelihood of their livestock and beasts, and the categories of human beings themselves, because the lesson in them is stronger. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]. Then He mentioned what encompasses the creatures, of what people know and what they do not know, across the different regions, generations and ages.

He placed the mention of plants first, giving it precedence in importance in this context, because it is more akin to the resurrection to which His words ﴿And all of them, will they all be brought before Us, assembled﴾ [Ya-Sin: 32] alluded.

The repetition of the particle "min" after the conjunction waw is for emphasis according to both interpretations.

The pronoun in "anfusihim" refers to the servants in His words ﴿Alas for the servants﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30], and what is meant by them are those who deny the Messenger (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 37:

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾ This is a transition to pointing out, through the manifest phenomena of the worlds, the fine order of creation in them, as is indicated by observation combined with reflection.

Beginning with it, the order of night and day is mentioned, because its occurrence repeats before the observation of every beholder. The phrase ﴿نَسْلَخُ مِنهُ النَّهارَ﴾ (naslakh minhu al-nahar, "We strip from it the day") admits all the aspects that we mentioned in the phrase "We have revived them" just before.

Al-salkh (stripping) is the removal of the skin from its animal. Its verb transitively reaches the skin that is removed directly, as the object. For this reason, the skin removed from the body of an animal is called silkh (with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam), meaning maslukh (stripped off). The body from which the skin has been removed is not called silkh. The verb salakha reaches the body from which the skin has been removed by means of the preposition, and most commonly it is with (min) of origin, but it also reaches with the preposition ʿan ("from"), because the stripping involves the meaning of separation and passing beyond after connection.

So the object of "naslakh" here is, without doubt, al-nahar (the day). The stripping has been transferred to the pronoun of the night by means of "min", so the meaning becomes: the night is a sign for them in the state of removing the covering of the light of day from it, so that the night remains over them. Thus the day is likened to the skin of a sheep or the like that covers what is beneath it, just as the day covers the darkness of the night in the morning. The uncovering and removal of the day is likened to the stripping of the skin from a sheep or the like, so the night is in the position of the body from which the skin has been stripped. The night is not itself the intended element of the comparison; rather, what is intended is likening the departure of the day from it, and this entails that the night remains like the body from which the skin has been removed. The basis of this is that darkness is the original state of the worlds before God created the luminous bodies that emit light; for darkness is a privation and light is an existence, and the existents were in darkness before God created the luminous stars and conveyed their light to the bodies that receive it, such as the earth and the moon.

And if darkness is the original state of existents, it does not follow that it is the original state of the earth, because the apparent view is that the earth separated from the sun luminous, and the darkness of one half of the terrestrial globe when the light of the sun overtakes it is considered like a body overtaken by its skin; so when the light is removed the darkness returns, and this is likened to the stripping of the skin from an animal, as He said, exalted is He, in its counterpart in Surah al-Ra'd: ﴿يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهارَ﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3].

Thus there is no evidence in the verse that the original condition of the terrestrial world is darkness; rather, it presents to people a reflection and an indication through a state observed by them, and it follows it with ﴿فَإذا هم مُظْلِمُونَ﴾ (fa-idha hum muzlimun, "behold, they are in darkness") based on what is commonly known.

The masters of rhetoric (ā'immat al-balaghah) have considered the metaphor in the verse to be an original, inherited metaphor (istiʿarah aslīyah taba'iyyah), and they did not make it an allegorical metaphor (tamthiliyyah), for the reason we have already presented: the intended element of the comparison is the state of the departure of the light of day from the horizon, which is succeeded by the darkness of night, by His saying ﴿فَإذا هم مُظْلِمُونَ﴾.

The attribution of muzlimun to the people is from the attribution of the verb of the form af'ala, in which the hamza indicates entry into a state, like asbaha and amsa ("they entered the morning" and "they entered the evening").

[Page 19]

﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ The word "the sun" (al-shams) may be in conjunction (ʿaṭf) with "the night" in His words ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾ [Yasin: 37], as the conjunction of a single noun with a single noun, and a predicate similar to the predicate of "the night" is to be supplied for it. The sense is: "And the sun is a sign for them." The clause "runs" (tajri) would then be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the sun," like the clause ﴿from which We strip away the day﴾ [Yasin: 37].

It may also be a conjunction of clause with clause, with His words "runs" being a predicate about "the sun." In either case, it is an elaboration (tafṣīl) of the general statement in ﴿And a sign for them is the night, from which We strip away the day﴾ [Yasin: 37], and so on, as is indicated by His later words ﴿nor can the night outstrip the day﴾ [Yasin: 40]. The apparent requirement of its being an elaboration would be that it not be conjoined, so that one would say: "The sun runs to a resting place for it." But the apparent requirement was departed from because this elaboration contains a particular sign, namely the sign of the movement of the sun and the moon.

The admonition about the sign of the night and the day was placed first for the reason we mentioned there, so the sign of the sun mentioned here is intended as another proof of the great craftsmanship of God, exalted is He, namely the order of the seasons.

The clause ﴿runs to a resting place for it﴾ admits the aspects we mentioned in the clause "We have given it life" (aḥyaynāhā), namely that it is a circumstantial clause, or an explanation (bayān) of the clause "a sign for them," or a comprehensive substitution (badal ishtimāl) from "a sign."

The literal meaning of running (jary) is the swift movement of creatures with legs. It was applied figuratively to the movement of a body from place to place with rapid movement relative to the movement of similar bodies. This application became common until it became equal to the literal meaning, and it is intended here to mean movement across very widely separated distances, which it covers in a short time relative to the distance of the earth around the sun. This is an argument from the well-known traces of that movement, known to people in a general way through what they reckon of time and the lengthening of night and day. This is the knowledge of those who have special knowledge through observing its states, who watch its stations of movement called the twelve zodiacal signs (burūj), and which is known in detail and by proof to the people of astronomical science (ʿilm al-hayʾa). All of these are addressed to take heed according to what their knowledge has reached.

"Al-mustaqarr" is the place of settling, that is, the place of rest or its time. The sīn and tāʾ in it are for emphasis, like "istajāba" meaning "ajāba" (he answered).

[Page 20]

The lām in "li-mustaqarrin" may be the lām of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) in its apparent sense, that is, it runs in order that it might settle, that is, in order that its running might come to an end, just as the traveller's journey ends when he reaches his place and settles there. It is connected to "runs" as its终 limit (nihāya), since the movement of the sun has as its limit its cessation, so cessation was treated as if it were the cause, as one says: "Beget for death and build for ruin."

Treating a limit as if it were a cause is used in speech, and among its examples is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. The meaning is that it moves a continuous movement, observed, until it reaches concealment from sight.

The lām may also carry the sense of "to" (ilā), that is, it runs to the place of its settling, which is the place of setting. Its setting out of sight is likened to the resting place and refuge to which a person returns at the end of the day after his labours.

This approximation has been transmitted in the hadith of Abu Dharr al-Harawi, in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhari and Muslim and the Jamiʿ of al-Tirmidhi, with various narrations whose general arrangement is that he said: "I was with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the mosque at sunset, and I asked him, or he said: 'This [sun] runs until it reaches its resting place beneath the Throne, and then it falls down in prostration. It remains thus until it is said to it: Rise up, return from where you came. So it returns and rises at dawn from its place of rising. Then it runs until it reaches its resting place beneath the Throne, and it falls down in prostration, and it remains thus until it is said to it: Rise up, return from where you came, so it returns and rises at dawn from its place of rising. Then it runs, and people find nothing strange in it, until it reaches that resting place beneath the Throne, and it is said to it: Rise up, rise at dawn from your west, so it rises at dawn from its west. That is its resting place, and its resting place is beneath the Throne.' That is the meaning of His words: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it.﴾"

This is an illustration and approximation of the daily movement of the sun, which begins with its rising over part of the spherical earth and ends with its setting over part of the earth, along fine lines, and by the repetition of its rising and setting the solar year is formed.

The place to which its movement ends has been described as "beneath the Throne." It is a specific direction which people have no way of knowing. It is the limit of the distance of its daily movement. At that point its movement ceases at the moment of cessation, which is when it rises from its west. That is when the movement of the earth around its ray ceases, because the motion of the bodies that follow its order ceases in consequence of the cessation of its own motion. That is the end of the persistence of this worldly knowledge.

The lām in His words "for it" (la-hā) is the lām of particularity (lām al-ikhtiṣāṣ), and it is a description of "mustaqarr." The construction was turned away from making "mustaqarr" an annexed noun (idāfa) to a pronoun for the sun, which would have made the lām unnecessary, to using the lām, so that "mustaqarr" could be indefinite in a way that signals the magnification of that resting place.

The words of the Prophet (ﷺ) here are an illustration of the states of sunset and sunrise in the daily cycle. The prostration of the sun was made an illustration of its subjection to God's subjugating it, just as speech was made an illustration of this in the verse ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: Come willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly﴾ [Fussilat: 11].

Know that His words "for a resting place for it" are an embedding (idmāj) of instruction within reminder, and it is not part of the sign of the sun for people, because people are not aware of it. It is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿That a specified term may be fulfilled﴾ [al-Anʿam: 60], following the expression of favour with His words: ﴿It is He who takes you back to Himself at night, and knows what you have committed by day; then He raises you up in it, that a specified term may be fulfilled; then to Him is your return﴾ [al-Anʿam: 60].

The demonstrative in ﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾ refers to what has been mentioned, either from His words ﴿And the sun runs﴾, that is, that running, or from it and from His words ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾ [Yasin: 37], that is, that which has been mentioned of the alternation of night and day.

The mention of the two attributes "the Almighty, the All-Knowing" corresponds to the meanings of the two in their relation to the order of the movement of the stars. Might suits the subjugation of this great star, and knowledge suits the wondrous and precise order. Its detailed treatment was given earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Furqan: 61], in Surat al-Furqan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 39:

﴿And the moon — We have determined for it phases, until it returns like the old dried-up stalk of a palm bunch.﴾

"Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Rawh from Ya'qub read (wal-qamaru) with a nominative ending (raf'), so it is either coordinated with "wa al-shamsu tajri" (and the sun runs) as a coordination of single words (ʿaṭf al-mufradāt), or it is a subject (mubtada') and the coordination is a coordination of clauses (ʿaṭf al-jumal)."

Page 22

"The clause qaddarnahu is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a predicate (khabar). Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, Ruways from Ya'qub, and Khalaf read (al-qamara) with a accusative ending (naṣb) as a case of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with the pronoun), so it is then a coordination of clauses."

The explanation of the "manazil" (phases) of the moon has already preceded at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He determined for it phases that you may know the number of years and the calculation﴾ [Yunus: 5] in Surat Yunus.

Taqdir (determination) is applied to making things with measure and firm order, and it is applied to fixing the quantity of something whose amount is sought to be known, such as the determination of times and the determination of quantities of things that are weighed or counted. Both senses are intended here. Indeed God determined for the sun and the moon the order of their courses, and by that He determined the reckoning of the seasons of the year, the months, the days and the nights.

The verb "qaddarna" is transitive to the pronoun of (al-qamar), which is a reference to its essence, whereas the determination is actually for its movement. But the determination was transferred to the name of its essence without mentioning the omitted noun, as an intensification of the movement's inseparability from it from the time of its creation, until it is as if the determination of its movement were the determination of its essence.

"Manazil" is in the accusative of place (ẓarfiyya makaniyya), like "sirtu amyalan" (I traveled miles), meaning: We determined its movement through phases, by whose movement it moves from one phase to another.

"Ḥattā" is initial (ibtida'iyya), meaning it is not a preposition, since what follows it is a clause. The meaning of limit (ghāya) never leaves "ḥattā," so the meaning of limit in it indicates an omitted goal, for a limit requires the beginning of something. The estimate: its light began and started to increase on a small night, then it began to diminish until it returned, that is, became like the old palm stalk, that is, similar to it.

It was expressed by this comparison because the light of the moon at the ends of its nights has no name by which it is known, unlike the first parts of its light, called the crescent (hilal), and because this comparison resembles its state at its beginning as it resembles its state at its end.

"'Ada" with the meaning of "ṣāra" (became): its shape to the viewer is like the stalk.

The ʿurjūn is the stalk that the palm tree produces, with the fruit at its end, and it is what remains attached to the palm after the cutting of the kibāsa from it, and the kibāsa is the cluster of date-stalks.

Page 23

The qadīm is the withered one, because when the fruit is cut off it curves, turns yellow and shrivels, so it resembles the form of what faces the earth of the moon's light at the end of the nights of the month and at the first night of it. The structure "﴿returned like the old palm stalk﴾" suits the moon's form on the last night, which is followed by the conjunction (muhāq), and its form on the first night of the month, which is the crescent (hilal).

The explanation of the moon's course and its phases has been elaborated for them, because they used to master its knowledge, unlike the course of the sun.
