**Ibn ʿĀshūr's commentary on Sūrah Yā-Sīn (36), verse 40:**

﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each is swimming in an orbit.﴾

When the mention of the sun and the moon came up in the context of the signs that point to God's sole act of creating and governing, and to the attributes of His divinity, among which is the connection of the attribute of power to the sign of the sun and its motion, and of the moon and its motion (some theologians called these "attributes of acts," ṣifāt al-afʿāl), and the people knew that the sun and the moon come close together as seen by observers, and they estimated their motion by means of constellations marked by star-signs, called *burūj* (zodiacal signs) in relation to the motion of the sun, and called *manāzil* (lunar mansions) in relation to the motion of the moon, and they knew how very close the lunar mansions are to the solar signs, since each sign is aligned with two or three mansions, and some of the mansion-stars are parts of the stars of the signs, God increased them in insight and instruction by showing that the sun has a motion that does not meet the motion of the moon, and the moon has a motion that does not meet the motion of the sun, and neither of them passes along the paths of the other's course; and that what appears to people of the closeness of the sun and the moon in one atmosphere and in two comparable sizes, and what appears to them of the closeness of the stars of the solar signs and the stars of the lunar mansions, is nothing but a deception of the eyes and a variation in the apparent magnitudes between the bodies and the distances.

The great sphere, like the sun, appears close in size to the sphere of the moon, and this is only due to the vast distances. The distances of the sun's orbit exceed the distances of the moon's orbit by hundreds of millions of miles, so that the sun's size appears to us close to the size of the moon.

God thus made clear that He has arranged the motion of the sun and the moon in an order that makes it impossible for either of the two spheres to reach the other, because of the great distances between their orbits.

[Page 24 ends.]

The meaning of ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ is the negation of its being fitting (*inbighāʾ*) for this, that is, the negation of its occurrence. This is because *inbaghā* is the reflexive form (*muṭāwiʿ*) of *baghā*, which means "to seek." So *inbaghā* indicates that a thing was sought and it came to the one who sought it; one says *baghāhu fa-inbaghā lahu* ("he sought it for him and it became fitting for him"). Thus the affirmation of *inbighāʾ* indicates the ability to attain a thing, and does not imply obligation; and the negation of *inbighāʾ* indicates the negation of its possibility, and for this reason it is used as a euphemism for what is forbidden. One says: *lā yanbaghī laka kadhā* ("it is not fitting for you to do such-and-such"). So distinguish between your saying *yanbaghī an lā tafʿala kadhā* and your saying *lā yanbaghī laka an tafʿala kadhā*. God the Exalted said:

﴿They said: Glory be to You, it was not for us to take any protectors besides You﴾ [al-Furqān 25:18]. The Exalted also said: ﴿It is not for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam 19:92], which occurred in Sūrat Maryam, and among the same usage is His saying: ﴿We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him﴾ [Yā-Sīn 36:69], in this same sūrah.

*Idrāk* (overtaking) means catching up with and reaching the goal. So His saying "an tudrika" ("that it overtake") is the subject (*fāʿil*) of *yanbaghī*. The sentence therefore conveys the negation of the fitness of the sun's overtaking the moon. The meaning is the negation that the sun should collide with the moon, contrary to what appears from the closeness of their lunar and solar stations; for that is due to alignment (*musāmatah*), not to actual approach.

The formulation of this in the form of a statement about the subject with a verbal predicate serves to strengthen the force of the negation, for that is more emphatic in denying it than if it had been said: "It is not fitting for the sun to overtake the moon."

Opening the sentence with the particle of negation before mentioning the negated verb, so that the negation becomes more firmly established in the hearer's mind, is stronger than if it had been said: "The sun, it is not fitting for it to overtake the moon." Thus in His saying ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ there are two distinctive features.

When He mentioned the sun and the moon, and the sun was associated in human imagination with the day, and the moon with the night, and there were benefits for people in the order of night and day, the mention of the order of the sun and the moon was inserted in the course of reflecting on the order of night and day. The meaning of ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ is that the night does not escape the day; so *sabq* here means escape and deliverance, as in the verse of Murrah ibn ʿAddāʾ al-Faqʿasī:

*"As if you had never been outstripped by time, once you attain what you were seeking."*

[Page 25 begins.]

And His saying the Exalted in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outstrip Us?﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 29:4]. The meaning is that the withdrawal of the day over the night is a matter subjected to order, and the night has no means of lagging behind it.

It does not suit the interpretation of *sabq* here to take its well-known meaning, which is precedence in motion, because that cannot be conceived in the alternation of night and day; nor that the meaning of *sabq* is the precedence of creation (its beginning), since no important purpose in the verse is connected with that. Moreover, the normal state is that darkness is prior in creation.

The purpose is to remind of the blessing of the night and the blessing of the day, for each of them has benefits for people. If one of them were to escape from the other and settle on the horizon, many great benefits of human and animal life would be disrupted.

There is an elliptical element in the speech; that is, the implied meaning is: "Nor does the moon overtake the sun, nor does the day outstrip the night."

His saying ﴿each is swimming in an orbit﴾ is coordinated (*ʿuṭifa*) to the clause ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾. The conjunction *wāw* is coordinating, giving preference to the informative aspect of this fact over the aspect of a concluding summation (*tadhyīl*); otherwise the proper form of a concluding summation would be disjunction (*faṣl*) without a conjunction.

What the word "kull" ("each") is attached to is omitted, and the nunation (*tanwīn*) of "kull" is the nunation of compensation for the omitted genitive, so the estimate is: "and each of the stars."

The context is reinforced by the plural pronoun in His saying "yasbaḥūn" ("they swim"), even though the previously mentioned items are two things and not many things. By this generalization the sentence takes on the function of a concluding summation.

*Falak* (orbit) is the imagined circle assumed to lie in the atmospheric void along which one of the stars moves in a regular course without deviating from it. When the early astronomers observed these paths and found them unchanging, and found that their ends join their beginnings, they imagined them as curved paths along which the stars travel, just as a ball rolls on the ground. Sometimes they went further in imagining and thought of them as solid tracks on which the stars rest in their motion, dragged by chains and hooks; and this was the belief of the Copts in Egypt.

[Page 26 begins.]

The Arabs called those paths *aflāk* (orbits), and the singular *falak* they derived from the name of the spindle-whorl (*falkat al-mighzal*), which is a rod with a round, flattened wooden disc at its top, like a large apple, on which a woman winds the threads of yarn she spins, turning it with her palms. The threads wind around it, so they imagined the orbit as a spherical body, and imagined the stars placed upon it, turning with its rotation. For this reason they measured time by the motion of the orbit, and they named the interval between the beginnings of the two periods [the span] until it returns to where the orbit's revolution began. But the Qur'ān went along with them in the linguistic term, because that is the limit of the language and most suitable for what they imagined, with His saying "yasbaḥūn" (they swim). Thus it became invalid that the bodies of the stars are attached to their orbits, and it follows from their being swimmers that their paths of motion are imaginary circles, because *sabḥ* here is swimming in the air, not in water, and in the air no lines or furrows are drawn.

The plural pronoun in "yasbaḥūn" is used although the two things previously mentioned are the sun and the moon, because the purpose is to convey the generalization of this judgment to the sun, the moon, and all the stars; and this is a scientific truth that the Qur'ān preceded.

The clause "kullun fī falak" ("each in an orbit") contains the rhetorical feature called *ṭard wa-ʿaks* (reversibility), for it can be read from its end as it is read from its beginning.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. And We created for them of its likeness that which they ride. And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout (of rescue) for them, nor are they saved, except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time."

This is a transition from enumerating signs in the earth and in the heavens to enumerating a sign in the sea, one that combines admonition and favor: the sign of the ship's being made to travel upon the water, and of the water's being made to bear it up so that it does not sink.

God has reminded people of a great sign that became so well known that it was as if they had witnessed it: the inspiration given to Noah to build the ark, so that it would carry the people who believed and carry from every kind of animal a pair, in order to save the species from destruction and extinction by drowning in the event of the Flood. Since this sign served the purpose of carrying pairs of animal kinds, the sign itself was made to be the carrying, as an incorporation of the favor within the admonition. It is as though it were said: "And a sign for them is the building of the ship, so that We might carry their offspring in it, and so We carried them."

The verb "carry" (ḥamalnā) is used figuratively, in the sense of rescue from drowning, by way of the figure of speech called al-majāz al-mursal (metonymy), based on the relationship of cause and effect: that is, "We rescued their offspring from drowning by carrying them in the ship at the time of the Flood."

Al-dhurriyyāt (the offspring) is the plural of dhurriyyah, which means the descendants of a human being.

Al-fulk al-mashḥūn (the laden ship) is the one known among people from the story of the Flood. Here it is singular, as indicated by the qualifier, and the qualifier is in the masculine form, al-mashḥūn, not al-mashḥūnah, as in His saying: ﴿And you see the ships therein plowing [the waves]﴾ [Fāṭir: 12]. It is the ship of Noah, which became well known by this description in the Qur'an, as in Sūrat al-Shu'arā': ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 119]. No ship other than Noah's is described by this description.

The transitive construction of "carried" (ḥamalnā) with the offspring as its object is a figurative extension of the object, and it is a rational metaphor (majāz 'aqlī). A rational metaphor is not confined to the predicate; rather, the figure lies in the attachment. The thing carried is in fact the origins of the offspring, not the offspring themselves together with their origins being associated with it.

Since the offspring of the addressees are among those whom God willed to remain on the earth when He commanded Noah to build the ship to save the species, and commanded him to carry pairs of people, they are the ones from whom humankind was generated after the Flood. He made all of humankind as though they were carried in the laden ship in the time of Noah. Mention of the offspring implies, by way of kināya (implicature), that their origins were carried, for the sake of brevity in speech, and that they themselves were carried likewise. It is as though it were said: "We carried their origins, and We carried them, and We carried their offspring," since, had the origins not been saved, the offspring would not have come into being. The wisdom in carrying the origins was the survival of the offspring, so the blessing encompassed all. This is like the favor in His saying: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 11], ﴿that We might make it for you a reminder﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 12].

The pronoun in "their offspring" (dhurriyyātihim) refers to the same thing to which the pronoun in "for them" refers, namely the servants, meaning the polytheists of Makkah, but here they are considered under the heading of their being part of humankind. The meaning is: "A sign for them: that We carried the offspring of humankind in Noah's ship, at the time when God commanded Noah to carry in it his family and those of his people who believed, for the survival of the offspring of humankind. That was a carrying of their offspring, as it continued in succession, as has been mentioned just above."

This is the interpretation of this verse. Al-Qurṭubī said: "It is among the most difficult things in the sūrah." Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: "Some people have confused matters to the point of saying that dhurriyyah is applied to the forefathers. This is not known from the language." It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring﴾ [al-A'rāf: 172], in Sūrat al-A'rāf.

Nāfi' and Ibn 'Āmir read dhurriyyātihim with the plural form. The rest read it without the alif, in the form of a collective noun; the meaning is the same.

From the indication of His saying "that We carried their offspring," both explicitly and by implicature, it is understood that this sign is continuing for every observer, since they witness their voyages and the voyages of their like upon the sea, especially the inhabitants of the shores and coasts, such as the people of Jeddah and Yanbu', as they travel to the lands of Yemen and the lands of Abyssinia. Thus it is understood that We carried, and We carry, and We will carry their forefathers, themselves, and their offspring. Ṭarafah described ships in his Mu'allaqah.

The clause ﴿And We created for them of its likeness that which they ride﴾ is a parenthetical insertion within the discussion of the sign of the sea, required by the principle of correspondence (murā'āt al-naẓīr), as a reminder of the blessing of the creation of camels suitable for journeys. Thus the sign of the inspiration to build the ship is related in respect of the great wisdom in the inspiration, the subjection of the sea to it, and its existence at the time of need for preserving the species. For this reason, in its regard, the verb of creation specific to bringing into existence was not used, unlike the making of people. The sign of taking mounts is related with the verb khalaqnā. A parallel to this comparison is His saying: ﴿and He made for you of the ships and the cattle that which you ride﴾. So what is meant by "that which they ride" here is specifically the mounts, because they are the ones that resemble the ship in being made capable of crossing sands, just as the ship was made suitable for traversing seas. The Arabs also called mounts "the ships of the land." The "min" in "of its likeness" is explanatory (bayāniyyah), with the explanation placed before the thing explained, which is permissible according to the more correct view; or it is emphatic (mu'akkidah), and its object originally is a circumstantial modifier of the relative "mā" in "that which they ride." What is meant is similarity in greatness, strength of carrying, continuity of travel, and also in form.

The clause ﴿And if We will, We drown them﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾, in view of its implicatory indication of the continuation of this sign and this favor, as a reminder that God, who bestowed favor upon them, if He wills, can make what is a blessing for people into a punishment for them, for a wisdom that He knows. This follows the Qur'an's custom of following encouragement with warning and the reverse, so that people neither become insolent through blessing nor despair of mercy.

Evidence for this is that in this clause the present tense is used, in a conditional context, purely because it refers to the future. This is like His saying: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the earth to swallow you on the side of the land or send against you a storm of stones, then you will not find for yourselves a guardian?﴾ [al-Isrā': 68], ﴿Or do you feel secure that He will not return you to it another time and send against you a hurricane of wind and drown you for what you disbelieved, then you will not find for yourselves against Us any pursuer?﴾ [al-Isrā': 69].

Al-ṣarīkh is the one who cries out, the one who seeks help and calls for rescue. The Arabs say: "The one crying out came to them," meaning the afflicted one who seeks rescue so that they might save him; it is the form fa'īl in the sense of fā'il. Al-ṣarīkh is also applied to the helper, in the form fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl, because when the one seeking help cries out to the one who rescues, the rescuer cries back responding with what reassures him of victory. The words of Salāmah ibn Jandal, recited by al-Mubarrad in al-Kāmil, combine both meanings:

Indeed, when a fearful crier comes to us, his cry is the sharpening of the spearheads.

Al-ẓanābīb: plural of ẓunbūb, a nail that is in the socket of a spearhead. "Qara'a al-ẓanābīb" means he examined the spearheads in preparation for going out.

The meaning: they find no one to call upon while they are in the depths of the sea, and no one rescues them from drowning.

Al-inqādh: pulling out of the water.

The placing of the subject before the verbal predicate in His saying "wa lā hum yunqadhūn" is for a benefit that strengthens the judgment, which is the negation of the judgment, namely the negation of anyone rescuing them.

The exception in His saying "illā raḥmatan" is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), since mercy is neither a cry for help nor a rescuer, but rather God's granting them relief by calming the sea and enabling them to swim upon the planks of the ship.

"Matā'an" is coordinated with "raḥmatan," meaning: except a mercy that is an enjoyment until a known term, since every living being is bound to death; when it escapes one death, another death confronts it. But God placed in human nature the love of increasing life, despite His knowledge that there is no escape for him from death.

Al-ṣarīkh is also applied to the helper, in the form fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl, because when the one seeking help cries out to the one who rescues, the rescuer cries back responding with what reassures him of victory. The words of Salāmah ibn Jandal, recited by al-Mubarrad in al-Kāmil, combine both meanings:

Indeed, when a fearful crier comes to us, his cry is the sharpening of the spearheads.

Al-ẓanābīb: plural of ẓunbūb, a nail that is in the socket of a spearhead. "Qara'a al-ẓanābīb" means he examined the spearheads in preparation for going out.

The meaning: they find no one to call upon while they are in the depths of the sea, and no one rescues them from drowning.

Al-inqādh: pulling out of the water.

The placing of the subject before the verbal predicate in His saying "wa lā hum yunqadhūn" is for a benefit that strengthens the judgment, which is the negation of the judgment, namely the negation of anyone rescuing them.

The exception in His saying "illā raḥmatan" is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), since mercy is neither a cry for help nor a rescuer, but rather God's granting them relief by calming the sea and enabling them to swim upon the planks of the ship.

"Matā'an" is coordinated with "raḥmatan," meaning: except a mercy that is an enjoyment until a known term, since every living being is bound to death; when it escapes one death, another death confronts it. But God placed in human nature the love of increasing life, despite His knowledge that there is no escape for him from death.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. And We created for them of its likeness that which they ride. And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout (of rescue) for them, nor are they saved, except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time."

This is a transition from enumerating signs in the earth and in the heavens to enumerating a sign in the sea, one that combines admonition and favor: the sign of the ship's being made to travel upon the water, and of the water's being made to bear it up so that it does not sink.

God has reminded people of a great sign that became so well known that it was as if they had witnessed it: the inspiration given to Noah to build the ark, so that it would carry the people who believed and carry from every kind of animal a pair, in order to save the species from destruction and extinction by drowning in the event of the Flood. Since this sign served the purpose of carrying pairs of animal kinds, the sign itself was made to be the carrying, as an incorporation of the favor within the admonition. It is as though it were said: "And a sign for them is the building of the ship, so that We might carry their offspring in it, and so We carried them."

The verb "carry" (ḥamalnā) is used figuratively, in the sense of rescue from drowning, by way of the figure of speech called al-majāz al-mursal (metonymy), based on the relationship of cause and effect: that is, "We rescued their offspring from drowning by carrying them in the ship at the time of the Flood."

Al-dhurriyyāt (the offspring) is the plural of dhurriyyah, which means the descendants of a human being.

Al-fulk al-mashḥūn (the laden ship) is the one known among people from the story of the Flood. Here it is singular, as indicated by the qualifier, and the qualifier is in the masculine form, al-mashḥūn, not al-mashḥūnah, as in His saying: ﴿And you see the ships therein plowing [the waves]﴾ [Fāṭir: 12]. It is the ship of Noah, which became well known by this description in the Qur'an, as in Sūrat al-Shu'arā': ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 119]. No ship other than Noah's is described by this description.

The transitive construction of "carried" (ḥamalnā) with the offspring as its object is a figurative extension of the object, and it is a rational metaphor (majāz 'aqlī). A rational metaphor is not confined to the predicate; rather, the figure lies in the attachment. The thing carried is in fact the origins of the offspring, not the offspring themselves together with their origins being associated with it.

Since the offspring of the addressees are among those whom God willed to remain on the earth when He commanded Noah to build the ship to save the species, and commanded him to carry pairs of people, they are the ones from whom humankind was generated after the Flood. He made all of humankind as though they were carried in the laden ship in the time of Noah. Mention of the offspring implies, by way of kināya (implicature), that their origins were carried, for the sake of brevity in speech, and that they themselves were carried likewise. It is as though it were said: "We carried their origins, and We carried them, and We carried their offspring," since, had the origins not been saved, the offspring would not have come into being. The wisdom in carrying the origins was the survival of the offspring, so the blessing encompassed all. This is like the favor in His saying: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 11], ﴿that We might make it for you a reminder﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 12].

The pronoun in "their offspring" (dhurriyyātihim) refers to the same thing to which the pronoun in "for them" refers, namely the servants, meaning the polytheists of Makkah, but here they are considered under the heading of their being part of humankind. The meaning is: "A sign for them: that We carried the offspring of humankind in Noah's ship, at the time when God commanded Noah to carry in it his family and those of his people who believed, for the survival of the offspring of humankind. That was a carrying of their offspring, as it continued in succession, as has been mentioned just above."

This is the interpretation of this verse. Al-Qurṭubī said: "It is among the most difficult things in the sūrah." Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: "Some people have confused matters to the point of saying that dhurriyyah is applied to the forefathers. This is not known from the language." It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring﴾ [al-A'rāf: 172], in Sūrat al-A'rāf.

Nāfi' and Ibn 'Āmir read dhurriyyātihim with the plural form. The rest read it without the alif, in the form of a collective noun; the meaning is the same.

From the indication of His saying "that We carried their offspring," both explicitly and by implicature, it is understood that this sign is continuing for every observer, since they witness their voyages and the voyages of their like upon the sea, especially the inhabitants of the shores and coasts, such as the people of Jeddah and Yanbu', as they travel to the lands of Yemen and the lands of Abyssinia. Thus it is understood that We carried, and We carry, and We will carry their forefathers, themselves, and their offspring. Ṭarafah described ships in his Mu'allaqah.

The clause ﴿And We created for them of its likeness that which they ride﴾ is a parenthetical insertion within the discussion of the sign of the sea, required by the principle of correspondence (murā'āt al-naẓīr), as a reminder of the blessing of the creation of camels suitable for journeys. What is meant is similarity in greatness, strength of carrying, continuity of travel, and also in form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 45–46:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you, that you may be shown mercy."﴾ ﴿And no sign of the signs of their Lord comes to them except that they turn away from it.﴾ The discourse moved from their failure to benefit from the signs that point to the oneness of God to their failure to benefit from the words conveyed to them in the Qur'an, namely the admonition and the reminder of what befell the nations that denied, lest the same befall them, and their failure to benefit from the Qur'an's reminder to them of the proofs of God's oneness and of the resurrection.

The verb "qīla" (it was said) is in the passive form because it is evident that the one who speaks is the Messenger (ﷺ) in conveying what he received from God Most High; that is, "it was said to them in the Qur'an."

"Mā bayna al-aydī" (what is before the hands) is intended to mean the future, and "mā khalf" (what is behind) is intended to mean the past. God Most High said, relating the words of 'Isa (peace be upon him): ﴿confirming what was before me of the Torah﴾ [al-Saff: 6], that is, what came before me. The origin of these two expressions is a figure of speech: sometimes they look at the position of the one referred to relative to a place, so that what is before him is what he will encounter, and what is behind him is what he has left behind him in his journey; and sometimes they look at the position of the one referred to relative to something else, so if it is before the one referred to, it has preceded him in the journey and is thus ahead of him, and if it is behind the one referred to, it has lagged behind him and thus comes after him.

This verse has been explained in both ways. It was said: "what is before you" refers to the matters of the Hereafter, and "what is behind you" refers to the conditions of the nations in this world. This is related from Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas.

It was also said: "what is before you" refers to the conditions of the nations in this world, and "what is behind you" refers to the conditions of the Hereafter.

Page 31

This is related from Qatadah and Sufyan. When one of the two relative clauses is taken to refer to the past conditions of the nations, it is necessary to supply two genitive nouns before "mā" (the relative), which are the object: that is, "fear the likes of the conditions of what is before you, or the conditions of what is behind you." It is not necessary to supply two nouns corresponding to the other, because the referent of "mā" in that case is the punishment of the Hereafter, which is the object of "fear." The words of God Most High ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what was before it and what was behind it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 66] have already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

"La'alla" (perhaps) here expresses hope, that is, the mercy of God is hoped for you, because when they fear, they beware of what leads to the one who fears being punished; they abstain, avoid, and hasten to repentance for what they neglected, so their Lord is pleased with them, shows them mercy with reward, and spares them punishment. The discussion of "la'alla" occurring in the speech of God Most High was mentioned earlier, at His words ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The answer to "idha" (when) is omitted, indicated by His words in the coordinated clause ﴿except that they turn away from it﴾. The implied sense here is: "they turned away."

The clause ﴿And no sign of the signs of their Lord comes to them except that they turn away from it﴾ is placed as a concluding generalization of what precedes it. It encompasses their conditions and the conditions of what is conveyed to them from the Qur'an, as if it were said: "And when it is said to them, 'Fear,' they turn away, and turning away is their habit in everything said to them."

"Al-ayat" (the signs) are the verses of the Qur'an that are revealed and that the Prophet (ﷺ) recites to them; the verb "ityan" (coming) is applied to their reaching them. Describing them as "from the signs of their Lord" serves to honor the signs and to censure them for turning away from the speech of their Lord, as ingratitude for the blessing of His creating them.

"Ma" here is negative, and the exception is from an omitted set of conditions; that is, no sign comes to them in any of their conditions except that they turn away from it. The clause "they turn away from it" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿When it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed? You are not but in clear error."﴾

They, together with the generosity that was among them, were stingy toward the poor among the Muslims, withholding from them giving out of spite toward them. So when they heard from the Qur'an what contained the command to spend, or when the poor among the Muslims asked them for some of their surplus wealth, or that they give them what they used to set aside for Allah from their wealth, which Allah related about them in His saying, ﴿And they assign to Allah a share of what He has produced of crops and livestock﴾ [al-An'am: 136], then perhaps those of the poor who had embraced Islam asked the polytheists for what they had been accustomed to giving them before their conversion, and they said, "Give from what Allah has provided you." They had heard from them Islamic expressions which they had not heard before. Perhaps they were arguing with them that Allah is the Provider, and nothing in existence happens except by His will. So the polytheists began to make excuses for withholding by way of mockery, saying, "We will not feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed." And if this is so, "Allah has provided him, so why has He not provided you? If Allah willed, He would feed you as He has fed us." Some of them may have said this out of ignorance, for they did not know how to place the attributes of Allah in their proper places, as Allah related about them: ﴿And they said, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20].

The use of the relative pronoun in His saying "those who disbelieve" in a position where the pronoun would ordinarily be expected, although the apparent requirement would be to say "they said, 'Shall we feed...'", serves the purpose of indicating that the utterance of this statement by them was for the sake of their disbelief and for the sake of the faith of those whom they were asked to spend upon.

Ibn 'Atiyyah related: The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the polytheists to spend on the needy during a hardship that afflicted the people, in which the wealthy were stingy toward the needy and withheld from them what they used to give them.

The lam in His saying "to those who believe" may be the lam of transitivity for the verb of saying, meaning they addressed the believers with their words, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?" It may also be the lam of causation, meaning, "those who disbelieve said for the sake of those who believe," i.e., they said things concerning those who believed, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Those who said to their brethren while they sat, "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168], and His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11], i.e., they said that as a pretext for not spending on the poor among the believers.

The interrogation in "Shall we feed" is one of denial, meaning, "We will not feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed them, according to your belief that Allah is the one who feeds."

The expression in their reply uses "feeding" although what was demanded is "spending," either merely for variety of expression, avoiding repetition of the word, since spending is intended to mean feeding; or because they were asked to spend, which is more general than feeding, since it includes clothing and housing, and they answered by withholding food, which is the easiest kind of spending; and because they used to reproach whoever was stingy with giving food, and if they refused the believers food, refusing what is above it is more fitting.

The clause ﴿You are not but in clear error﴾ is part of the speech of the polytheists addressing the believers, meaning: you, in your saying "Spend from what Allah has provided you" and what is similar to it, in believing that Allah disposes of our affairs, are not but in obvious error, of which you have made yourselves capable. They called it error because of their ignorance of the attributes of Allah, and they called it clear because they judge by the apparent causes of acquiring wealth and of its absence.

The clause is an explanation for the denial implied by the interrogation.

[Page 33]

﴿They say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿They are only waiting for a single blast that will seize them while they are disputing.﴾ ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest (tawsiyah), nor will they return to their families.﴾ He mentions this after their mockery of the believers, when they prevented them from spending, on the pretext that if God had willed, He would have fed them. This is another mockery of the believers, regarding their threat to the polytheists of a punishment that will descend upon them. So they would ask them about this promise mockingly, as indicated by His words, ﴿if you are truthful﴾. The interrogative is therefore used as an allusion (kinayah) to derision and denial.

The word "promise" (al-wa'd) is applied to warning and threat of evil, because wa'd is more general and is specified for good or evil by context.

The demonstrative "this" (hadha) for "the promise" is used to belittle the threat of punishment, as in the words of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*Whenever this death comes, it will find no need of mine
Except that I have already fulfilled its fulfillment.*

Since their mockery was distressing to the Muslims, God informed His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers that the promise is certain to occur, and that they are awaiting nothing but a blast that will seize them, so they will not escape its grip.

[Page 34]

The verb "they await" (yanzurun) is derived from *nazrah*, meaning expectation. It was discussed previously in His words, ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels come to them?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], in Surat al-A'raf. *Al-sayhah* is an intense sound that comes out of a person's throat, either to scold or to call for help. The word *sayhah* is applied in several places in the Qur'an to the sound of a thunderbolt, as in His words concerning Thamud: ﴿So the blast seized them﴾ [al-Hijr: 83]. Here, then, *sayhah* admits of metaphor, meaning: they are only awaiting a thunderbolt or a great blast. The intended meaning is the first blast, by which the order of life in this world will end, and the second blast, from which the second creation arises, which is eternal life. Thus the style of the speech departs from the wise style by turning away from answering them, since they did not intend a true question. They are therefore answered that what has been prepared for them of punishment is more deserving of their expectation.

The meaning of "seize them" (ta'khudhuhum) is that it destroys them suddenly. The descent of the blast of punishment is likened to the descent of raiders upon a tribe to seize its livestock and capture its women. So the verb "seize" is applied to that descent, as in His words, ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, and He seized them with a severe seizing﴾ [al-Haqqah: 10], meaning: it descends upon them while they are disputing. Attributing the seizing to the blast is a rational literal attribution (haqiqah 'aqliyyah), because they perish by its thunderclap. It is also possible that the blast is literal, namely the cry of criers, meaning: they are only awaiting a cry to be raised against them, announcing the imminence of slaughter, and this would be a warning of worldly punishment. Perhaps it is the cry of the crier who came to them with news of the Muslims' attack on the trade caravan of Quraysh at Badr.

"They dispute" (yakhassimun) comes from *khusumah* and *khisam*, which mean contention. It was discussed previously in His words, ﴿and do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ [al-Nisa': 105] in Surat al-Nisa', and His words, ﴿These two are two adversaries﴾ [al-Hajj: 19] in Surat al-Hajj. Its origin is *yakhtasimun*; the *ta'* was changed to *dad* because the two articulation points are close, seeking lightness through assimilation (idgham). The reciters differed on how to pronounce it. All of them read it with a fatha on the *ya'*, and they differed concerning the rest. Warsh, from Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr in one of his transmissions, read *yakhassimun* with a shadda on the *sad* and a kasra, treating the converted *ta'* as a *sad* and quiescent for the sake of assimilation, and its vowel was transferred to the *kha'*, which had been quiescent.

[Page 35]

Qalun, from Nafi', and Abu 'Amr in the well-known transmission from him, read it with a quiescent *kha'*, slightly elided, with a fatha to avoid meeting two quiescent letters, and with a kasra and shadda on the *sad*. 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read *yakhiṣṣimun*, with a kasra on the *kha'* and a kasra with shadda on the *sad*. Hamzah read *yakhsimun*, with a quiescent *kha'*, a kasra and no shadda on the *sad*, the imperfect of *khasama*, which is said to mean "to dispute." Abu Ja'far read *yakhiṣṣimun*, with a quiescent *kha'*, a kasra and shadda on the *sad*, to combine two quiescent letters.

"Disputing" (ikhtisam) means their dispute concerning going out to Badr, or concerning determining who would go out, because of the surprises that befell them, while they dispute between one who believes and one who denies the warner. Attributing the seizing to the blast on this interpretation is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the blast is the time of the seizing, but it is in fact the swords of the Muslims that seize them. Placing the subject before the predicate verb in His words, ﴿and they are disputing﴾, serves to emphasize the strength of the judgement, namely that the blast seizes them.

Following from "seizes them" is the clause, ﴿so they will not be able to make a bequest﴾, meaning they will not be able to make a bequest concerning their families and property after them, as is the case with one who is dying. If the intended blast is the blast of the event, then His words, ﴿so they will not be able to make a bequest﴾, are an allusion to the great speed between the blast and their destruction, since its explicit meaning is not intended, for they do not leave others behind them, because destruction comes upon all people. If the intended blast is the blast of war, the meaning is that they will rush to the places of battle on the day of Badr, or they will await the arrival of the army of conquest on the day of the Conquest, and so they will not be able to speak with those whom they would entrust with their families. "Bequest" (tawsiyah) is the verbal noun of *awsa*, a doubled form, and its indefiniteness is for diminution, meaning: they will not be able to make any bequest at all.

[Page 36]

His words, ﴿nor will they return to their families﴾, may be a conjunction with "a bequest," meaning: they will not be able to return to their families, as is the case with one overtaken by terror, who hastens to check on the condition of his family out of that fear. It may also be a conjunction with the clause "they will not be able," so that it falls under the consequence introduced by the particle *fa'* (so). That is, "so they will not return to their families," meaning: they are doomed on both interpretations. However, on the interpretation that the intended blast is the blast of war, the pronoun in "they return" is restricted to the great men of Quraysh who perished on the day of Badr, because they were the ones who bore the greatest burden of denial and obstinacy, or to those who were completed in destruction on the day of the Conquest, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Khatal, who was killed on the day of the Conquest.

﴿And the Horn is blown, and behold, they rise from their graves toward their Lord, hastening.﴾

The waw (و) may be a circumstantial waw (wāw al-ḥāl), and the clause then occupies the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning: "They await nothing but a single blast, while the Horn has already been blown, etc." It may also be a parenthetical waw (wāw i'tirāḍiyya), and this parenthesis falls between the clause ﴿They await nothing but a single blast﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 49], etc., and the clause ﴿And had We willed, We would have obliterated﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 66].

The purpose is to admonish them with the resurrection that they denied and with what lies beyond it.

The past tense (al-māḍī) is used here to express the certainty of the occurrence, like ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Naḥl: 1]. The meaning is: "And the Horn is blown," that is, a blower blows into the Horn, and he is the angel entrusted with it, whose name is Isrāfīl. This is the second blast mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Then it is blown a second time, and behold, they are standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68].

The particle "idhā" (إذا) here is for suddenness (lil-mufājaʾa, the particle of sudden occurrence), which means that the content of the clause that follows it happens quickly and without preparation. The pronoun in "hum" (هم) refers back to what the preceding pronouns referred to. It may also refer to something understood from the context, meaning: "Behold, all the people, including those being spoken of."

Al-ajdāth (الأجداث) is the plural of jadath (جدث), with a vowelled ʿayn-less pattern (بالتحريك, i.e., with a fatḥa on the second radical), and it means the grave.

Yanslūn (ينسلون) means they walk swiftly. Its verb is of the pattern ḍaraba (ضرب), and it occurs rarely in the pattern naṣara (نصر). The verbal noun is al-naslān (النسلان), on the pattern of al-ghalayān (الغليان), because of what the verb implies of turning and agitation; this was discussed at the end of Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ.

This implies that they were buried after the blast. If the blast that is meant is the one that seized them, then al-ajdāth is what lies over them of dust during the period between the blast and the blowing of the Horn. It has been reported that between the two there are forty years, since after that blast no human being remains to bury those among them who have died. If, however, the blast is the blast of terror leading to death, then al-ajdāth is in its literal sense, like the well of Badr (qalīb Badr).

The meaning of "ilā Rabbihim" (إلى ربهم) is toward the judgment of their Lord and His reckoning, and it is connected to "yanslūn."

[Page 37]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 52:

﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us up from our sleeping place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers told the truth."﴾ This is a explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because describing this state after the narration of their denial of resurrection and their deeming it impossible prompts the question of one who asks about their words when they see the reality of resurrection.

"Ya waylana" (Woe to us!) is a phrase said by one who is in calamity or who is regretful. Al-wayl (woe) means a bad state, and they only said this because they saw the punishment prepared for them when they were resurrected. It has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Their saying is related in the past tense, following the relating of what precedes it in the past tense, to affirm that it has occurred.

The particle of address (harf al-nida') attached to "waylana" is for alerting, and the woe is treated as one who hears and is called to be present. It has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He, "She said: Woe to me (ya waylata)" in Surat Hud.

"Man" (who) is an interrogation about the agent of the resurrection, used to express wonder and regret at the occurrence of the resurrection. Since resurrection was impossible in their view, they expressed wonder at its occurrence by wondering at its agent, because strange events direct the minds to seek knowledge of their agent. For when they were resurrected and driven toward the punishment, they knew that it was a resurrection done by one who wished to punish them.

Al-marqad is the place of rest. The original meaning of ruqad is sleep. They used ruqad to refer to death and lying in graves, by way of likening it to the state of one who sleeps.

Then, not long after, their souls brought to mind what they had been warned of in the world, and they resumed, from their wonder, saying: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers told the truth.﴾

صفحة ٣٨

This statement is a report used for a necessary benefit, namely that they knew the cause of what they had wondered at, so the wonder ceased. It is permissible that they say this as one who is regretful speaks to himself, and that some of them say it to others, each thinking that his companion has not perceived the cause, so he wants to inform him of it.

They used the attribute "al-Rahman" in place of the Divine Name (Allah) in order to complete the regret over their denial of resurrection, by mentioning what accompanied the resurrection in their denial, namely their rejection of this name, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 60].

The demonstrative in His saying "this" (hadha) refers to the visible state of all of them, which is the state of their emerging from the earth.

The clause "and the messengers told the truth" is conjoined to the clause "this is what the Most Merciful promised," and it is used to express regret over having denied the messengers.

The plural "al-mursalin" (the messengers), although what is related is the speech of the polytheists who say, "When is this promise?", is either because they recalled that their denial of Muhammad ﷺ was prompted by their deeming it impossible that God would send a human being as a messenger; so this was because they did not accept anyone who brings a message from God, as He related of them, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being."﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. So when they regretted their error, they mentioned it in a manner that includes it and its cause, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 105] in Surat al-Shu'ara', and His saying in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37]. Or it is because that saying issued from all the disbelievers raised from the nations, so every nation knew its error in denying its messenger and the error of others in denying their messengers, and so they all uttered what expresses both errors. It has already passed that the pronoun in "fa-idha hum jami'" may refer to all people.

Some exegetes made His saying, "This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers told the truth," part of the speech of the angels, answering with it the statement of the disbelievers, "Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" So this is an answer that includes the explanation of who raised them, together with rebuking them for their denial of it in the life of the world, when the messengers conveyed to them that matter from God, exalted is He. The name "al-Rahman" is then part of the speech of the angels, to increase the reproach of the disbelievers for their disregard of it in the world.

صفحة ٣٩

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 53:

﴿It will be but one shout, and then they will all be brought before Us.﴾ This is a summary (fadhlakah) of the whole passage from ﴿They are waiting for nothing but one shout﴾ [Yasin: 49] to His words ﴿and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ [Yasin: 52]. This is because the blowing (al-nafkh) is synonymous with the shout (al-sayhah) in its figurative usage. The feminine marker in the verb "كانت" (kānat, "it was") is therefore due to interpreting the blowing, drawn from ﴿and the Trumpet is blown﴾, in the sense of "the blast." The reference to it as "ṣayḥatan" (a shout) is so that it is described as "wāḥidatan" (one), because that description is the intended meaning of the exceptive construction (al-istithnā' al-mufarragh, an exception whose stated object is omitted). The sense is: that blowing was nothing but one shout, which is not repeated to summon them to attend; rather, the single blast brings them out of their graves, drives them on, and brings them to the reckoning.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom Allah wills. Then it is blown again, and behold, they are standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68], that is a preceding blast that falls upon people in this world, by which people will perish. Its mention will come in surah al-Zumar.

Since His words ﴿It will be but one shout﴾ carry the force of a repetition and emphasis of His words ﴿and the Trumpet is blown﴾, what follows it, His words ﴿and behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾, stands in the position of a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on His words ﴿and behold, they will rush from the graves to their Lord﴾ [Yasin: 51]. It is as though it were like: ﴿and the Trumpet is blown, and behold, they rush from the graves to their Lord﴾ [Yasin: 51] and ﴿behold, they are all brought before Us﴾. The repetition of the particle of sudden occurrence (ḥarf al-mufājaʾah, the "fa" of suddenness, here "idhā") indicates that the content of the two sentences, which are linked by this particle, happens in the twinkling of an eye, so that both occur suddenly at one time.

The discussion of the parallel of this structure has already preceded.

"Jamīʿun" (all) is a qualifier (naʿt) of the subject (mubtadaʾ), meaning "they are all of them." The tanwīn (nunation) in "jamīʿun" replaces the omitted genitive complement that links the qualifier to the qualified, i.e., they are gathered together, not brought in groups and bands. His words, exalted is He, ﴿And all of them, all of them, will be brought before Us﴾ [Yasin: 32], have already occurred in this surah.

[Page 40]
The majority (al-Jumhūr) read "ṣayḥatan" with the accusative (naṣb). Abu Ja'far read it with the nominative (raf'), on the basis that "kāna" is complete (tāmmah, not requiring a predicate). Its parallel has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 54:

﴿So today no soul will be wronged in the least, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾ If His saying, ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52], is a quotation of the words of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, then this is speech from Allah, the Exalted, conveyed through the angels. The fa' in His saying ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in the least﴾ is a fa' fasihah (the "eloquent" fa', i.e., the one that reveals and points to an unstated utterance), which arises from His saying ﴿and when they will all be brought before Us, present﴾ [Ya-Sin: 53]. So this is an address to those who said, "Who has raised us from our resting place?" The meaning is: "You have now certainly known that Allah's promise is true and that the messengers spoke the truth, so today is the Day of Recompense, just as the messengers used to warn you."

If His saying ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52] is from the words of the angels, then the fa' is a consequence (tafriʻ) of it, and the clause ﴿It will be only one blast﴾ [Ya-Sin: 53], etc., is a parenthetical insertion between the consequent and that upon which it is based.

"Al-yawm" (today) is a adverb of time (zarf), and its definiteness is for a known reference (al-ʻahd), namely a known presence, meaning the Day of Recompense. The benefit of mentioning this is to draw attention to that day as a day of justice.

His saying "no soul will be wronged in the least" hints, by allusion (ta'rid), that they will meet a harsh recompense, but it is just, with no injustice in it, because negating injustice suggests that the recompense might be imagined to exceed the equivalence of the crime. This is the meaning of ﴿and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, i.e., only in accordance with what you used to do and in its measure. "Shay'an" (in the least) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), i.e., "any part of injustice."

The occurrence of "nafs" (soul) and "shay'an" (anything), both indefinite nouns in the context of negation, generalizes the negation of all of that from every soul and the negation of every aspect of the reality of injustice, and this encompasses all souls. But the intended reference is the souls of those being punished, i.e., that their recompense according to their evil deeds is a just recompense. Since its determination is from Allah, the Exalted, who is Knowing of everything, the reality of justice was realized in the measure of their recompense, for every justice other than the justice of Allah is subject to increase and decrease in the reality of the matter, but it operates according to the judgment (ijtihad) of those who judge. Allah did not charge the judge except with exerting his effort to hit the truth. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "If a judge exerts his effort and is correct, he has two rewards; and if he exerts his effort and errs, he has one reward."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 55–57:

﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in enjoyment, reclining.﴾ ﴿They and their spouses are in shade, reclining upon couches.﴾ ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for.﴾ This is from the speech of the one who is addressed by the angels, and the sentence is resumptive (mustanaf'a). It is said to those who deserve the punishment, to inform them of the descent of their rank below the ranks of the people of the Garden, as a proclamation of the realities (i'lanan bil-haqa'iq), since that is the world of realities, and to bring regret upon them for what they neglected of seeking success in the Hereafter.

This indicates that the people of the Garden were hastened to bliss before the people of the Fire are brought to the Fire, and that the people of the Garden are not present at that gathering.

The definiteness of "al-yawm" is for familiarity (al-'ahd), as has preceded. The benefit of mentioning the temporal adverb "al-yawm" is to draw attention to that day as the day of favour upon the believing God-fearing ones.

Al-shughl (busyness) is the verbal noun of shaghalahu, when it diverts him, i.e., occupies him. It is said: shaghalahu bi-kadha 'an kadha, fa-shtaghala bihi (he occupied him with such-and-such from such-and-such, so he became occupied with it). The adverbial sense of "fi" is figurative: their being engaged in busyness is treated as though they were enclosed within it, i.e., busyness encompassed them, diverting them from witnessing the scene of the people of punishment. God turned them away from the sight of distressing things, since witnessing them is not free of the constriction of souls. Because this is the intended meaning, He omitted mention of what occupies them, as there is no purpose in mentioning it. Thus His saying "fi shughl" is the predicate of "inna," and "fakihun" is a second predicate.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read "shughlin" with a damma and then a sukun. The rest read it with two dammas, and both are dialectal variants of the word.

Al-fakihah: one who is in fukaha, with a damma on the fa', which is joking through speech that is pleasant and amusing; it is an ism al-masdar (a noun of the verbal action). The verb is fakiha with a kasra on the kaf, meaning he joked and was pleased. It is reported from some lexicographers that no triliteral verb has been heard from it, and it seems he meant that its use is rare. As for non-triliteral verbs from this root, it has come in the proverb: "Do not joke with your mother, and do not urinate on the blind one (la tufakih amah wa la tabul 'ala akmah)." And God Most High said: ﴿So you would have been amazed (fazaltum tafakkahun)﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65].

The majority read "fakihun" in the form of the active participle. Abu Ja'far read it without an alif, in the form of the intensive pattern (mithal al-mubalaghah).

The clause ﴿They and their spouses are in shade...﴾ to its end stands in the position of explanation (bayan) for the clause "Indeed, the companions of the Garden..." The intended meaning of "azwajuhum" (their spouses) is the spouses prepared for them in the Garden. Among them are those who were their spouses in this world, if they were not barred from the Garden. God Most High said: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their descendants﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23].

The word "al-zilal" was read by the majority in the pattern fi'al, with a kasra on its first letter, as the plural of zill, i.e., the shade of the Gardens. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "zulal" with a damma on the za' and a fatha on the lam, the plural of zullah, which is what provides shade like domes.

"Al-zilal" is pluralized in both readings to correspond with the plural "the companions of the Garden," so each of them is in a shade or in a canopy.

Al-ara'ik: the plural of arikah. Al-arikah is the name for the collection of the bed and the canopy (al-hajalah); when the bed is within the canopy, the whole is called arikah. This is among the words denoting a thing composed of two things, like "al-ma'idah," which is the name for the table upon which there is food.

Al-ittika' (reclining) is a posture between lying down and sitting; it is lying on one side without placing the head and shoulder on the bedding. It is an ifti'al form from wak'a (with a hamza), when one leans on something; its waw was changed to ta', as it was changed in "tuja" and "turath." From it is derived the verb ittaka'a, because the one reclining steadies his seat and firms it through a kind of lying down. The noun from it is al-tuka'ah, on the pattern of humazah, which is the sitting of one seeking rest and prolonged comfort; it is the posture of the people of luxury. It was already discussed at His saying ﴿and she prepared for them a reclining couch (muttaka')﴾ [Yusuf: 31] in Surat Yusuf. Among the pampered peoples of the civilised nations, those who ate reclining were common; this was the custom of the lords of the Persians and the Romans and whoever imitated them among the Arabs. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ said: "As for me, I do not eat reclining." This is because reclining helps the stomach to expand, so it accepts more food; for this reason reclining while eating was disliked, due to excess in luxury.

As for reclining outside the state of eating, the Prophet ﷺ did recline in his assembly, as in the hadith of Dimam ibn Tha'labah, envoy of the Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr: that he "entered the mosque and asked about the Prophet ﷺ, and it was said to him: 'That is the fair one, the one reclining (al-azhar al-muttaki')'."

Al-fakihah: what is eaten for pleasure, not for satiety, such as fruits and dried sweets. It was singled out for mention because it is rare to obtain for people in this world, and because reclining brought it to mind, since the habit of those who recline is to occupy themselves with taking fruits.

Then He generalised what was prepared for them with His saying "and for them is whatever they call for." "Yaddda'un" may be derived from du'a' (to call) or from id-di'a' (to claim). That is, whatever they call for, or whatever they claim within themselves to be theirs through divine inspiration. The form of ifti'al was used for it to intensify the meaning, so the pattern of "yaddda'un" is yaftali'un. Its origin is yadtai'yun; the vowel of the ya' was transferred to the 'ayn to seek lightness, because the damma on the ya' is heavy after the deletion of the vowel of the 'ayn; so the ya' remained quiescent, and after it is the waw of the plural, because it conveys the sense of attribution to a plural.

This ifti'al you may take from "da'a." The ifti'al here makes the verb da'a intransitive, so a prepositional phrase should be attached to it. The estimate is: "what they call for for themselves," like the saying of Labid:

"He roasted on a windy night and gathered the fat (ishtawa layalata rihin wa-jtamal)."

Ishtawa means he roasted for himself, and ijtamala means he gathered fat for himself, that is, he gathered the melted fat, which is the ihalah.

If you take it from id-di'a', its meaning is that they claim that as a right of theirs, i.e., their souls speak of it, and it returns to the sense: "and they wish within themselves without needing to ask by speech." Therefore it has been said that the meaning of yaddda'un is yatamannawn (they wish). One says: "Call for what you will against me," i.e., wish for what you will against me; and "so-and-so is in the best of what he claims," i.e., in the best of what he wishes. From it is His saying: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you call for﴾ [Fussilat: 31], in Surat Fussilat.
