As for non-triliteral verbs from this root, it has come in the proverb: "Do not joke with your mother, and do not urinate on the blind one (la tufakih amah wa la tabul 'ala akmah)." And God Most High said: ﴿So you would have been amazed (fazaltum tafakkahun)﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65].

The majority read "fakihun" in the form of the active participle. Abu Ja'far read it without an alif, in the form of the intensive pattern (mithal al-mubalaghah).

The clause ﴿They and their spouses are in shade...﴾ to its end stands in the position of explanation (bayan) for the clause "Indeed, the companions of the Garden..." The intended meaning of "azwajuhum" (their spouses) is the spouses prepared for them in the Garden. Among them are those who were their spouses in this world, if they were not barred from the Garden. God Most High said: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their descendants﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23].

The word "al-zilal" was read by the majority in the pattern fi'al, with a kasra on its first letter, as the plural of zill, i.e., the shade of the Gardens. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "zulal" with a damma on the za' and a fatha on the lam, the plural of zullah, which is what provides shade like domes.

"Al-zilal" is pluralized in both readings to correspond with the plural "the companions of the Garden," so each of them is in a shade or in a canopy.

Al-ara'ik: the plural of arikah. Al-arikah is the name for the collection of the bed and the canopy (al-hajalah); when the bed is within the canopy, the whole is called arikah. This is among the words denoting a thing composed of two things, like "al-ma'idah," which is the name for the table upon which there is food.

Al-ittika' (reclining) is a posture between lying down and sitting; it is lying on one side without placing the head and shoulder on the bedding. It is an ifti'al form from wak'a (with a hamza), when one leans on something; its waw was changed to ta', as it was changed in "tuja" and "turath." From it is derived the verb ittaka'a, because the one reclining steadies his seat and firms it through a kind of lying down. The noun from it is al-tuka'ah, on the pattern of humazah, which is the sitting of one seeking rest and prolonged comfort; it is the posture of the people of luxury. It was already discussed at His saying ﴿and she prepared for them a reclining couch (muttaka')﴾ [Yusuf: 31] in Surat Yusuf. Among the pampered peoples of the civilised nations, those who ate reclining were common; this was the custom of the lords of the Persians and the Romans and whoever imitated them among the Arabs. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ said: "As for me, I do not eat reclining." This is because reclining helps the stomach to expand, so it accepts more food; for this reason reclining while eating was disliked, due to excess in luxury.

As for reclining outside the state of eating, the Prophet ﷺ did recline in his assembly, as in the hadith of Dimam ibn Tha'labah, envoy of the Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr: that he "entered the mosque and asked about the Prophet ﷺ, and it was said to him: 'That is the fair one, the one reclining (al-azhar al-muttaki')'."

Al-fakihah: what is eaten for pleasure, not for satiety, such as fruits and dried sweets. It was singled out for mention because it is rare to obtain for people in this world, and because reclining brought it to mind, since the habit of those who recline is to occupy themselves with taking fruits.

Then He generalised what was prepared for them with His saying "and for them is whatever they call for." "Yaddda'un" may be derived from du'a' (to call) or from id-di'a' (to claim). That is, whatever they call for, or whatever they claim within themselves to be theirs through divine inspiration. The form of ifti'al was used for it to intensify the meaning, so the pattern of "yaddda'un" is yaftali'un. Its origin is yadtai'yun; the vowel of the ya' was transferred to the 'ayn to seek lightness, because the damma on the ya' is heavy after the deletion of the vowel of the 'ayn; so the ya' remained quiescent, and after it is the waw of the plural, because it conveys the sense of attribution to a plural.

This ifti'al you may take from "da'a." The ifti'al here makes the verb da'a intransitive, so a prepositional phrase should be attached to it. The estimate is: "what they call for for themselves," like the saying of Labid:

"He roasted on a windy night and gathered the fat (ishtawa layalata rihin wa-jtamal)."

Ishtawa means he roasted for himself, and ijtamala means he gathered fat for himself, that is, he gathered the melted fat, which is the ihalah.

If you take it from id-di'a', its meaning is that they claim that as a right of theirs, i.e., their souls speak of it, and it returns to the sense: "and they wish within themselves without needing to ask by speech." Therefore it has been said that the meaning of yaddda'un is yatamannawn (they wish). One says: "Call for what you will against me," i.e., wish for what you will against me; and "so-and-so is in the best of what he claims," i.e., in the best of what he wishes. From it is His saying: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you call for﴾ [Fussilat: 31], in Surat Fussilat.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah Yā-Sīn (36), verse 58:**

﴿Peace: a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf qaṭʿ*, a new sentence not grammatically joined to what precedes it), not coordinated with what came before, in order to draw attention to its content. That content is the indication of honour and special favour toward the people of Paradise from the side of the Holy (*al-Quds*), since the greeting of God (*salām Allāh*) is directed to them in a speech by which they know that it is a word from God. This may be through the angels, or through the creation of sounds which they are certain have been made for the sake of their hearing, just as Mūsā (Moses) heard the speech of God when He called him from the right side of the Mount (*al-Ṭūr*), from the tree. After mentioning what He had bestowed on them of blessings, pointing to the roots of its kinds, He informed them that they have something higher and loftier, which is being honoured by being greeted. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the good pleasure of God is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72].

*Salām* is in the nominative (*marfūʿ*) in all the well-known recitations. It is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*, the topic of the nominal sentence), and its indefiniteness (*tankīr*) is for magnification. Its being in the nominative indicates permanence and certainty. Its original form is the accusative, as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*, a cognate object standing in for the verb), as in His saying, "they say, 'Peace'" [al-Furqān: 63]. When permanence was intended, it was given in the nominative, as in His saying, "He said, 'Peace'" [Hūd: 69]. The explanation of this has already been given under His saying: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Yūnus: 10].

The predicate (*khabar*) of *salām* is omitted, because the absolute object *qawlan* ("a word"), which is in the accusative, stands in for the predicate. Its full form would be: "Peace is said to them, a word from God." What required the omission of the verb and the substitution of the verbal noun for it is that the verbal noun is apt to receive *tanwīn* (nunation), which indicates magnification. What required that the verbal noun be in the accusative, rather than given in the nominative, is what the accusative suggests: that the verbal noun came as a substitute (*badal*) for the verb. The *min* in *min Allāh* is inceptive (*ibtidāʾiyyah*, indicating origin).

The nunation of *rabb* is for magnification. For this reason, the expression was turned away from annexing *rabb* to their pronoun. Instead, the Exalted Essence was described by the attribute of Lordship (*al-rubūbiyyah*), because it is most suitable for honouring them and for being pleased with them, by mentioning that they worshipped Him in the world and so acknowledged His lordship.

Surah 36, verse 59 (Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir)

صفحة ٤٥ [page 45]

﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones.﴾ This may be a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, enjoying themselves﴾ [Ya-Sin: 55]. It may also be conjoined upon "Peace, a word [spoken]" (salamun qawlan), meaning: and it is said, "Separate yourselves today, O guilty ones," in contrast to what is said to the companions of the Garden. The sense is: "Peace" is said to the people of the Garden as a word, and it is said to the guilty: "Separate yourselves," so this is of the distribution of two addresses within one setting, like His saying, ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and [you, wife], ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Yusuf: 29].

Imtaza is the reflexive (muṭāwiʿ) of mazahu, meaning: he separated it (afradahu) from what had been mixed with it. The command is addressed to them to separate themselves, as an intensification in hastening the occurrence of the separation (al-mayz), because this command is a command of creation (amr takwin), so it is expressed in the form of its effect. Thus the separation is expressed by framing the command from the root of the reflexive, for your saying "Let the bottle break (li-tankasira al-zujajatu)" is more emphatic in hastening the occurrence of breaking in it than saying "Break the bottle." The intended meaning is their separation by distancing themselves from the Garden, which happens by their going to the Fire, so it returns to the meaning: "Enter the Fire."

This indicates that they were in the place of gathering (al-mahshar) waiting to see what would be done to them, as we pointed out earlier at His saying, ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy﴾ [Ya-Sin: 55]. When what the companions of the Garden have of bliss is related, at the time it is said to the companions of the Fire ﴿So today no soul will be wronged at all﴾ [Ya-Sin: 54], that is related, then it is said to the polytheists ﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones.﴾

The repetition of the word "today" (al-yawm) three times in this narration serves as a rebuke (taʿrid) to those addressed in it, namely the disbelievers who used to deny the occurrence of that day, together with emphasizing its mention upon their ears by His saying ﴿So today no soul will be wronged﴾, and His saying ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy﴾ [Ya-Sin: 55], and His saying ﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones.﴾

Their address with the title "the guilty" (al-mujrimun) is to indicate the reason for their separation from the people of the Garden, namely that they are guilty. The lam in "al-mujrimun" is relative (mawsulah), meaning: O you who committed crimes (ajramu).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 60–62:

﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ ﴿And that you should worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾ ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. Did you not then use reason?﴾ This is an address to all of mankind gathered at the Gathering (al-Mahshar), except the people of Paradise who were hastened to Paradise. It therefore encompasses all the people of misguidance, from among the polytheists and others, and perhaps it also includes the people of al-A'raf (the Heights). It is both a witnessing against the polytheists and a rebuke to them.

The interrogative (al-istifham) is taqriri (confirmatory, drawing an affirmation). They were addressed with the title "children of Adam" because the situation of rebuke over their worship of Satan requires reminding them that they are the sons of the one whom Satan made an enemy to himself, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"If there is for the two graves a grave in Jilaq, and a grave in Sidaa, the one near Harib..."

And for al-Harith al-Jafni, the lord of his people,
he will surely seek with the army the abode of the one who wars [against him],
meaning the lands of those who fought his origins.

The covenant (al-'ahd) is a charge (wisaya), and the charge of God through Adam, that they should not worship Satan, is what has been established and become well known among the nations through what the messengers brought in past ages, so its denial is not possible. In this sense, denial is directed at them in their state, which resembles the state of one who denies this covenant.

Know that in the words of the Exalted, "a'had" (أعهَدْ), there is a succession of the 'ayn and the ha', and these are two letters whose articulation points are close, among the letters of the throat. However, their succession did not produce a heaviness in pronouncing the word that would contradict eloquence according to the requirement of the dissonance of letters (tanafur al-huruf), because the movement of the tongue in the articulation point of the 'ayn from the middle of the throat to the articulation point of the ha' from the farthest part of the throat lightened the pronunciation of both. Likewise, the transition from a sukun to a harakah increased that lightness. A similar case is the words of the Exalted, "wa sabbihhu" (وسَبِّحْهُ), which contain a ha' (ح), from the middle of the throat, and a ha' (ه), from its farthest part, except that the first is quiescent and the second vowelled, and they are close in articulation point; this is not counted as dissonance of letters. It is illustrated by the verse of Abu Tammam:

"Generous: when I praise him, I praise him, while the people are with me; and when I blame him, I blame him alone."

The phrase "amdahhu" (أمْدَحْهُ) is not counted as dissonant in its letters, yet its repetition created some heaviness in it, so it is not like the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"His locks, raised upward..." (ghadara'uhu mustashziratun ila al-ula)

which is made an example of dissonance, for the dissonance of its letters arises from the succession of three letters: the sin, the shin, and the zay. Had the separation between the sin and the shin by the ta' not been there, it would have been far more dissonant.

The causes of dissonance are many, and their source is the speed of movement of the tongue among the articulation points of letters that are very close or very distant, together with accidents that befall them from the attributes of letters: jahr and hams, or shiddah and rakhw, or isti'la' and istifal, or infitah and intibaq, or ism and inthilaq, and from their vowels and quiescences. There is no consistent rule for this, but it is referred to the taste of the eloquent. Ibn Sinan al-Khafaji attempted to reduce it to the closeness of the articulation points of letters, but Ibn al-Athir refuted him with what leaves him no escape.

When the situation requires, by the right of eloquence, the preference of a word for mention, since nothing else can take its place, and some heaviness arises in one of its inflections, the eloquent requirement of the situation does not necessitate its being uttered.

The "an" (أنْ) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah); it explains the generality of the covenant, because the covenant contains the meaning of saying without its letters, so the "an" that follows it is explanatory.

The worship of Satan is worship of what he commands to be worshipped, such as idols and the like.

The clause "indeed, he is to you a clear enemy" is a reason (ta'lil) for the clause "do not worship Satan," and "an" has dispensed with the causal fa' (fa' al-sababiyyah), as has been mentioned more than once.

"Mubin" is an active participle from abana, meaning "bana" (to become clear), for emphasis; that is, his enmity is evident. The manner of its evidence is that when a person observes the consequences of the deeds which his own soul whispers to him, and suspects them and presents them to the precepts of the prophets and the wise, he finds their consequences to be ruinous, and it becomes clear to him that they are from Satan through whispering, and that the one who whispered them is an enemy to him, for if he were a friend he would not have led him into calamities, nor would it be supposed that he would cause that without insight. The repetition of such whisperings to a person and to those like him who reveal their states to him indicates that these are deliberate whisperings aimed at casting one into ruin; thus it is known that the one who suggests them is a fierce enemy. Perhaps this meaning is what is referred to by the words of the Exalted, "And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. Did you not then use reason?"

The clause "and that you should worship Me" is coordinated with "that you should not worship Satan," by repeating the explanatory "an," so the two clauses explain two covenants.

The expression took the form not of a restrictive construction (qasr), because in bringing these two clauses there is additional benefit: among the people of misguidance are the naturalists (al-dahriyyin) and the deniers (al-mu'attilin), who, although they do not worship Satan, have not worshipped God either, and so they are rebuked for breaking the covenant.

The demonstrative in His words "this is a straight path" refers to the covenant understood from the verb "a'had," or to what is mentioned in its explanation from the two clauses "do not worship Satan" and "and that you worship Me"; that is, "this that is mentioned is a straight path," meaning like the upright road in reaching the intended goal. The tanwin is for magnification.

The Exalted's words "And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude" are coordinated with "indeed, he is to you a clear enemy." So his enmity is evident by the evidence of experience, and it was therefore a cause for the prohibition of worshipping what he commands them to worship.

The meaning is: his enmity is as evident as the straight path, because it has been established among people, and generations and ages have borne witness to it; for he has never ceased to lead people astray, a misguidance whose matter has been transmitted widely and whose denial is impossible.

"Jibillan" (الجِبِلُّ), with a kasra on the jim and a kasra on the ba' and a shaddah on the lam, is as recited by Nafi', 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited it with a damma on the jim, a damma on the ba', and a light lam. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr recited it with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the ba'.

"Jibill" means a great multitude, and it is derived from "jabl" (الجَبْل) with a sukun on the ba', in the sense of creation.

The rebuke for scarcity of intellects is derived from it in His words, "Did you not then use reason?" So the interrogative is denunciatory (inkari) regarding their not reasoning, that is, not perceiving, since if they had been reasoning they would have grasped Satan's casting them into the abysses of destruction.

The addition of the verb "kana" (كان) indicates that reason did not come into being in them, nor are they those who possess it.

A similar case is the words of the Exalted, "wa sabbihhu" (وسَبِّحْهُ), which contain a ha' (ح), from the middle of the throat, and a ha' (ه), from its farthest part, except that the first is quiescent and the second vowelled, and they are close in articulation point; this is not counted as dissonance of letters. It is illustrated by the verse of Abu Tammam:

"Generous: when I praise him, I praise him, while the people are with me; and when I blame him, I blame him alone."

The phrase "amdahhu" (أمْدَحْهُ) is not counted as dissonant in its letters, yet its repetition created some heaviness in it, so it is not like the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"His locks, raised upward..." (ghadara'uhu mustashziratun ila al-ula)

which is made an example of dissonance, for the dissonance of its letters arises from the succession of three letters: the sin, the shin, and the zay. Had the separation between the sin and the shin by the ta' not been there, it would have been far more dissonant.

The causes of dissonance are many, and their source is the speed of movement of the tongue among the articulation points of letters that are very close or very distant, together with accidents that befall them from the attributes of letters: jahr and hams, or shiddah and rakhw, or isti'la' and istifal, or infitah and intibaq, or ism and inthilaq, and from their vowels and quiescences. There is no consistent rule for this, but it is referred to the taste of the eloquent. Ibn Sinan al-Khafaji attempted to reduce it to the closeness of the articulation points of letters, but Ibn al-Athir refuted him with what leaves him no escape.

When the situation requires, by the right of eloquence, the preference of a word for mention, since nothing else can take its place, and some heaviness arises in one of its inflections, the eloquent requirement of the situation does not necessitate its being uttered.

The "an" (أنْ) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah); it explains the generality of the covenant, because the covenant contains the meaning of saying without its letters, so the "an" that follows it is explanatory.

The worship of Satan is worship of what he commands to be worshipped, such as idols and the like.

The clause "indeed, he is to you a clear enemy" is a reason (ta'lil) for the clause "do not worship Satan," and "an" has dispensed with the causal fa' (fa' al-sababiyyah), as has been mentioned more than once.

"Mubin" is an active participle from abana, meaning "bana" (to become clear), for emphasis; that is, his enmity is evident. The manner of its evidence is that when a person observes the consequences of the deeds which his own soul whispers to him, and suspects them and presents them to the precepts of the prophets and the wise, he finds their consequences to be ruinous, and it becomes clear to him that they are from Satan through whispering, and that the one who whispered them is an enemy to him, for if he were a friend he would not have led him into calamities, nor would it be supposed that he would cause that without insight. The repetition of such whisperings to a person and to those like him who reveal their states to him indicates that these are deliberate whisperings aimed at casting one into ruin; thus it is known that the one who suggests them is a fierce enemy. Perhaps this meaning is what is referred to by the words of the Exalted, "And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. Did you not then use reason?"

The clause "and that you should worship Me" is coordinated with "that you should not worship Satan," by repeating the explanatory "an," so the two clauses explain two covenants.

The expression took the form not of a restrictive construction (qasr), because in bringing these two clauses there is additional benefit: among the people of misguidance are the naturalists (al-dahriyyin) and the deniers (al-mu'attilin), who, although they do not worship Satan, have not worshipped God either, and so they are rebuked for breaking the covenant.

The demonstrative in His words "this is a straight path" refers to the covenant understood from the verb "a'had," or to what is mentioned in its explanation from the two clauses "do not worship Satan" and "and that you worship Me"; that is, "this that is mentioned is a straight path," meaning like the upright road in reaching the intended goal. The tanwin is for magnification.

The Exalted's words "And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude" are coordinated with "indeed, he is to you a clear enemy." So his enmity is evident by the evidence of experience, and it was therefore a cause for the prohibition of worshipping what he commands them to worship.

The meaning is: his enmity is as evident as the straight path, because it has been established among people, and generations and ages have borne witness to it; for he has never ceased to lead people astray, a misguidance whose matter has been transmitted widely and whose denial is impossible.

"Jibillan" (الجِبِلُّ), with a kasra on the jim and a kasra on the ba' and a shaddah on the lam, is as recited by Nafi', 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited it with a damma on the jim, a damma on the ba', and a light lam. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr recited it with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the ba'.

"Jibill" means a great multitude, and it is derived from "jabl" (الجَبْل) with a sukun on the ba', in the sense of creation.

The rebuke for scarcity of intellects is derived from it in His words, "Did you not then use reason?" So the interrogative is denunciatory (inkari) regarding their not reasoning, that is, not perceiving, since if they had been reasoning they would have grasped Satan's casting them into the abysses of destruction.

The addition of the verb "kana" (كان) indicates that reason did not come into being in them, nor are they those who possess it.

This is Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 63–64:

﴿This is Hell which you were promised.﴾ ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve.﴾

It is an address directed to those who worshipped objects of worship that Satan had adorned for them, when Hell appears to them in such a way that it is pointed to and they recognise that it is the very Hell they were warned of in the world, and when the period of life is mentioned to them in the threat. The command in His words ﴿اصْلَوْها﴾ (iṣlawhā, "burn therein") is used in the sense of humiliation and rebuke.

"Iṣlawhā" is an imperative of ṣalā yaṣlā (صَلِيَ يَصْلى), meaning to warm oneself at the heat of the fire. The application of ṣalī (الصَّلْي) to burning is a sarcastic usage (tahakkum).

The definite article in "al-yawm" (اليَوْم, "today") is the definite of prior reference (ta'rīf al-'ahd), meaning "this present day." It is intended as an answer to what they used to say in the worldly life about delaying the promise and denying it, when they would say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"

The bāʾ in "bi-mā kuntum takfurūn" (بِمَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ, "for what you used to disbelieve") is causal (sababiyyah), meaning "because of your disbelief in the world."

Regarding the word *al-yawma*, the discussion is the same as for its three similar occurrences mentioned earlier. It serves to draw attention to the occurrence of this astonishing state in it, namely the transfer of speech from its usual place to the hands and feet.

Page 50
The pronouns of the third person in (*afwahihim*, *aydihim*, *arjulihim*, *yaksibuna*) refer to those who were addressed by His saying ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾ [Yasin: 63], by way of *iltifat* (a shift from address to third-person reference). The underlying construction is: "Today We seal upon your mouths, and your hands speak to Us, and your feet bear witness to what you used to earn." Addressing them with this information is a way of making them despair, since they cannot deny what they have seen of the records of their deeds, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Read your record; sufficient is your own soul today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra': 14].

Some of what is detailed in other verses has been left implicit in this verse. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah: "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ [al-An'am: 22]. ﴿Then their trial will be only that they will say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. And He said: ﴿And their partners will say: "You did not used to worship us."﴾ [Yunus: 28]. ﴿So Allah suffices as a witness between us and you, that we were indeed unaware of your worship.﴾ [Yunus: 29].

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A servant will address his Lord, saying: 'O Lord, did You not protect me from injustice?' He will say: 'Indeed, I do not permit against myself except a witness from Myself.' Then Allah will say: 'Sufficient is your own soul today as a witness against you.' Then He will seal upon his mouth. Then it will be said to his limbs: 'Speak!' So they will speak of his deeds. Then he will be left free to speak, and he will say: 'Away with you, destruction! It was for your sake that I was contending.'" The one who called them to this speech is omitted, because no purpose connected with it is relevant here, so the text confines itself to the intended meaning.

It may seem that there is a contradiction between this verse and His saying ﴿On the day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. There is no contradiction, because the verse of Yasin concerns the condition of the polytheists, while the verse of Surat al-Nur concerns the condition of the hypocrites.

By the speaking of the hands is meant their speaking with testimony, and by the witnessing of the feet is meant their uttering testimony. Thus in both clauses there is *ihtibak* (an elliptical construction in which each part omits what the other supplies). The estimated sense is: "Their hands speak to Us, so they bear witness; and their feet speak to Us, so they bear witness."

The phrase *bima kanu yaksibuna* ("for what they used to earn") is connected to each of the two verbs *tukallimuna* ("speak") and *tashhadu* ("bear witness") by way of *tanazu'* (the grammatical contention in which two verbs share one complement). What they earned is polytheism and its branches, and their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the harms they inflicted upon him.

[Page 51]

﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, so they would race toward the path, but how could they see?﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places, so they would not be able to proceed, nor could they return.﴾

This is an extension of the phrase ﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾. The place of these two verses within what precedes them is as follows: when God mentioned that He compelled them to acknowledge their polytheism after denying it on the Day of Resurrection, this was likely to prompt the believers' hearts to wish that God had, in this world, dealt with them through a similar compulsion, so that He would compel them to affirm His oneness, to confirm His Messenger, and to follow His religion. So God informed them that, had His will been directed to that in this world, He would have done it. This is an allusion to the fact that His exalted will brings about its objects in accordance with His exalted knowledge and wisdom. He has made the order of this world run according to the occurrence of things through their causes, which God entrusted with producing their effects, consequences, and offspring. When this world is replaced by the world of reality, He will arrange all affairs upon the true course, which admits of no other, in accordance with the paths of reason and wisdom. The meaning is: We compel them, in the Hereafter, to acknowledge that what they were upon in this world was polytheism and falsehood. And if We willed, We would have shown them Our signs in this world, so that they would be restrained and would turn back from their disbelief and their evil denial.

Since ﴿law﴾ ("if") entails the impossibility of one thing because of the impossibility of another, it implies the meaning: "But We did not will that; so We left them in their condition as a respite (istidraj) and as a means of distinguishing the wicked from the good." This is a statement addressed to the Muslims, and its purpose is to give the believers insight and to guide them to patience with what they encounter from the polytheists, until God's help arrives.

Thus, the obliteration (ṭams) and transformation (maskh), which are connected to the conditional clause of impossibility, refer to an obliteration and a transformation in this world, not in the Hereafter.

Ṭams is the effacing of the features of the eye by removing its blackness and whiteness, or by mixing them together, and it is blindness or squinting. It is said: "a ṭarīq maṭmūsa" (an obliterated road) when there are no traces of travelers in it for the traveler to follow. The preposition ʿalā (on) indicates the firmness of the obliteration; otherwise, ṭamasa is transitive by itself.

Al-istibāq is an iftiʿāl form from al-sabq, and the iftiʿāl form indicates exertion and striving in the action, meaning: they hastened.

Al-ṣirāṭ is the road on which one walks. The verb of racing is made to govern it by omitting "ilā" (to), in the manner of omission and connection. The poet, who is among the examples cited in the book (Sībawayh's), said:

"You pass through the abodes and do not turn aside."

He meant: "You pass by the abodes."

Or the verb istabaqū is taken to include the meaning of ibtadarū (rushed), meaning: they rushed toward the road, racing one another, that is, hastening because of what overtook them, hoping to reach their homes before they perished, but they did not see the road. God's words ﴿Indeed we went racing one another﴾ in Surat Yusuf were mentioned earlier.

And ﴿annā﴾ is an interrogative meaning "how," used here in denial: they cannot see, though their eyes have been obliterated. That is: if We willed, We would have hastened for them a punishment in this world by which they would be restrained, so that they would desist from their polytheism.

Maskh is changing the body of a human into the form of a body not of its own kind. This was discussed earlier at God's words ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised"﴾ [al-Baqara 2:65] in Surat al-Baqara.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the one who is transformed does not live more than three days. On this basis, none of the existing things at present is a remnant of a transformation.

Al-makāna is the feminine of al-makān (place), treated as a patch of ground. Similarly they say: muqām and muqāma, dār and dāra. The meaning is: if We willed, We would have transformed the disbelievers in this world in their place where they displayed their denial of the Messengers, so they would be unable to turn away toward what they had come out for, nor to return to what they had come from. Rather, they would remain in their place, because human reason would have departed from them through the transformation.

The expected parallel would have been: "nor a return," but he deviated to ﴿nor do they return﴾ for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fāṣila). So His words ﴿nor do they return﴾ were made a coordination with the clause ﴿they were not able﴾, and it is not a coordination with "muḍiyyan" (proceeding), because the verb istaṭāʿa does not govern clauses. The implied meaning is: "they did not proceed, nor did they return." Thus We made the punishment for them in this world before the Hereafter, and We relieved the believers of them, and We left them as a lesson and an admonition for those who come after them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 68:

﴿And whomever We cause to live long, We reverse him in creation. Will they not then reason?﴾ It may appear at first glance that the placement of this verse is strange within its context, so that one supposes it to be a fresh statement, the subject of the discourse having shifted from the polytheists, their conditions, and being granted respite, to a reminder of a wondrous matter of God's making, to the extent that one imagines that what necessitated the placement of this verse in this position is that it was revealed at a time separate from the revelation of the verses before it, for a reason that required its revelation. Many of the exegetes therefore made its position the position of inference (istidlal) that God's power is not difficult for Him to exercise, whether in obliterating their eyes or transforming them, just as He changed the constitution of the long-lived from strength to weakness. This would be a qiyas of approximation of the kind called in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) al-qiyas al-khafi (the hidden analogy) and bi-al-adwan (the lesser analogy). It would then be coordinated with a presumed cause in the speech, as if it were said: "If We willed, We would obliterate..." etc., because We are capable of reversing conditions. Do they not see how We turn the creation of man, making him other than what We created him at first? After all of this, the placement of the conjunctive waw is not very cohesive.

Some exegetes made its position the position of inference concerning the distant place, meaning that He who is capable of changing their creation from youth to decrepitude is capable of resurrecting them after death. This too is a qiyas of approximation by the hidden and the lesser analogy.

Among them are those who spoke on it while disregarding what precedes it, so they spoke on its meaning and the lesson within it, without explaining the manner of its connection to what precedes it.

Among them are those who took it to cut off the excuse of the polytheists on that Day, when they would say: "We did not remain in the world except for a short time, and had we lived long, there would have been no shortcoming on our part." This is far from the implication of His words ﴿We reverse him in creation﴾. All these interpretations revolve around taking "creation" in the verbal-noun sense, i.e., in his constitution or in the effect of his creation.

All these interpretations are far from the composition of the speech. What appears is that what impelled the exegetes to this was the familiar usage of "ta'mir" (granting long life) for the lengthening of the lifespan of one who is made to live long. When they interpreted it in this sense, they attached the interpretation of "nunakkisuhu fi al-khalq" to suit that.

My view is that since the sentence "wa man nu'ammiruhu" (And whomever We cause to live long) is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾ [Ya-Sin: 67], it is a conditional sentence coordinated upon a conditional sentence. The sentence coordinated upon is a conditional of impossibility (shart imtina'i), and the coordinated sentence is a conditional of contingency (shart ta'liqi). The first sentence expressed their being granted respite and being given leeway, and the coordinated sentence expressed warning them of an undesirable outcome and threatening them with its befalling them. That is: if We have not transformed them nor obliterated their eyes, then We have left them alive so that they would be defeated and humiliated. Thus the meaning of "wa man nu'ammiruhu" is: whomever We leave alive from among them.

So ta'mir here means letting remain, i.e., whomever We leave alive from among them and do not uproot from among them, i.e., from among the polytheists, making him humiliated among the nations. The ta'mir intended here is like the ta'mir in His words ﴿Did We not grant you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed in it?﴾ [Fatir: 37], in that its meaning is: Did We not leave you for a period of life sufficient for the one who reflects, which is what is implied by His words ﴿for whoever would take heed to take heed in it﴾ [Fatir: 37].

The ta'mir in this verse does not mean the lengthening of life and reaching decrepitude as in the saying "so-and-so is among the long-lived," for that did not befall all the people of the Fire who were addressed by His words "Did We not grant you a long life?" A sentence has been elided in the speech whose estimate is: "And if We willed, We would have destroyed them," indicated by His words "whomever We cause to live long," i.e., leave alive.

Al-nakṣ (نكس) is literally the turning of the upper part downward, or what is near the bottom. He said, Exalted is He, ﴿Those who hang their heads down﴾ [As-Sajdah: 12]. It is used figuratively for returning from a good condition to a bad one; hence one says "so-and-so is nakis" when he is weak and not hoped for in valor, and it is a verb in the sense of a passive participle, as if he were overturned in the qualities of manhood. Thus "nunakkisuhu" is undoubtedly figurative, though we take it as figurative for humiliation after honor and a bad condition after its brightness.

Al-khalq (الخلق) is the verbal noun of khalaqahu, and it is often used for the created thing and for people. In the hadith of 'A'isha concerning the church that Umm Salama and Umm Habiba saw in Abyssinia, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And those are the worst of creation in the sight of God on the Day of Resurrection," meaning the worst of people.

The occurrence of the particle "fi" (في) here specifies that al-khalq is intended to mean people, i.e., We make him a sign among the people. This is more fitting to this meaning than the meaning "in his constitution," because reversal does not occur in the original constitution but in its stages. This has been explained by His words ﴿and He increased you in creation in breadth﴾ [Al-A'raf: 69], i.e., He increased you in strength and breadth among the nations, i.e., among the nations contemporary with you. So it is a threat to them and a promise to the believers of victory over the polytheists and their coming under the authority of the Muslims, for those who were chiefs of the polytheists in the Jahiliyya became captives of the Muslims on the Day of Badr, and were under their judgment on the Day of the Conquest, so they were called the Tulaqa' (the freed ones).

The majority read "nankusuhu" with a fathah on the first nun, sukun on the second nun, and a damma on the kaf, lightened, which is the imperfect of the transitive nakasa, as one says nakasa ra'sahu (he lowered his head). ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it with a damma on the first nun, a fathah on the second nun, and a kasra on the kaf, doubled, the imperfect of nakkasa, the intensive form.

Following the three conditional sentences and what is derived from them, the words ﴿Will they not then reason?﴾ come as a reproachful resumption, for their failure to reflect on the great power of God Most High, which indicates that if He willed He would obliterate their eyes, and if He willed He would transform them in their places, and that if He does not do that, they will not be safe from His support of the Muslims against them. For if they measured the observable powers of God Most High, they would know that His power to transform them, and what is less than that of bringing down a disliked thing upon them, is easier than His power to create the great and perfected creatures, and that there is no barrier between the attachment of His power to transforming them except that He does not will that, for a wisdom He knows, since power is only attached to what is within its capacity in accordance with the will.

Nafi' and Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Abu 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read "a-fa-la ta'qilun" with the ta' of address, and it is an address to those to whom His words were directed, ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ [Ya-Sin: 66], and so on. The rest read it with the ya' of the third person, because those conditional sentences are not free from a confrontation by allusion with those spoken about, so they were deserving that they understand its import and comprehend its meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 69–70 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him. It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿That it may warn whoever is alive, and that the word may be justified against the disbelievers.﴾ This verse refers back to what is contained in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾ [Ya-Sin: 46].

So the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 48], as a narrative conjoined to a narrative and a purpose to a purpose. It is also possible that it is a fresh, initial resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), with the waw being for resumption; for this reason it confined itself here to declaring the Qur'an free from being poetry and the Prophet ﷺ free from being a poet, without addressing a declaration of his freedom from being a sorcerer or a madman, because the purpose is the response to their turning away from the Qur'an. Do you not see that when it intended to nullify their statements about the Qur'an, it said in the other verse ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41] ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42].

The pronoun in "'allamnahu" refers to something known from the context of refutation, and not to something mentioned, since no antecedent had preceded it.

The refutation was built upon them in the manner of metonymy (kinayah), by negating that the Prophet ﷺ was taught poetry, because this conveys that the Qur'an is taught to the Prophet ﷺ by Allah, exalted is He, and that it is not poetry, and that the Prophet ﷺ is not a poet.

"Poetry" (al-shi'r) is in the accusative as a second object of the verb "'allamnahu." This verb is one of the verbs of knowledge, and its unaugmented form transitively takes one object in most cases, such as "he knew the matter" ('alima al-mas'alah). It takes two objects whose original form is the subject and predicate; when it takes the intensive form (tad'if), it becomes transitive to two objects only, on the basis that its unaugmented form is transitive to one, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when I taught you the Book and wisdom﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110] in Surah al-Ma'idah, and His saying ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾ in this Surah Ya-Sin.

Page 57

This is a distinction in usage left to the testing of the people of the language, which al-Radi noted in his commentary on al-Kafiyah in the chapter on the transitivity of the verbs of the heart to two objects, that its origin is transitive to one.

So the meaning is estimated as: We taught him the Qur'an, ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾. The Qur'an was revealed to him by teaching from Allah, and what He revealed to him is not poetry. Thus the meaning is: the Qur'an has nothing whatsoever of poetry. Therefore this sentence was a response to their saying "he is a poet" in the manner of metonymy, because it is a movement from the necessary consequence to the thing necessitated.

What indicates that this is the intended meaning of ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾ is His saying after it, ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, that is: what We taught him is nothing but a reminder and a Qur'an, and it is not poetry.

Teaching here means revelation, that is: We did not reveal poetry to him. Teaching has been used for revelation in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is only a revelation that is revealed, taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 4], and He said ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisa': 113].

How could the Qur'an be poetry, when poetry is speech that is metrical and rhymed, having meanings suited to its aims, most of which are jest and entertainment? Where is the meter in the Qur'an, where is the rhyme, where are the meanings that poetry produces, where is the arrangement of their speech compared with its arrangement, and their styles compared with its styles? It is among the marvels of audacity that such a statement should issue from people of language and eloquence, while they have no basis whatsoever for it; so their saying this is nothing but slander.

What the style of the Qur'an is built upon, namely the equality of the closing rhyming units (fawasil), does not make them equivalent to the rhymes (qawafi), as the people of the craft know, and everyone who has practiced the rudiments of rhyme among the muwallads. I do not think they called it poetry except out of haste in nullifying it, or as a deception to mislead the unwary. They spread among the Arabs that Muhammad ﷺ is a poet and that his speech is poetry. From this suspicion arises the report of Unays ibn Junadah al-Ghifari, brother of Abu Dharr. al-Bukhari related it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muslim from 'Abdullah ibn al-Samit, one of them adding to the other, and both said: "Abu Dharr said to his brother: 'Ride to this valley and learn for me the news of this man who claims that he is a prophet, to whom news comes from heaven, and listen to his speech, then come back to me.' So the brother set out until he arrived, heard his speech, then returned to Abu

Dharr." He said to him: "I saw him commanding noble character, and speech that is not poetry at all." Abu Dharr said: "What do the people say?" He said: "They say: a poet, a soothsayer, a sorcerer." Unays was one of the poets. Unays said: "I have heard the speech of the soothsayers, and it is not like theirs. I have set his speech against the recitations of poetry, and it does not agree on the tongue of anyone after me that it is poetry. By Allah, he is truthful, and they are liars." Then he related the report of Abu Dharr's conversion to Islam. It appears that this was at the beginning of the mission.

Similar is the report of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, which al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Ishaq related: that he gathered the Quraysh at the time of the season (of pilgrimage) to consult about the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. He said to them: "The delegations of the Arabs come to you, so agree upon one opinion about him, so that some of you do not contradict others." They said: "Shall we say he is a soothsayer?" He said: "By Allah, he is not a soothsayer, nor is he of their murmuring or their rhymed prose." They said: "Shall we say he is possessed?" He said: "By Allah, he is not possessed, nor of their choking or their whispering." He mentioned their hesitation in describing him until they said: "Shall we say he is a poet?" He said: "He is not a poet. I have known poetry in its entirety: its rajaz, its hazaj, its qarid, its mabsut and its maqbud, and he is not a poet."

To the end of the story.

So the meaning of ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾ is: We did not reveal to him poetry that We taught him.

It is not meant that Allah did not place in the nature of the Prophet ﷺ the capacity to compose poetry, because that capacity is not called teaching so that it would be negated. This meaning is rather derived from His saying after it, ﴿nor is it befitting for him﴾, and we will speak on it shortly.

The verse has required the negation that the Qur'an is poetry. This requirement has raised objections from the heretics and problems for the sincere. For there are found passages of the Qur'an that complete the measure of some of the poetic meters, some of which form a complete line of verse, and some of which form a single hemistich, and you do not find more than that. So this entails the occurrence of poetry in the verses of the Qur'an.

The heretics have raised this objection, and therefore Abu Bakr al-Baqillani addressed its refutation in his book (I'jaz al-Qur'an), and he was followed by al-Sakkaki and Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. As for al-Baqillani, he stood alone with a response in which he said: a single line does not get called poetry, let alone a hemistich that does not complete a line. I consider this insufficient here, because it cannot be ensured that the designation of poetry is negated from the hemistich, and even more so from the line.
