It is said to them, before considering what they have brought forward: have they distorted by addition or subtraction, a vowel or a letter, or not? And before we look at whether they observed the rules of the science of prosody in the meters and the forms of the feet (a'arid wa-darub) mentioned earlier, or not. And before we look at whether they acted upon the preferred of the two positions on the meaning of poetry as previously mentioned, or not. By the two positions I mean: the position of those who said poetry is not poetry unless its speaker intended it to be metrical, and the position of those who said: intending the meter is not obligatory, rather it suffices that it be found metrical even without the intention of its speaker for the meter. The first position has been supported. Glory be to Allah! They have considered all of that as poetry. Is it not correct, by the judgment of predominance, that what they have pointed out, due to its scarcity, should not be paid attention to, and the Qur'an should be treated as free of poetry, so that it is said, in accordance with the requirements of eloquence: (﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾)? End of his words. He has inclined with it toward two matters:

One: that what occurs in the Qur'an of metrical speech is not intended by it to be metrical, so it is not poetry according to the opinion of the majority who require the intention to meter, because Allah, exalted is He, did not concern Himself with its being metrical.

Two: even if we concede that intention is not required, the negation that the Qur'an is poetry proceeds according to what is predominant. So its speaker is not counted as a liar or ignorant, and it does not contradict the certainty that the Qur'an is from Allah, which He taught to Muhammad ﷺ.

Ibn al-'Arabi, in Ahkam al-Qur'an, inclined to the view that what they have taken pains to extract from the Qur'an, passages on poetic measures, does not hold true except by one of several matters, such as cutting off the speech, adding a silent letter, or dropping a letter or two. He mentioned examples of that, some of which do not complete, so refer to it.

There is no escape from acknowledging that the Qur'an includes metrical passages from which a line or a hemistich is formed. As for what falls short of a line, it is as nothing, since poetry is not less than a line. There is no benefit in the objection from bringing what is found metrical, for the occurrence of what equals a complete line from a meter of Arabic poetry, even if rarely, or with a variant or an altered form, suffices to keep the problem in place. So there is no need for what Ibn al-'Arabi followed in his refutation, nor is what al-Sakkaki followed in his book sufficient, because those against whom the refutation is directed have latitude to adopt what suits their doctrine from the weakest positions concerning the reality of poetry and concerning its variations and its prosodic defects. After all this, al-Baqillani and al-Sakkaki did not delve

Page 61

**[Page 61 continues]** ...to uproot the objection that the second answer raises, in their statement that there was no intention to produce metre. From this it follows that the matter would be hidden from God's knowledge. So why not place, in the position of those metrical phrases, phrases that are free of metre?

I have not seen any of the exegetes or those who delve into the aspects of the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an take up the task of uprooting this doubt, though a period of time has passed since it was raised. I was never convinced by those responses, nor did I find them satisfying, and I saw that they did not reach the final goal of the race-course's horses.

What appeared to me is this: the Qur'an was revealed in the most eloquent of the languages of mankind, those that people have agreed upon and established. Had there been a speech more eloquent than the speech of the Arabs, or a nation more naturally inclined than the Arab nation, God would have chosen it for the manifestation of the best laws, the most noble messengers and the most honoured divine books.

It is known that the Qur'an came as a miracle to the eloquent Arabs. Its structures and meanings reached a degree of eloquence that every eloquent person among them falls short of, to the extent that the Arabic language can accommodate in terms of fluency and rhetoric. When the requirement of the situation (*muqtaḍā al-ḥāl*) in a particular context of discourse demands, to render the right of fluency and rhetoric, words, structure and arrangement, and it happens that the totality of its vowels and consonants conforms to the scale of Arabic poetry in its metres (*a'ārīḍ*) and their variants (*ḍurūb*), that speech would not be counted as poetry if such a thing occurred in human speech unintentionally. Its occurrence in human speech may not be noticed by its speaker, and if he noticed it, it would not be difficult to change it, because it is not the ultimate of what the situation requires, unless it was intended as a stylistic variation (*tafannun*) in producing a speech whose outward form is prose while its disassembled form is verse.

As for its occurrence in the speech of God the Exalted, it is excluded from all of that for three reasons:

First: God is not unaware of its occurrence in a speech that He revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ).

Second: it is not permissible to replace that totality of words with others, because their totality is all that the situation requires and has reached the limit of inimitability.

Third: God does not wish the revealed speech from Him to include the embellishment of combining prose and verse, because He willed to exalt His speech above any trace of poetry.

Know that the wisdom behind the Qur'an not being poetry, although those challenged by it are the eloquent Arabs, and most of them are poets, and their eloquence is deposited in their poetry, is that it combines inimitability with closing the door to the doubt that would befall them if the Qur'an had come according to the measures of poetry. That doubt is like an error or a sophistry, by counting the Prophet (ﷺ) among the poets. Thus the majority of people, whose perceptions do not penetrate to the realities, would think that what the Messenger brought is not extraordinary, and that the one who brought it is not a prophet but a poet. So the Qur'an was a miracle to the eloquent Arabs by being of the kind of their speech, which they could not deny. Yet it is not of the category called poetry; rather it surpasses their poetry in its eloquent beauties. It is not in the style of poetry with the metres they were accustomed to, but in the style of the heavenly books and the Remembrance.

The wisdom of the All-Knower of the unseen has indeed become manifest in this. When the polytheists heard the Qur'an, they hastened to challenge its being sent down from God, by saying of the Messenger: "He is a poet," meaning that his speech is poetry, until their intellectuals awakened them from their heedlessness, such as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and Unays ibn Junāda, and until the Qur'an struck them with this verse: ﴿We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him. It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾.

After this, the composing of poetry does not leave the poet free from altering the arrangement of speech at times in ways that eloquence does not require, such as what happened to some poets of verbal convolution, and such as the anteriorization and posteriorization contrary to the requirement of the situation. These are excused by the excuse of poetic necessity (*ḍarūra*). So if the Qur'an had come as poetry, it would have fallen short in some places of fulfilling the whole requirement of the situation.

We will mention, when explaining His saying "and it is not fitting for him," aspects most of which correspond to what His saying here indicates: ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said that the pronoun governed by the preposition *lām* in His saying "and it is not fitting for him" may refer to the Qur'an, as will come.

His saying "and it is not fitting for him" is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*) placed between the two conjoined clauses. Its purpose is to follow the negation that the Qur'an revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) is poetry, with the negation that the Prophet (ﷺ) is a poet in what he says apart from what was revealed to him. That is, God created the Prophet (ﷺ) with an aversion between his verbal faculty and the poetic faculty. That is, He did not give him the faculty of the practitioners of versifying, because He willed to cut off from the souls of the deniers the root of the idea that the Prophet (ﷺ) is a poet, or that his Qur'an is poetry; so that their calumny becomes clear to anyone with even a little discernment of speech. Many of them are among the Arabs, their men, and many of their women, except the wife of 'Abd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa and her like. The *wāw* is parenthetical (*i'tirāḍiyya*).

The pronoun in "yanbaghī" refers to poetry. The pronoun in "lahu" may refer to what the pronoun of the absent in His saying "'allamnāhu" refers to, which is the apparent reading. Ibn 'Aṭiyya allowed that it refers to the Qur'an that the verb "'allamnāhu" contains, and so made the clause "and it is not fitting for him" stand in the position of a justification for the clause ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾.

The meaning of "wa mā yanbaghī lahu" is: what poetry is not attainable for him. The explanation of this was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿It is not fitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92] in Surat Maryam, and before that, shortly, at His saying ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ [Yasin: 40]. The basic meaning of "yanbaghī" is "responds to *al-baghy*," i.e. urgent seeking. Then it came to mean "is attainable and proper," and the sense of reciprocity was forgotten from it, so that "yanbaghī" came to mean "is attainable," as one says: "such-and-such is not yanbaghī," i.e. is not attainable. Al-Ṭībī said: it is narrated from al-Zamakhsharī that he said in the book of Sībawayh: every verb which involves treatment (*'ilāj*) comes with a reflexive form of passivity (*infi'āl*), like *ḍaraba*, *ṭalaba* and *'alima*; and what does not involve treatment, like *'adima* and *faqada*, does not at all take the reflexive passive form in its reflexive.

The meaning of poetry being "not fitting for him" is that the composing of poetry is not fitting for him, since poetry is a kind of speech that has measures and rhymes. The Prophet (ﷺ) is exempt from versifying and composing it; that is, the formation of poetic measures is not among the natural dispositions of his faculty. The intended meaning is not that he does not recite poetry, because reciting poetry is not the same as learning to compose it. How many transmitters of poetry and critics of poetry cannot compose poetry! Likewise the Prophet (ﷺ) had criticised poetry, pointed out some of its merits, and preferred some poets over others, yet he did not compose poetry. Sometimes he recited a verse and forgot the arrangement of its words, so its metre was sometimes broken in his recitation. This is part of the complete incompatibility between the faculty of his eloquence and the faculty of the poets. Do you not see that it was not consistent, for at times he recited a verse that was metrically correct?

This is the side of the composition of poetry and its measures. Likewise the side of the substance of poetry and its meanings: poetry has modes of subject matter, such as amatory verse (*ghazal*), erotic prelude (*nasīb*), satire (*hijā'*), panegyric (*madīḥ*) and witticisms (*mulaḥ*); and modes of meanings, such as extreme exaggeration to the point of hyperbole, and the poet's claiming for himself states of passion, travel or courage of which he is devoid of their reality. This is a forgivable falsehood in the craft of poetry. Such a thing does not befit the highest station of the perfections of the soul, which is the station of the greatest of the messengers, God's blessings be upon him and upon them. If the Prophet (ﷺ) had composed poetry without bringing into it the artifices of the poets, his poetry would have been counted a deficiency, and that deficiency would have been a cause for people to reproach him, impairing the sanctity of his perfection in the souls of his people, a matter in which enemy and friend would equally share.

Moreover, the poets of that time were held in disrepute by people of honour and dignity, because of their dissolute conduct, their devotion to drinking, gambling, women and the like. It suffices you what is well known about the story of Ḥujr al-Kindī disinheriting his son Imru' al-Qays. God the Exalted has said ﴿And the poets are followed by the misguided﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 224], and so on. So if the Messenger (ﷺ) had brought poetry or uttered it, people would have looked at him with the eye with which the lofty value of his station and the noble nature of his honour are not looked upon. The consideration in this matter is the prevalent and common case. Otherwise, the Prophet (ﷺ) has said: "Indeed, there is wisdom in some poetry," and said: "The truest word ever spoken by a poet is the word of Labīd:

*Certainly, everything except God is vain.*"

So the exempting of the Prophet (ﷺ) from uttering poetry is part of safeguarding the inimitability of the Qur'an and safeguarding the station of prophethood, just like his exemption from knowing writing.

Abū Bakr ibn al-'Arabī said: this verse is not a defect in poetry, just as His saying ﴿You did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾ [al-'Ankabūt: 48] was not a defect in writing. Since illiteracy was not a defect in writing, likewise the negation of composition from the Prophet (ﷺ) is not a defect in poetry.

Because of the usefulness and influence that poetry has in spreading the call of Islam, the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded Ḥassān and 'Abd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa to compose poetry, and he showed his approval of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr when he recited to him the famous ode, "Su'ād has departed."

What is said about the words spoken by the Prophet (ﷺ) that are metrical, such as his saying on the day of Uhud: "I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib," is like what is said about what occurred in the Qur'an of similar things, which we have explained just above.

The clause ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ is a explanatory resumption (*isti'nāf bayānī*), because the negation of poetry from the Qur'an raises a question from an inquirer who says: "What then is this which was revealed to Muḥammad (ﷺ)?" So His saying ﴿It is only a reminder﴾ is the answer to his demand.

The pronoun "huwa" refers to the Qur'an understood from "'allamnāhu," i.e. what was taught to him is only a reminder and a Qur'an. Or it refers to the thing that We taught him, i.e. to the taught thing contained in "'allamnāhu." Or it refers to "dhikr" in His saying "illā dhikr," which is "mubīn." This is one of the places where a pronoun refers to something that comes later in wording and rank, because the explanatory element is like an apposition. Its parallel has occurred in His saying ﴿It is only our life of this world﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 37] in Surat al-Mu'minūn.

The exclusive form that restricts the revelation to the attribute of being a reminder and a Qur'an is a restriction of reversal (*qaṣr qalb*), that is: it is not poetry as you claim. Through this, a thorough refutation of them is achieved, and the emphasis of His saying ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾ is established, and the meaning implied by His saying ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾ is confirmed, namely that the Qur'an is poetry.

"Dhikr" is a verbal noun described as the attribute of the Book sent down to Muḥammad (ﷺ), as an intensive description, i.e. it is only one who reminds people of what they have forgotten or did not know. The discussion of "dhikr" has already been covered at His saying ﴿They said: O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are truly mad﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 6] in Surat al-Ḥijr.

"Qur'an" is the verbal noun of *qara'a*, used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e. the recited speech. Its explanation was given at His saying ﴿and you do not recite from it any Qur'an﴾ [Yūnus: 61] in Surat Yūnus.

"Mubīn" is the one that makes the intended meaning clear with eloquence and rhetoric.

His saying "li-tundhira" is connected to His saying "'allamnāhu," in view of what is joined to it of the negation of its being poetry, then the affirmation of its being a reminder and a Qur'an. That is, because the clause ﴿It is only a reminder﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it, having the force of saying: "And We did not teach him anything but a reminder and a clear Qur'an, so that he may warn," or "so that you may warn." Ibn 'Aṭiyya made it connected to "mubīn."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 36, verses 69–70 (part 3 of 3):**

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read *"litundhira"* with the second-person ta' (*ta' al-khitab*), as an *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person) from the third-person pronoun in His saying *"'allamnahu"* to a second-person pronoun. The rest read it with the third-person ya', meaning the Prophet whom We taught.

*Al-indhar* (warning) is informing someone of a matter from which one must guard oneself.

*Al-hayy* (the living) is used figuratively for one of complete intellect and sound perception. This is an eloquent comparison: whoever is like the living in understanding.

The intended meaning is an indirect reproach of those who turn away from the proofs of the Qur'an: they are like the dead, having no benefit from their minds, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs in retreat﴾ [al-Naml: 80].

The phrase *﴿wa-yahiqqa al-qawlu 'ala al-kafirin﴾* (and the word will be justified against the disbelievers) is coordinated with *"litundhira"* by *'atf al-majaz 'ala al-haqiqah* (coordination of the figurative with the literal). This is because the *lam* that the conjunction *waw* stands in for is not a *lam* of purpose, but *lam al-'aqibah* (the lam of consequence), like the *lam* in His saying ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. Thus there is a *isti'arah tab'iyyah* (a contextual metaphor) in the *waw*, and this is close to the use of a homonym in both of its meanings.

In this consequence there is also *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one term is omitted from each of two parallel clauses, each being implied by the other). The implied sense is: that you may warn whoever is living, so that he increases in life by heeding the Reminder and thereby succeeds; and whoever is dead, who does not benefit from the warning, so that the word is justified against him. This is as He said at the beginning of the surah ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a noble reward﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11], combining for him warning at the outset and good tidings at the end.

*Al-qawl* (the word) is the statement that came with the threat against those who did not benefit from the warning of the Messenger ﷺ.

[Page 67]

By *al-kafirin* (the disbelievers) is meant those who persisted in their disbelief. Otherwise, the warning was addressed to people at first, and all of them were disbelievers.

The mention of warning returns to what the surah opened with, His saying ﴿that you may warn a people whose fathers were never warned﴾ [Ya-Sin: 6]. It is like *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr* (repeating the end of a passage at its beginning). With this, the field of argument against them is complete and their doubts are refuted, and the discourse proceeds to the favour that follows in His saying ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, from what Our hands have made, cattle, of which they are the owners?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71], up to His saying ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 73].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 69–70 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him. It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿That it may warn whoever is alive, and that the word may be justified against the disbelievers.﴾ This verse refers back to what is contained in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾ [Ya-Sin: 46].

Page 56

We have already explained that the intended meaning of "the signs" is the signs of the Qur'an. Their turning away from the Qur'an takes various forms: some of it is through not complying with what it commands them of good, together with mocking the Muslims, and this is His saying, ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47] and so on. Some of it is through denying what it warns them of regarding recompense, and this is His saying, ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 48]. And among their turning away from it is their slandering of the verses of the Qur'an in various statements, among them their saying: "It is the saying of a poet." So when the Qur'an took up the task of refuting their denial with a warning of recompense on the Day of Gathering, and what followed of speech on that, it returned here to their slander of the wording of the Qur'an, from their saying ﴿Rather he has invented it; rather he is a poet﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5], which necessarily implies that they say: the Qur'an is poetry.

So the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 48], as a narrative conjoined to a narrative and a purpose to a purpose. It is also possible that it is a fresh, initial resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), with the waw being for resumption; for this reason it confined itself here to declaring the Qur'an free from being poetry and the Prophet ﷺ free from being a poet, without addressing a declaration of his freedom from being a sorcerer or a madman, because the purpose is the response to their turning away from the Qur'an. Do you not see that when it intended to nullify their statements about the Qur'an, it said in the other verse ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41] ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42].

The pronoun in "'allamnahu" refers to something known from the context of refutation, and not to something mentioned, since no antecedent had preceded it.

The refutation was built upon them in the manner of metonymy (kinayah), by negating that the Prophet ﷺ was taught poetry, because this conveys that the Qur'an is taught to the Prophet ﷺ by Allah, exalted is He, and that it is not poetry, and that the Prophet ﷺ is not a poet.

"Poetry" (al-shi'r) is in the accusative as a second object of the verb "'allamnahu." This verb is one of the verbs of knowledge, and its unaugmented form transitively takes one object in most cases, such as "he knew the matter" ('alima al-mas'alah). It takes two objects whose original form is the subject and predicate; when it takes the intensive form (tad'if), it becomes transitive to two objects only, on the basis that its unaugmented form is transitive to one, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when I taught you the Book and wisdom﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110] in Surah al-Ma'idah, and His saying ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾ in this Surah Ya-Sin.

Page 57

This is a distinction in usage left to the testing of the people of the language, which al-Radi noted in his commentary on al-Kafiyah in the chapter on the transitivity of the verbs of the heart to two objects, that its origin is transitive to one.

So the meaning is estimated as: We taught him the Qur'an, ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾. The Qur'an was revealed to him by teaching from Allah, and what He revealed to him is not poetry. Thus the meaning is: the Qur'an has nothing whatsoever of poetry. Therefore this sentence was a response to their saying "he is a poet" in the manner of metonymy, because it is a movement from the necessary consequence to the thing necessitated.

What indicates that this is the intended meaning of ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾ is His saying after it, ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, that is: what We taught him is nothing but a reminder and a Qur'an, and it is not poetry.

Teaching here means revelation, that is: We did not reveal poetry to him. Teaching has been used for revelation in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is only a revelation that is revealed, taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 4], and He said ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisa': 113].

How could the Qur'an be poetry, when poetry is speech that is metrical and rhymed, having meanings suited to its aims, most of which are jest and entertainment? Where is the meter in the Qur'an, where is the rhyme, where are the meanings that poetry produces, where is the arrangement of their speech compared with its arrangement, and their styles compared with its styles? It is among the marvels of audacity that such a statement should issue from people of language and eloquence, while they have no basis whatsoever for it; so their saying this is nothing but slander.

What the style of the Qur'an is built upon, namely the equality of the closing rhyming units (fawasil), does not make them equivalent to the rhymes (qawafi), as the people of the craft know, and everyone who has practiced the rudiments of rhyme among the muwallads. I do not think they called it poetry except out of haste in nullifying it, or as a deception to mislead the unwary. They spread among the Arabs that Muhammad ﷺ is a poet and that his speech is poetry. From this suspicion arises the report of Unays ibn Junadah al-Ghifari, brother of Abu Dharr. al-Bukhari related it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muslim from 'Abdullah ibn al-Samit, one of them adding to the other, and both said: "Abu Dharr said to his brother: 'Ride to this valley and learn for me the news of this man who claims that he is a prophet, to whom news comes from heaven, and listen to his speech, then come back to me.' So the brother set out until he arrived, heard his speech, then returned to Abu

Page 58

Dharr." He said to him: "I saw him commanding noble character, and speech that is not poetry at all." Abu Dharr said: "What do the people say?" He said: "They say: a poet, a soothsayer, a sorcerer." Unays was one of the poets. Unays said: "I have heard the speech of the soothsayers, and it is not like theirs. I have set his speech against the recitations of poetry, and it does not agree on the tongue of anyone after me that it is poetry. By Allah, he is truthful, and they are liars." Then he related the report of Abu Dharr's conversion to Islam. It appears that this was at the beginning of the mission.

Similar is the report of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, which al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Ishaq related: that he gathered the Quraysh at the time of the season (of pilgrimage) to consult about the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. He said to them: "The delegations of the Arabs come to you, so agree upon one opinion about him, so that some of you do not contradict others." They said: "Shall we say he is a soothsayer?" He said: "By Allah, he is not a soothsayer, nor is he of their murmuring or their rhymed prose." They said: "Shall we say he is possessed?" He said: "By Allah, he is not possessed, nor of their choking or their whispering." He mentioned their hesitation in describing him until they said: "Shall we say he is a poet?" He said: "He is not a poet. I have known poetry in its entirety: its rajaz, its hazaj, its qarid, its mabsut and its maqbud, and he is not a poet."

To the end of the story.

So the meaning of ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾ is: We did not reveal to him poetry that We taught him.

It is not meant that Allah did not place in the nature of the Prophet ﷺ the capacity to compose poetry, because that capacity is not called teaching so that it would be negated. This meaning is rather derived from His saying after it, ﴿nor is it befitting for him﴾, and we will speak on it shortly.

The verse has required the negation that the Qur'an is poetry. This requirement has raised objections from the heretics and problems for the sincere. For there are found passages of the Qur'an that complete the measure of some of the poetic meters, some of which form a complete line of verse, and some of which form a single hemistich, and you do not find more than that. So this entails the occurrence of poetry in the verses of the Qur'an.

The heretics have raised this objection, and therefore Abu Bakr al-Baqillani addressed its refutation in his book (I'jaz al-Qur'an), and he was followed by al-Sakkaki and Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. As for al-Baqillani, he stood alone with a response in which he said: a single line does not get called poetry, let alone a hemistich that does not complete a line. I consider this insufficient here, because it cannot be ensured that the designation of poetry is negated from the hemistich, and even more so from the line.

It is said to them, before considering what they have brought forward: have they distorted by addition or subtraction, a vowel or a letter, or not? And before we look at whether they observed the rules of the science of prosody in the meters and the forms of the feet (a'arid wa-darub) mentioned earlier, or not. And before we look at whether they acted upon the preferred of the two positions on the meaning of poetry as previously mentioned, or not. By the two positions I mean: the position of those who said poetry is not poetry unless its speaker intended it to be metrical, and the position of those who said: intending the meter is not obligatory, rather it suffices that it be found metrical even without the intention of its speaker for the meter. The first position has been supported. Glory be to Allah! They have considered all of that as poetry. Is it not correct, by the judgment of predominance, that what they have pointed out, due to its scarcity, should not be paid attention to, and the Qur'an should be treated as free of poetry, so that it is said, in accordance with the requirements of eloquence: (﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾)? End of his words. He has inclined with it toward two matters:

One: that what occurs in the Qur'an of metrical speech is not intended by it to be metrical, so it is not poetry according to the opinion of the majority who require the intention to meter, because Allah, exalted is He, did not concern Himself with its being metrical.

Two: even if we concede that intention is not required, the negation that the Qur'an is poetry proceeds according to what is predominant. So its speaker is not counted as a liar or ignorant, and it does not contradict the certainty that the Qur'an is from Allah, which He taught to Muhammad ﷺ.

Ibn al-'Arabi, in Ahkam al-Qur'an, inclined to the view that what they have taken pains to extract from the Qur'an, passages on poetic measures, does not hold true except by one of several matters, such as cutting off the speech, adding a silent letter, or dropping a letter or two. He mentioned examples of that, some of which do not complete, so refer to it.

There is no escape from acknowledging that the Qur'an includes metrical passages from which a line or a hemistich is formed. As for what falls short of a line, it is as nothing, since poetry is not less than a line. There is no benefit in the objection from bringing what is found metrical, for the occurrence of what equals a complete line from a meter of Arabic poetry, even if rarely, or with a variant or an altered form, suffices to keep the problem in place. So there is no need for what Ibn al-'Arabi followed in his refutation, nor is what al-Sakkaki followed in his book sufficient, because those against whom the refutation is directed have latitude to adopt what suits their doctrine from the weakest positions concerning the reality of poetry and concerning its variations and its prosodic defects. After all this, al-Baqillani and al-Sakkaki did not delve

Page 61

**[Page 61 continues]** ...to uproot the objection that the second answer raises, in their statement that there was no intention to produce metre. From this it follows that the matter would be hidden from God's knowledge. So why not place, in the position of those metrical phrases, phrases that are free of metre?

I have not seen any of the exegetes or those who delve into the aspects of the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an take up the task of uprooting this doubt, though a period of time has passed since it was raised. I was never convinced by those responses, nor did I find them satisfying, and I saw that they did not reach the final goal of the race-course's horses.

What appeared to me is this: the Qur'an was revealed in the most eloquent of the languages of mankind, those that people have agreed upon and established. Had there been a speech more eloquent than the speech of the Arabs, or a nation more naturally inclined than the Arab nation, God would have chosen it for the manifestation of the best laws, the most noble messengers and the most honoured divine books.

It is known that the Qur'an came as a miracle to the eloquent Arabs. Its structures and meanings reached a degree of eloquence that every eloquent person among them falls short of, to the extent that the Arabic language can accommodate in terms of fluency and rhetoric. When the requirement of the situation (*muqtaḍā al-ḥāl*) in a particular context of discourse demands, to render the right of fluency and rhetoric, words, structure and arrangement, and it happens that the totality of its vowels and consonants conforms to the scale of Arabic poetry in its metres (*a'ārīḍ*) and their variants (*ḍurūb*), that speech would not be counted as poetry if such a thing occurred in human speech unintentionally. Its occurrence in human speech may not be noticed by its speaker, and if he noticed it, it would not be difficult to change it, because it is not the ultimate of what the situation requires, unless it was intended as a stylistic variation (*tafannun*) in producing a speech whose outward form is prose while its disassembled form is verse.

As for its occurrence in the speech of God the Exalted, it is excluded from all of that for three reasons:

First: God is not unaware of its occurrence in a speech that He revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ).

Second: it is not permissible to replace that totality of words with others, because their totality is all that the situation requires and has reached the limit of inimitability.

Third: God does not wish the revealed speech from Him to include the embellishment of combining prose and verse, because He willed to exalt His speech above any trace of poetry.

Know that the wisdom behind the Qur'an not being poetry, although those challenged by it are the eloquent Arabs, and most of them are poets, and their eloquence is deposited in their poetry, is that it combines inimitability with closing the door to the doubt that would befall them if the Qur'an had come according to the measures of poetry. That doubt is like an error or a sophistry, by counting the Prophet (ﷺ) among the poets. Thus the majority of people, whose perceptions do not penetrate to the realities, would think that what the Messenger brought is not extraordinary, and that the one who brought it is not a prophet but a poet. So the Qur'an was a miracle to the eloquent Arabs by being of the kind of their speech, which they could not deny. Yet it is not of the category called poetry; rather it surpasses their poetry in its eloquent beauties. It is not in the style of poetry with the metres they were accustomed to, but in the style of the heavenly books and the Remembrance.

The wisdom of the All-Knower of the unseen has indeed become manifest in this. When the polytheists heard the Qur'an, they hastened to challenge its being sent down from God, by saying of the Messenger: "He is a poet," meaning that his speech is poetry, until their intellectuals awakened them from their heedlessness, such as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and Unays ibn Junāda, and until the Qur'an struck them with this verse: ﴿We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him. It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾.

After this, the composing of poetry does not leave the poet free from altering the arrangement of speech at times in ways that eloquence does not require, such as what happened to some poets of verbal convolution, and such as the anteriorization and posteriorization contrary to the requirement of the situation. These are excused by the excuse of poetic necessity (*ḍarūra*). So if the Qur'an had come as poetry, it would have fallen short in some places of fulfilling the whole requirement of the situation.

We will mention, when explaining His saying "and it is not fitting for him," aspects most of which correspond to what His saying here indicates: ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said that the pronoun governed by the preposition *lām* in His saying "and it is not fitting for him" may refer to the Qur'an, as will come.

His saying "and it is not fitting for him" is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*) placed between the two conjoined clauses. Its purpose is to follow the negation that the Qur'an revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) is poetry, with the negation that the Prophet (ﷺ) is a poet in what he says apart from what was revealed to him. That is, God created the Prophet (ﷺ) with an aversion between his verbal faculty and the poetic faculty. That is, He did not give him the faculty of the practitioners of versifying, because He willed to cut off from the souls of the deniers the root of the idea that the Prophet (ﷺ) is a poet, or that his Qur'an is poetry; so that their calumny becomes clear to anyone with even a little discernment of speech. Many of them are among the Arabs, their men, and many of their women, except the wife of 'Abd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa and her like. The *wāw* is parenthetical (*i'tirāḍiyya*).

The pronoun in "yanbaghī" refers to poetry. The pronoun in "lahu" may refer to what the pronoun of the absent in His saying "'allamnāhu" refers to, which is the apparent reading. Ibn 'Aṭiyya allowed that it refers to the Qur'an that the verb "'allamnāhu" contains, and so made the clause "and it is not fitting for him" stand in the position of a justification for the clause ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾.

The meaning of "wa mā yanbaghī lahu" is: what poetry is not attainable for him. The explanation of this was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿It is not fitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92] in Surat Maryam, and before that, shortly, at His saying ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ [Yasin: 40]. The basic meaning of "yanbaghī" is "responds to *al-baghy*," i.e. urgent seeking. Then it came to mean "is attainable and proper," and the sense of reciprocity was forgotten from it, so that "yanbaghī" came to mean "is attainable," as one says: "such-and-such is not yanbaghī," i.e. is not attainable. Al-Ṭībī said: it is narrated from al-Zamakhsharī that he said in the book of Sībawayh: every verb which involves treatment (*'ilāj*) comes with a reflexive form of passivity (*infi'āl*), like *ḍaraba*, *ṭalaba* and *'alima*; and what does not involve treatment, like *'adima* and *faqada*, does not at all take the reflexive passive form in its reflexive.

The meaning of poetry being "not fitting for him" is that the composing of poetry is not fitting for him, since poetry is a kind of speech that has measures and rhymes. The Prophet (ﷺ) is exempt from versifying and composing it; that is, the formation of poetic measures is not among the natural dispositions of his faculty. The intended meaning is not that he does not recite poetry, because reciting poetry is not the same as learning to compose it. How many transmitters of poetry and critics of poetry cannot compose poetry! Likewise the Prophet (ﷺ) had criticised poetry, pointed out some of its merits, and preferred some poets over others, yet he did not compose poetry. Sometimes he recited a verse and forgot the arrangement of its words, so its metre was sometimes broken in his recitation. This is part of the complete incompatibility between the faculty of his eloquence and the faculty of the poets. Do you not see that it was not consistent, for at times he recited a verse that was metrically correct?

This is the side of the composition of poetry and its measures. Likewise the side of the substance of poetry and its meanings: poetry has modes of subject matter, such as amatory verse (*ghazal*), erotic prelude (*nasīb*), satire (*hijā'*), panegyric (*madīḥ*) and witticisms (*mulaḥ*); and modes of meanings, such as extreme exaggeration to the point of hyperbole, and the poet's claiming for himself states of passion, travel or courage of which he is devoid of their reality. This is a forgivable falsehood in the craft of poetry. Such a thing does not befit the highest station of the perfections of the soul, which is the station of the greatest of the messengers, God's blessings be upon him and upon them. If the Prophet (ﷺ) had composed poetry without bringing into it the artifices of the poets, his poetry would have been counted a deficiency, and that deficiency would have been a cause for people to reproach him, impairing the sanctity of his perfection in the souls of his people, a matter in which enemy and friend would equally share.

Moreover, the poets of that time were held in disrepute by people of honour and dignity, because of their dissolute conduct, their devotion to drinking, gambling, women and the like. It suffices you what is well known about the story of Ḥujr al-Kindī disinheriting his son Imru' al-Qays. God the Exalted has said ﴿And the poets are followed by the misguided﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 224], and so on. So if the Messenger (ﷺ) had brought poetry or uttered it, people would have looked at him with the eye with which the lofty value of his station and the noble nature of his honour are not looked upon. The consideration in this matter is the prevalent and common case. Otherwise, the Prophet (ﷺ) has said: "Indeed, there is wisdom in some poetry," and said: "The truest word ever spoken by a poet is the word of Labīd:

*Certainly, everything except God is vain.*"

So the exempting of the Prophet (ﷺ) from uttering poetry is part of safeguarding the inimitability of the Qur'an and safeguarding the station of prophethood, just like his exemption from knowing writing.

Abū Bakr ibn al-'Arabī said: this verse is not a defect in poetry, just as His saying ﴿You did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾ [al-'Ankabūt: 48] was not a defect in writing. Since illiteracy was not a defect in writing, likewise the negation of composition from the Prophet (ﷺ) is not a defect in poetry.

Because of the usefulness and influence that poetry has in spreading the call of Islam, the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded Ḥassān and 'Abd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa to compose poetry, and he showed his approval of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr when he recited to him the famous ode, "Su'ād has departed."

What is said about the words spoken by the Prophet (ﷺ) that are metrical, such as his saying on the day of Uhud: "I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib," is like what is said about what occurred in the Qur'an of similar things, which we have explained just above.

The clause ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ is a explanatory resumption (*isti'nāf bayānī*), because the negation of poetry from the Qur'an raises a question from an inquirer who says: "What then is this which was revealed to Muḥammad (ﷺ)?" So His saying ﴿It is only a reminder﴾ is the answer to his demand.

The pronoun "huwa" refers to the Qur'an understood from "'allamnāhu," i.e. what was taught to him is only a reminder and a Qur'an. Or it refers to the thing that We taught him, i.e. to the taught thing contained in "'allamnāhu." Or it refers to "dhikr" in His saying "illā dhikr," which is "mubīn." This is one of the places where a pronoun refers to something that comes later in wording and rank, because the explanatory element is like an apposition. Its parallel has occurred in His saying ﴿It is only our life of this world﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 37] in Surat al-Mu'minūn.

The exclusive form that restricts the revelation to the attribute of being a reminder and a Qur'an is a restriction of reversal (*qaṣr qalb*), that is: it is not poetry as you claim. Through this, a thorough refutation of them is achieved, and the emphasis of His saying ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾ is established, and the meaning implied by His saying ﴿and We did not teach him poetry﴾ is confirmed, namely that the Qur'an is poetry.

"Dhikr" is a verbal noun described as the attribute of the Book sent down to Muḥammad (ﷺ), as an intensive description, i.e. it is only one who reminds people of what they have forgotten or did not know. The discussion of "dhikr" has already been covered at His saying ﴿They said: O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are truly mad﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 6] in Surat al-Ḥijr.

"Qur'an" is the verbal noun of *qara'a*, used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e. the recited speech. Its explanation was given at His saying ﴿and you do not recite from it any Qur'an﴾ [Yūnus: 61] in Surat Yūnus.

"Mubīn" is the one that makes the intended meaning clear with eloquence and rhetoric.

His saying "li-tundhira" is connected to His saying "'allamnāhu," in view of what is joined to it of the negation of its being poetry, then the affirmation of its being a reminder and a Qur'an. That is, because the clause ﴿It is only a reminder﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it, having the force of saying: "And We did not teach him anything but a reminder and a clear Qur'an, so that he may warn," or "so that you may warn." **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 36, verses 69–70 (part 3 of 3):**

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read *"litundhira"* with the second-person ta' (*ta' al-khitab*), as an *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person) from the third-person pronoun in His saying *"'allamnahu"* to a second-person pronoun. The rest read it with the third-person ya', meaning the Prophet whom We taught.

*Al-indhar* (warning) is informing someone of a matter from which one must guard oneself.

*Al-hayy* (the living) is used figuratively for one of complete intellect and sound perception. This is an eloquent comparison: whoever is like the living in understanding.

The intended meaning is an indirect reproach of those who turn away from the proofs of the Qur'an: they are like the dead, having no benefit from their minds, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs in retreat﴾ [al-Naml: 80].

The phrase *﴿wa-yahiqqa al-qawlu 'ala al-kafirin﴾* (and the word will be justified against the disbelievers) is coordinated with *"litundhira"* by *'atf al-majaz 'ala al-haqiqah* (coordination of the figurative with the literal). This is because the *lam* that the conjunction *waw* stands in for is not a *lam* of purpose, but *lam al-'aqibah* (the lam of consequence), like the *lam* in His saying ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. Thus there is a *isti'arah tab'iyyah* (a contextual metaphor) in the *waw*, and this is close to the use of a homonym in both of its meanings.

In this consequence there is also *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one term is omitted from each of two parallel clauses, each being implied by the other). The implied sense is: that you may warn whoever is living, so that he increases in life by heeding the Reminder and thereby succeeds; and whoever is dead, who does not benefit from the warning, so that the word is justified against him. This is as He said at the beginning of the surah ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a noble reward﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11], combining for him warning at the outset and good tidings at the end.

*Al-qawl* (the word) is the statement that came with the threat against those who did not benefit from the warning of the Messenger ﷺ.

[Page 67]

By *al-kafirin* (the disbelievers) is meant those who persisted in their disbelief. Otherwise, the warning was addressed to people at first, and all of them were disbelievers.

The mention of warning returns to what the surah opened with, His saying ﴿that you may warn a people whose fathers were never warned﴾ [Ya-Sin: 6]. It is like *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr* (repeating the end of a passage at its beginning). With this, the field of argument against them is complete and their doubts are refuted, and the discourse proceeds to the favour that follows in His saying ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, from what Our hands have made, cattle, of which they are the owners?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71], up to His saying ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 73].

[Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah Yā Sīn, verses 71–73]

﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, from what Our hands have made, livestock, and they are their owners?﴾ ﴿And We have made them subservient to them, so some of them are for their riding, and from some of them they eat.﴾ ﴿And for them in them are benefits and drinks. Will they not then give thanks?﴾

After the refutation of the bases of the polytheists' associationism had ended, the discourse began to turn to the purpose of reminding them of God's blessings upon them, and how they met them with ingratitude, turned away from thanking the Benefactor and worshipping Him, and took gods for their worship, claiming that these would benefit them and ward off harm from them. Included in this reminder is the statement that the livestock are created by the power of God.

So the sentence is conjoined by ʿaṭf al-gharaḍ (conjunction of purpose) to the preceding purpose.

The interrogative (istifhām) expresses denial and wonder at their not seeing the evidences of the blessing. If "seeing" (al-ru'yah) is intellectual, the denial is in accordance with the apparent meaning. If "seeing" is visual, then the denial is contrary to the apparent meaning, by treating their observation of those mentioned things as the equivalent of not seeing, because they do not act in accordance with the knowledge that arises from seeing those observed things and seeing their conditions. On both possibilities, the verbal clause (the clause made into a verbal noun) takes the place of the two objects of the intellectual seeing, or the verbal noun derived from it is the object of visual seeing.

Within this favour there is the inclusion of some indications of God's sole authority over creation, which invalidate their association of others with Him in worship. This is found in His saying "that We have created," and His saying "from what Our hands have made," and His saying "We have made them subservient," and His saying "for them in them are benefits and drinks." For its meaning is: We have deposited for them, in their loins, milk they drink, and in their bodies wool and hair from which they benefit.

His saying "for them" (lahum) is the locus of the favour, that is, for their sake. All the benefits on earth that God created were created for the sake of humankind, by way of honouring them, as was mentioned in His saying: ﴿He it is who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29] in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

The working of hands, which is what is customary in manufacture, is used figuratively (istiʿārah) for bringing into existence the origins of the kinds without any prior source of procreation or the like. This is attributed to the hands of God, the Exalted, because it is evident that those origins were not generated from a cause, as in His saying: ﴿And the heaven We built with hands﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 47]. So "from" (min) in His saying "from what [Our hands] have made" is for the beginning (ibtidāʾiyyah), because the livestock they possess are generated from origins, until they end at their original origins, which God created, just as He created Adam. He expressed that creation as being by the hand of God, as a figurative metaphor (istiʿārah tamthīliyyah) to bring closer the matter of the hidden and wondrous creation, like His saying: ﴿For what I created with My two hands﴾ [Ṣād: 75]. The indication of this metaphor is what has been established, that "there is nothing like unto Him" and that He does not resemble created things, and this is among the definitive articles of belief in Islam.

As for those who held back from interpreting such metaphors, and called them the ambiguous (mutashābih), they only meant that we do not reach the reality of what we express by the essence (al-kunh). As for those who interpreted them by way of metaphor (majāz), they acknowledge that their interpretation is a bringing closer and a making easy for the throats of expression to swallow. As for those who affirmed the attributes of God according to their outward meanings, what moved them was extreme fear (of error), and the early generation (al-salaf) had an excuse in this which does not extend to the people of the eras in which unbelief and atheism spread, for these are far from persuading the questioners; and the pen of lengthy discussion on this is a spindle of no use.

The livestock (al-anʿām) are camels, cattle, sheep and goats. He made it a consequence of their being created for humankind that "they are their owners," that is, capable of using them as they wish, because ownership (al-milk) is the types of disposal. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Ḍabuʿ al-Fazārī, one of the long-lived poets of the Jāhiliyyah, said:

"I have become one who no longer bears arms, nor owns the head of a camel if it bolts."

This is an inclusion of the favour within the course of the reminder.

The fronting of "for them" (lahā) before "owners" (mālikūna), of which it is the complement, is to increase the presence of the livestock in the minds of the listeners before hearing its complement, so that both come in the most possible firm position, by fronting and by arousing suspense. The preservation of the verse-ending (fāṣilah) also necessitated this.

They turned away from saying "they are owners" (fahum mālikūna) to "so they are, for them, owners" (fahum lahā mālikūna), so that indefiniteness could be achieved, which conveys, by magnifying the owners of the livestock, a metonymy (kināyah) for magnifying ownership, that is, through the abundance of benefit. This is what He indicated in detail and in summary by His saying: ﴿And We have made them subservient to them﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and for them in them are benefits and drinks﴾. And the addition (iḍāfah) of the adjective that resembles the verb, although it does not give the annexed noun definiteness, does not strip it of the features of indefiniteness, such as tanwīn.

The nominal sentence is used to convey the permanence and durability of this ownership.

Taḏlīl (making subservient) is making a thing humble (dhalīl). The humble is the opposite of the mighty, and it is the one who does not repel from himself what he dislikes. The meaning of making the livestock subservient is the creation of their submissiveness to humankind within their nature, such that they do not proceed to resist what he wants from them, for they have strengths by which some of them repel others from themselves. So when a person drives them away or commands them, they become submissive to him and obey him, despite their dislike, in what he wants from them: of movement, carrying, milking, taking their offspring, or slaughter.

His saying ﴿so some of them are for their riding, and from some of them they eat﴾ has indicated this.

Rakūb, with a fatḥah on the rāʾ, means the thing ridden, like ḥalūb (the milked one), and it is on the pattern faʿūl in the sense of mafʿūl. Therefore it agrees with the thing it describes; one says "a riding camel" (baʿīr rakūb) and "a milked she-camel" (nāqah ḥalūbah).

"From" (min) is partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), that is: and some of them are other than that, such as for ploughing and fighting, as He said: ﴿And for them in them are benefits and drinks﴾. And al-mashārib is the plural of mashrab, which is a mīmī verbal noun in the sense of drinking, but it is intended as the object, that is: drinks (mashrūbāt).

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases with "from" (min) before where they should be placed later is for the reason mentioned in His saying: ﴿So they are, for them, owners﴾.

The saying ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾ [Yā Sīn: 35] is a consequence of the reminder and favour, as a wondering interrogative, for their abandoning the repetition of thanks for these numerous blessings. Therefore the present tense is used, which indicates renewal and continuity, because those blessings follow one another in succession at every moment. And since they were marvelled at for not repeating thanks, the conveying of wonder at not giving thanks at all is understood by implication; and for this reason He followed it with His saying: ﴿And they took, besides God, gods﴾ [Yā Sīn: 74].

It is also possible to make it a conjunction on the two preceding sentences that were built upon it (al-jumlatayn al-mufarraʿatayn). The purpose of the report that they take gods besides God is to express astonishment at their conduct, which runs contrary to the due response to blessings, and then their opposition to what the proof of Oneness requires, a proof embedded in the mention of the blessings.

The use of the proper name of majesty (ism al-jalāla), God, rather than a pronoun of clear reference, in a place where a pronoun would normally be used, is because of the greatness of divinity that his proper name conveys. It hints that taking gods besides Him is a monstrous audacity, so that this prepares for His saying after it: ﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾ [Yasin: 76], that is, for they have said what is even more outrageous.

As for the pronoun in His saying in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿And they take besides Him gods that create nothing, while they themselves are created﴾ [al-Furqan: 3], it is because the mention of His sole divinity was explicitly stated earlier in His saying: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and who created everything and determined it precisely﴾ [al-Furqan: 2].

As for His saying ﴿hoping they will be helped﴾, the particle laʿalla (perhaps/hopefully) occurs here in an unusual way, because its function is normally to express the speaker's own hope, and that is not fitting here. The commentators have neglected to explain it, and the grammarians and lexicographers have ignored this use of laʿalla. Therefore, one of the following must be the case:

Either laʿalla is a metaphorical allegory (tamthīliyya makniyya), in which the situation of God regarding what He reports about them is likened to the situation of one who hopes, from those he speaks of, that a result of laʿalla should come about for them. The mention of the particle laʿalla is a sign pointing to the accompaniment of the likened element (radīf al-mushabbah bihi). Thus the sentence ﴿hoping they will be helped﴾ is parenthetical (muʿtaraḍa) between "gods" and its attribute, which is the sentence ﴿they cannot help them﴾.

Or the speech is taken to have the sense of interrogation, an interrogation of denial or mockery (istifhām inkārī aw tahakkumī), and the sentence is likewise parenthetical.

Or the hope is considered to refer to the hope of those being spoken of, that is, hoping that those gods will help them, and with an implied verb of saying, meaning: saying, "Perhaps we will be helped." The verb "they will be helped" is then reported in meaning, according to one of the two ways of reporting speech, as in one says: "He said, I will do such-and-such," and "He said, he will do such-and-such." In this case the sentence ﴿they cannot help them﴾ is a resumed statement (istiʾnāf) answering them.

Or you may make laʿalla express causation (lil-taʿlīl), according to the view of al-Kisaʾi, so that the sentence ﴿they cannot help them﴾ is a resumed statement.

The intended meaning is to point out that the disbelievers claim that the idols intercede for them with God in worldly matters, and they say: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18]. In this claim they follow the path of what they are accustomed to in pride through alliance and pacts among the tribes, and in belonging to their leaders. The honour of a tribe is in proportion to the number of its clients (mawālī). So they measured their situation with their Lord by their situation among themselves, and measuring the affairs of divinity by the conditions of humans is among the deepest abysses of error.

The pronoun of the plural of rational beings is applied to the idols in His saying ﴿they cannot help﴾, because they named them with the names of rational beings and ascribed to them perception.

The pronoun in ﴿and they﴾ may refer to the gods, following the pronoun in ﴿they cannot﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿for them﴾ refers to the polytheists. That is: and the idols are a host brought forward for the polytheists. A "jund" (host) is a large number, and a "muḥḍar" is one who is brought in order to be present at a scene. The meaning is: they cannot help, despite their presence at the place of the polytheists, to witness their punishment, and despite being a great number, and they are not able to help those who hold fast to them. It is also possible to reverse it: the polytheists are a host for their idols, brought forward to serve them. This may also be a report about their condition with their idols in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 76–77:

﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾ is a consequence of His words ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah﴾ [Ya-Sin: 74], diverting the Prophet ﷺ from being grieved by their words. That is, he is warned not to grieve over what they say about it, for they have said about Allah what is more grievous.

(And "their speech") is an idafah to a generic noun, so it is general: that is, let not their speech grieve you, regarding their association of partners with Allah, their denial of the Resurrection, their denial of the message, and the harm they inflict upon the Messenger ﷺ and the believers. For this reason the object of the speech is omitted; that is, "their speech which is of such a nature as to grieve you" shall not grieve you.

The prohibition of grief is a prohibition of its cause, which is the preoccupation of the Messenger's mind with their turning away from accepting the true religion. It also entails a command to adopt the means that divert grief from himself, such as consoling himself with the care of Allah the Exalted and His punishment of those who oppose and show enmity to Him.

* * *

﴿Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the prohibition of grief over their speech.

The statement is a metonymy (kinayah) for holding them accountable for what they say; that is, We record their words and what their souls conceal of what they do not openly declare, and We will hold them accountable for all of it, requiting them with a punishment equal to it, and with Your victory over them, and the like. In His words ﴿what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ there is a generalization, which makes the causal explanation also a concluding phrase (tadhyil).

And ﴿inna﴾ (indeed, the particle "inna") takes the place of the causative particle "fa" (so/therefore) in the context where it occurs, for the mere purpose of emphasizing the assertion conveyed by the sentence. It is not a fresh, independent sentence, but is connected to what precedes it.

[Page 73]

Nafi' read ﴿yahzunka﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the zāy, from aḥzana (to cause grief), meaning he caused him to experience grief. The rest of the readers read it with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the zāy, from ḥazana, and both have the same meaning.

He placed concealing first to give it importance, because it is a stronger indication of the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge of their circumstances. He mentioned revealing after it because it is the locus of the report, and to indicate that Allah the Exalted's knowledge encompasses both the particulars and the universals of affairs.

Stopping at His words ﴿And let not their speech grieve you﴾ [Yunus: 65], with a new start at His words (﴿Indeed, We know﴾), is better than continuing, because it is clearer in meaning. It is not obligatory, since no hearer would imagine that they say, "Indeed Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal." And if they had said it, it would not have been something that grieves the Prophet ﷺ, so how could he be forbidden from grieving over it?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verses 78–79:

﴿Has not man considered that We created him from a drop of semen, and yet he is an open adversary?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 77] ﴿And he presents to Us an example and forgets his own creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ ﴿Say, "He will give them life who created them the first time, and He is Knowing of all creation."﴾ When the doubts of the polytheists were refuted, both their association of others with the worship of God and their deeming His power to resurrect impossible, and their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) in what he reported of that, a complete refutation, the discourse turned to the disparagement of partial statements made by the leaders of those who denied the resurrection, rebuking them for their impudence and for their disbelief in the blessing of their Lord. They were men of Mecca. I reckon that they used to embellish proofs and adorn disputation for people, and came to them with persuasive statements conforming to the understanding of the common folk. It is said that "the man" (al-insan) refers to Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It is also said that it refers to al-'As ibn Wa'il, and it is said Abu Jahl, and there are narrations with chains of transmission about this. Probably this occurred several times, each of these men being responsible for some of it.

They said in the narrations: "One of these three came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) holding a decayed human bone. He crumbled it and scattered it in the wind, and said: 'O Muhammad, do you claim that God will give life to this after it has decayed (i.e., become worn away)?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Yes. God will cause you to die, then give you life, then cause you to enter Hell.'"

Page 74

The definite article in "al-insan" is the definite article of prior reference (ta'rif al-ahd), referring to a specific, known man who made this statement on that day. It has already been mentioned in Surah Maryam that His saying, ﴿And man says, "When I die, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66] was revealed concerning one of these men, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira was mentioned together with them. A parallel to this verse is His saying, ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3] in Surah al-Qiyamah.

The reason for interpreting the definite article here as the definite article of prior reference is that it cannot be understood otherwise: if it were for the genus, it would imply that the whole human race denies resurrection, when among them are believers and adherents of the religions. Interpreting it as comprehensive (al-istighraq) is further removed, unless it is meant as customary comprehensiveness (al-istighraq al-'urfi), and such a context is not among its appropriate uses. As for His saying in Surah al-Nahl, ﴿He created man from a drop, and yet he is an open adversary﴾ [al-Nahl: 4], it is the definite article of comprehensiveness, meaning every human being was created, since the context is one of true comprehensiveness.

What is meant by "khasim" (adversary) in that verse is: he is fierce in obstinacy after having originally been a drop. The sentence is thus conjoined to the sentence ﴿Have they not seen that We created for them…﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71], and so on.

The interrogative is like the interrogative in the sentence conjoined to it.

The seeing here is of the heart (qalbiyyah). The clause "﴿that We created him﴾" [Ya-Sin: 77] takes the place of the two objects, as was mentioned in His saying, ﴿Have they not seen that We created for them, of what Our hands have made, livestock?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71].

"Idha" here is for surprise (lil-mufajaah). The point of the surprise is that this man was created to worship God and to know what befits Him; when he does not act accordingly, it is as though he has sprung upon one with what was not expected from him, together with conveying that the dispute over matters of divinity was what he rushed into as soon as he came to reason.

"Khasim" is an intensive form (fa'il) in the sense of mufa'il, meaning one who disputes intensely.

"Mubin" is from abana, in the sense of bana, meaning: evident in that.

Striking an example (darb al-mathal) means producing it, as one says: "He struck a tent" and "he struck a dinar." Its explanation has already been given at His saying, ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to strike an example, of anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The "mathal" is the depiction of a state. The meaning is: he displayed to people and brought them a comparison between the state of Our power and the state of human incapacity, since Our giving life to bones after they had decayed was deemed impossible by him. It is like His saying,

Page 75

﴿So do not strike for God examples﴾ [al-Nahl: 74], that is, do not liken Him to His creation, so that you make partners for Him, since it occurs after ﴿and they worship besides God what does not possess for them any provision from the heavens and the earth, anything﴾ [al-Nahl: 73].

The interrogative in His saying "Who will give life to bones" is denunciatory (inkari). "Man" (man) is general for everyone to whom the predicate is attributed. The meaning is: no one gives life to bones while they are decayed. Its generality included their denial that God Most High could give life to bones while they were decayed, that is, in the state of being decayed.

The clause ﴿He said, "Who will give life to bones"﴾ explains the clause "He struck for Us an example," like His saying, ﴿So Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120], where the clause "He said, O Adam" explains the clause "whispered."

The forgetting in His saying "and forgets his creation" is a metaphor for the absence of knowledge from its root, that is, for not being guided to the manner of the first creation: he forgot that We created him from a drop, meaning he did not realize that this is more marvelous than the restoration of his bone, like His saying, ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation? Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15].

The mention of the drop here prepares for the surprise of his being a fierce adversary immediately after being created, meaning: that one of humble origin has become a stubborn adversary; and so that His saying afterward, "and forgets his creation," may be built upon it, meaning he forgot his weak creation, so he became arrogant and overstepped. Also, because his creation from a drop is more marvelous than giving him life when he is a bone, this is a concession to his claim as to what is within the bounds of possibility, though God gives life to what is weaker than bones: He gives life to the human being from his ashes, from his dust, from the "coccyx" bone, and from one of whom nothing remains.

"Rameem" means decayed; one says: "the bone decayed and became decayed (arramma)" when it wears away. It is of the form fa'il in the sense of the verbal noun; one says, "the bone decayed (ramma) rameeman," so it is a predicate by means of the verbal noun, and for that reason it did not agree in number with the subject, which is plural (bila).

The command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to say to him, ﴿He will give them life who created them﴾, is a command to answer in the manner of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), by turning the questioner's interrogative toward something other than its intended meaning, because when he said, ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾, he was not seeking to specify the one who gives life, but intended impossibility; so he was answered as one who seeks knowledge. It was said to him, ﴿He will give them life who created them the first time﴾.

Page 76

Therefore the answer was built on the verb of giving life, with the agent attributed to the one who gives life, and the answer is suitable to be a refutation of the negation intended by the denying interrogative, as if it were said: "Rather, He will give them life who created them the first time." The answer was not built on demonstrating the possibility of giving life; rather, the demonstration of possibility was placed in making the predicate-subject a relative clause, so that the relative clause indicates the possibility, and both aims are achieved. Thus the relative pronoun here is a hint toward the reason for the predicate's construction, which is "He will give them life," meaning: He will give them life because He created them the first time, so He is capable of creating them a second time. He, Most High, said, ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62], and He said, ﴿And it is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27].

This argument is concluded with the clause ﴿And He is Knowing of all creation﴾, meaning: He is of vast knowledge, encompassing all the means of creation that we do not know: like creation from a drop, creation from an atom, and creation from closed-off plant parts such as the weevil of the broad bean and the weevil of wood. These are more marvelous than the formation of a human from his bones.

In linking giving life to bones there is an indication that the bones of a living being are inhabited by life just as its flesh and blood are, and are not like reeds and wood. This is the view of Malik and Abu Hanifa, and for this reason the bones of an animal that died without slaughter are considered impure. Al-Shafi'i is reported to have held that bone is not inhabited by life, so it does not become impure by death. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The adherents of the schools have been inconsistent on this, and what we have mentioned is the correct view," meaning that some attributed to al-Shafi'i agreement with the view of Malik, and this is the view of Ahmad, so it becomes a consensus. Physicians affirm life and sensation in bones. Ibn Zuhr the Andalusian physician said in the book al-Taysir: "Galen's statements about bones were inconsistent as to whether they have sensation, and what appears to me is that they have slow sensation."
