Interpreting it as comprehensive (al-istighraq) is further removed, unless it is meant as customary comprehensiveness (al-istighraq al-'urfi), and such a context is not among its appropriate uses. As for His saying in Surah al-Nahl, ﴿He created man from a drop, and yet he is an open adversary﴾ [al-Nahl: 4], it is the definite article of comprehensiveness, meaning every human being was created, since the context is one of true comprehensiveness.

What is meant by "khasim" (adversary) in that verse is: he is fierce in obstinacy after having originally been a drop. The sentence is thus conjoined to the sentence ﴿Have they not seen that We created for them…﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71], and so on.

The interrogative is like the interrogative in the sentence conjoined to it.

The seeing here is of the heart (qalbiyyah). The clause "﴿that We created him﴾" [Ya-Sin: 77] takes the place of the two objects, as was mentioned in His saying, ﴿Have they not seen that We created for them, of what Our hands have made, livestock?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71].

"Idha" here is for surprise (lil-mufajaah). The point of the surprise is that this man was created to worship God and to know what befits Him; when he does not act accordingly, it is as though he has sprung upon one with what was not expected from him, together with conveying that the dispute over matters of divinity was what he rushed into as soon as he came to reason.

"Khasim" is an intensive form (fa'il) in the sense of mufa'il, meaning one who disputes intensely.

"Mubin" is from abana, in the sense of bana, meaning: evident in that.

Striking an example (darb al-mathal) means producing it, as one says: "He struck a tent" and "he struck a dinar." Its explanation has already been given at His saying, ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to strike an example, of anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The "mathal" is the depiction of a state. The meaning is: he displayed to people and brought them a comparison between the state of Our power and the state of human incapacity, since Our giving life to bones after they had decayed was deemed impossible by him. It is like His saying,

Page 75

﴿So do not strike for God examples﴾ [al-Nahl: 74], that is, do not liken Him to His creation, so that you make partners for Him, since it occurs after ﴿and they worship besides God what does not possess for them any provision from the heavens and the earth, anything﴾ [al-Nahl: 73].

The interrogative in His saying "Who will give life to bones" is denunciatory (inkari). "Man" (man) is general for everyone to whom the predicate is attributed. The meaning is: no one gives life to bones while they are decayed. Its generality included their denial that God Most High could give life to bones while they were decayed, that is, in the state of being decayed.

The clause ﴿He said, "Who will give life to bones"﴾ explains the clause "He struck for Us an example," like His saying, ﴿So Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120], where the clause "He said, O Adam" explains the clause "whispered."

The forgetting in His saying "and forgets his creation" is a metaphor for the absence of knowledge from its root, that is, for not being guided to the manner of the first creation: he forgot that We created him from a drop, meaning he did not realize that this is more marvelous than the restoration of his bone, like His saying, ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation? Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15].

The mention of the drop here prepares for the surprise of his being a fierce adversary immediately after being created, meaning: that one of humble origin has become a stubborn adversary; and so that His saying afterward, "and forgets his creation," may be built upon it, meaning he forgot his weak creation, so he became arrogant and overstepped. Also, because his creation from a drop is more marvelous than giving him life when he is a bone, this is a concession to his claim as to what is within the bounds of possibility, though God gives life to what is weaker than bones: He gives life to the human being from his ashes, from his dust, from the "coccyx" bone, and from one of whom nothing remains.

"Rameem" means decayed; one says: "the bone decayed and became decayed (arramma)" when it wears away. It is of the form fa'il in the sense of the verbal noun; one says, "the bone decayed (ramma) rameeman," so it is a predicate by means of the verbal noun, and for that reason it did not agree in number with the subject, which is plural (bila).

The command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to say to him, ﴿He will give them life who created them﴾, is a command to answer in the manner of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), by turning the questioner's interrogative toward something other than its intended meaning, because when he said, ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾, he was not seeking to specify the one who gives life, but intended impossibility; so he was answered as one who seeks knowledge. It was said to him, ﴿He will give them life who created them the first time﴾.

Page 76

Therefore the answer was built on the verb of giving life, with the agent attributed to the one who gives life, and the answer is suitable to be a refutation of the negation intended by the denying interrogative, as if it were said: "Rather, He will give them life who created them the first time." The answer was not built on demonstrating the possibility of giving life; rather, the demonstration of possibility was placed in making the predicate-subject a relative clause, so that the relative clause indicates the possibility, and both aims are achieved. Thus the relative pronoun here is a hint toward the reason for the predicate's construction, which is "He will give them life," meaning: He will give them life because He created them the first time, so He is capable of creating them a second time. He, Most High, said, ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62], and He said, ﴿And it is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27].

This argument is concluded with the clause ﴿And He is Knowing of all creation﴾, meaning: He is of vast knowledge, encompassing all the means of creation that we do not know: like creation from a drop, creation from an atom, and creation from closed-off plant parts such as the weevil of the broad bean and the weevil of wood. These are more marvelous than the formation of a human from his bones.

In linking giving life to bones there is an indication that the bones of a living being are inhabited by life just as its flesh and blood are, and are not like reeds and wood. This is the view of Malik and Abu Hanifa, and for this reason the bones of an animal that died without slaughter are considered impure. Al-Shafi'i is reported to have held that bone is not inhabited by life, so it does not become impure by death. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The adherents of the schools have been inconsistent on this, and what we have mentioned is the correct view," meaning that some attributed to al-Shafi'i agreement with the view of Malik, and this is the view of Ahmad, so it becomes a consensus. Physicians affirm life and sensation in bones. Ibn Zuhr the Andalusian physician said in the book al-Taysir: "Galen's statements about bones were inconsistent as to whether they have sensation, and what appears to me is that they have slow sensation."

[Page 77]

﴿The One who made for you fire from the green tree, and then you kindle from it.﴾ This is a *badal* (apposition, substitution) of ﴿He who created it﴾ [Yasin: 79], a *badal mutabiq* (an apposition that matches its referent exactly). The relative clause was not joined to the previous relative clause by conjunction, which would have spared repeating the relative pronoun, because repeating the relative pronoun emphasizes the first and draws attention to the second, so that the listener's soul becomes alert to receive what follows and grasps the strangeness of this creation, which is the bringing into being of an opposite from its opposite: fire, the extreme of heat, from its opposite, moisture. This is the reason for describing the tree as *al-akhdar* (green). The intended meaning of "green" is not the color but its necessary concomitant, which is moisture, since a tree remains green as long as it is alive. When it dries out and life leaves it, its color changes to dusty grey, so greenness becomes a *kinayah* (metonymy) for the moisture and life of the plant. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"And when she grazed on the *rumm* [a plant], she left neither dry stalks of what they gather, nor green ones."

The description of the tree, which is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) of *shajarah*, is feminine in meaning, yet it is described by *al-akhdar* without the feminine marker, in consideration of the wording of the described noun, which lacks a feminine sign. This is the dialect of the people of Najd. The people of the Hijaz, however, say *shajarun khadra'* in consideration of the meaning of plurality. The Qur'an has come with both in His saying: ﴿Indeed they will eat from it and fill their bellies from it﴾ [al-Saffat: 66], ﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water﴾ [al-Saffat: 67].

The tree intended here is the *al-markh* (a tree whose name is pronounced with a fatha on the *mim* and a sukun on the *ra'*) and the *al-'affar* (a tree whose name is pronounced with a fatha on the unpointed *'ayn* and a fatha on the *fa'*). These are two trees from whose branches fire is struck: a branch of one is taken together with a branch of the other, about the size of a *miswak* (tooth-stick), and both are green, dripping water. The *markh* is rubbed against the *'affar* and fire is struck. It has been said that the *'affar* is placed on top and the *markh* below, and it has been said the reverse, because al-Jawhari and Ibn Sidah in *al-Mukhassas* said: the *'affar* is the *zand* (fire-drill), which is the male, and the *markh* is the female, which is the *zandah*. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: the *markh* is the male and the *'affar* is the female, and the fire is the *siqt al-zand* (the spark of the fire-drill), which is what comes out when striking, blazing; something combustible, such as straw or cloth with oil on it, is placed beneath it, and the fire is caught in it.

The surprise conveyed by ﴿then you kindle from it﴾ indicates the wondrous inspiration of God to mankind to use striking with the green tree and their being guided to its special property.

*Al-iqad* (kindling) is lighting the fire; it is said *awqada* and *waqada*, with the same meaning.

The predicate is expressed as a present tense verb to convey the recurrence and continuity of this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 81:

Page 78

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them? Yes indeed, and He is the Supreme Creator, the All-Knowing.﴾ This assertion is connected to the previous arguments addressed to man, the one meant in His words, ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a drop of semen?﴾ [Ya Sin: 77]. This is because, once it became clear that reasoning from the creation of things proves the possibility of creating their like, the verse advances to reasoning from the creation of great created things to the possibility of creating what is less than them.

This argument is presented in the form of an interrogative of affirmation (taqrir), because its clarity leaves the one being questioned no choice but to affirm it. Intuition dictates that whoever created the heavens and the earth is more capable of creating people after death.

The affirmation was directed toward the negation of what is affirmed, in order to give latitude to the one being affirmed, if he intends denial while being certain that denial is not open to him. Thus his affirmation, after the question is directed at him, is a negation of the intended meaning, evidence that he cannot do other than affirm. Examples of this interrogative of affirmation are numerous.

The majority of readers recited (﴿bi-qadirin﴾) with the single bi' and an alif after the qaf, and the noun is in the genitive by the added bi' in negation for emphasis. Ruways, from Ya'qub, read it with a yā' at the beginning in the imperfect form "yaqdiru."

Because this is so, after the affirmation an answer is given to what was affirmed, with the word "bala" (Yes indeed), which serves to refute the negation, meaning: yes indeed, He is capable of creating their like.

The pronoun in "mithlahum" (their like) refers to man in His words ﴿Does man not see﴾ [Ya Sin: 77], taking it as referring to people in general, whether the intended "man" in His words ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a drop of semen﴾ [Ya Sin: 77] was a specific individual or not. The intended meaning is him and those like him who follow his belief, namely the polytheists of Makkah. That is: He is capable of creating their like, meaning bodies in their forms and likenesses, because the bodies created for resurrection are the likes of the people who existed in this world, composed of their parts. The re-creation does not necessarily require gathering scattered bodies, but may be from non-existence, and perhaps this involves various modes. The dead whose bodies remain have life breathed into them, and the dead whose limbs have scattered and decayed are re-fashioned, and bodies from which nothing remains are re-made as bodies in their forms, so that their souls may be deposited in them. Do you not see that the human body changes from its state at birth, grows, and its features alter, and it is renewed every day with blood and flesh in proportion to what has dissolved and evaporated? That change is not considered a substitution of its essence, for he perceives that he is himself, and people distinguish him from others by the non-change of the soul. The Qur'an contains indications of these states of the Return, and for this reason the scholars of the Sunnah differed on whether resurrection is from non-existence or from dispersal, as Sayf al-Din al-Amidi indicated in Abkar al-Afkar, and their souls, which used to govern their bodies, are deposited in them, for souls remain after the bodies perish.

The clause ﴿and He is the Supreme Creator, the All-Knowing﴾ is parenthetical at the end of the statement, and the waw is parenthetical, meaning: He creates many kinds of creatures, and He has broad knowledge of their states and the subtleties of their arrangement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 36, verse 82:

﴿Indeed, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ This is the summation of the argument (fadhlakat al-istidlal) and the decisive statement (fasl al-maqal). For this reason it is separated from what precedes it, just as the conclusion clause (jumlat al-natijah) is separated from the two premises of a syllogism (qiyas). What follows from what has preceded is that when He, exalted is He, intends a thing, His power becomes attached to bringing it into existence by the creative command (al-amr al-takwini), which is expressed by its approximation as "Be" (kun), and this is the most concise word expressing command to existence (al-kawn), that is, the attribution of being (al-ittisaf bil-wujud).

The word "command" (al-amr) in His saying ﴿Indeed, His command﴾ carries the meaning of "affair" (al-sha'n), because this suits their denial of His power to revive the decayed bones. That is, there is no affair for God at the time of His intending the bringing into being of any existent, except His determining that He brings it into existence. He expressed that determination, to which the thing created submits, by the word "Be," so as to make known that He does not practise His making with a hand, nor with an instrument, nor by kneading the material from which He creates, as craftsmen and engineers do. This is because the polytheists had come to imagine the impossibility of resurrection from the non-existence of materials, let alone preparing and shaping them. Thus the restriction (al-qasr) is relative (idafi), to reverse their belief that He needs to gather material, shape it, and let a period of time pass to complete it.

"Idha" (when) is a temporal adverb (zarf zaman) in a position of accusative as an adverbial object (al-maf'ul fihi), that is, at the time of His intending a thing.

Page 80
The majority (al-jumhur) read ﴿fa-yakunu﴾ in the nominative, on the estimate: "that He says to it, 'Be,' so it is." Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it in the accusative, as a conjunction (ataf) upon the accusative "yaqula."

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 36, verse 83:**

﴿So glory be to the One in whose hand is the dominion (malakūt) of all things, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ The *fa'* here is the *fa' faṣīḥa* (the "eloquent" *fa'*, which indicates an implied condition). The meaning is: when all the proofs you have heard of God's great power, His unique divinity, and that He will restore you after death have become clear, then His transcendence above their statements about Him, which would diminish His greatness, is affirmed, because in His hand is the complete dominion over every existing thing.

*Malakūt* is an intensive form (*mubālagha*) of *mulk* (with a kasra on the *mīm*). The pattern *faʿalūt* occurs rarely in the Arabic language. Examples of it include *rahbūt* and *raḥamūt*. Among their proverbial sayings is: *rahbūt khayrun min raḥamūt*, meaning: to be feared by people is better than to be shown mercy by them. That is, being powerful, whose might is feared, is better than being gentle, whom people pity. It was previously discussed at His words, ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the malakūt of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Anʿām: 75], in Surah al-Anʿām.

The clause ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ is coordinated with the clause of glorification (*tasbīḥ*), as a declarative sentence coordinated with an imperative one, so it falls under what the *fa' faṣīḥa* encompasses. The meaning is: it has become clear that you are going to Him, not escaping the grip of His dominion, and this is through the restoration of your creation after death.

The placing of *ilayhi* (to Him) before *turjaʿūn* (you will be returned) is for emphasis and to preserve the rhyme (*fāṣila*), because they did not claim that there was a return to other than Him. Rather, they denied the Resurrection (*maʿād*) altogether.

[Page 81]

**In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful**
**Surah al-Ṣāffāt**

Its well-known and agreed-upon name is "al-Ṣāffāt." It is by this name that it is referred to in the books of tafsir, the books of Sunnah, and in all the copies of the Qur'an. Nothing has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning its naming. In *al-Itqān* (by al-Suyūṭī), it says: "I have seen in the words of al-Jaʿbarī that Surah al-Ṣāffāt is called 'the Surah of the Sacrificed One' (*sūrat al-dhabīḥ*), and this requires a textual basis."

The reason it is named "al-Ṣāffāt" is the occurrence of this word in it with the meaning intended as a description of the angels. Although this word occurs in Surah al-Mulk, it is there with a different meaning, since what is intended there is a description of birds. Moreover, the more well-known view is that Surah al-Mulk was revealed after Surah al-Ṣāffāt.

It is Meccan by consensus. It is the fifty-sixth in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surah al-Anʿām and before Surah Luqmān.

Its verses are counted as one hundred and eighty-two by the majority of those who count verses. The Basrans counted them as one hundred and eighty-one.

* * *

Its purposes are: affirming God's oneness, and presenting many proofs for this which show that He alone created the great creations that no other can create, namely the heavenly worlds with their parts and inhabitants, and no one on earth has any means to dispute this.

Also: affirming that resurrection is followed by gathering (*ḥashr*) and recompense.

[Page 82]

Also: describing the condition of the polytheists on the Day of Recompense and some of them falling upon others.

Also: describing the good condition and bliss of the believers.

Also: recounting what used to take place between them and some of the polytheists who were their companions in the pre-Islamic period (*jāhiliyya*), and their attempts to turn them away from Islam.

Then it moves on to drawing a parallel between the call of Muḥammad (ﷺ) to his people and the call of the messengers before him, and how God helped His messengers, raised their status, and blessed them.

Woven into this are some of their virtues, excellences, and their strength in the religion of God, and how God saved them from the calamities that surrounded them. Especially the excellence of the Sacrificed One (*al-dhabīḥ*), with an indication that he was Ismāʿīl.

Also: describing what befell the nations who denied their messengers.

Then the refutation of the polytheists for the corruption of their beliefs about God, their attributing partners to Him, their saying "the angels are God's daughters," the angels' rejection of them before the assembled witnesses, and their statements about the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Qur'an, and how they used to wish that they had a book.

Then God promised His messenger victory, as was His custom with the messengers and with the earlier believers, and that God's punishment would descend upon the polytheists, and the good outcome would belong to the believers.

Its opening was appropriate to its purposes, in that swearing by the angels is suitable for establishing God's oneness, because the idols were not claimed to have angels, and whoever the angels serve is the true God. Also, because the angels are among the created beings, whose creation indicates the greatness of the Creator, and the oath indicates that they are the most noble of the higher created beings.

Furthermore, the attributes considered in the oath by them are suitable for the purposes mentioned after it. *Al-Ṣāffāt* (those who line up) is suitable to the greatness of their Lord. *Al-Zājirāt* (those who drive) is suitable to the casting out of the devils from the heavens, and suitable to the guiding of the stars and their preservation from one overtaking another. It is also suitable to their driving people in the place of gathering.

[Page 83]

And *al-tālīyāt dhikran* (those who recite the remembrance) is suitable to the conditions of the Messenger and the messengers (peace be upon them) and what they were sent with to their peoples.

This is it. In opening with an oath there is an arousing of curiosity about what is sworn to, so that the listener attends to it with his whole being.

Thus the opening of the surah has been completed in the finest and most perfect modes of eloquent expression.
